title: The watcher test fails intermittently on Windows
description:
﻿`test/studio/watch.test.ts` fails intermittently, and it has now been seen twice.

Two agents on unrelated branches reported it independently, and the orchestrator
saw a third unidentified single failure earlier the same day:

- dbmd-25''s agent: *"one unrelated flake seen once: `test/studio/watch.test.ts >
  says so on the status`, green on every run since."*
- dbmd-71''s agent: *"`test/studio/watch.test.ts` failed once on the first run and
  passed on two re-runs — a filesystem-watch timing test on Windows."*

Twice is this project''s threshold for fixing a thing rather than absorbing it.
**An intermittently red gate is corrosive in a way a slow one is not**: people
learn to re-run rather than to read, and then a real failure gets re-run too.

The orchestrator could not reproduce it: six consecutive runs of that file alone,
all green, plus repeated full-suite runs.

## Where to look

`src/studio/watch.ts` and `test/studio/watch.test.ts`. This is a **different**
test from the one dbmd-36 fixed; that was a directory listing catching the
writer''s temp file, and it is closed.

`fs.watch` on Windows is the obvious suspect and the item should confirm rather
than assume it. Things that are true and worth checking against:

- **`fs.watch` is allowed to be late.** ADR 0019 says so explicitly and builds
  the safety property at the write rather than in the watcher for that reason. A
  test that waits a fixed number of milliseconds for an event is asserting
  something the design deliberately does not promise.
- **An editor saving by rename produces more than one event**, and the watcher
  debounces. A test that counts events, or that asserts on the state after one
  debounce window, races the debounce.
- The status the failing case is about, `says so on the status`, is served by a
  poll rather than pushed, so there are two timers in play rather than one.

## What done looks like

- **Reproduce it deliberately** rather than by waiting for luck. Force the
  ordering, mock the clock, or drive the watcher directly. dbmd-36''s agent mocked
  `rename` to park the writer mid-write and that is the standard to match.
- Fix the test, not the watcher, **unless the watcher is genuinely wrong**. If the
  test is asserting a promise `fs.watch` does not make, the test is wrong. If the
  watcher misses a real change, that is much more serious and it is data loss.
  Say which you found.
- **Do not add a sleep or a retry.** dbmd-36''s brief said the same and the reason
  holds: sleeping hides a real race, slows the suite, and makes the next race
  harder to see.
- Check the other timing-sensitive assertions in that file for the same shape,
  whether or not they have been unlucky yet.

## Watch out for

- dbmd-48 is rewriting how the client learns about the model and touches
  `src/studio/`. Coordinate or wait; do not both edit the watcher.
- CI runs Linux and development is Windows. If the flake is Windows-only, say so,
  because it means CI will never catch a regression in whatever you fix.
close_reason: PR #44 merged: the racing settle helper was the cause, replaced by POST /api/flush. No product defect; the diff is tests only.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
﻿## Third sighting, and it is not Windows-only

The dbmd-51 agent hit it on **CI's Linux runner**, on a documentation-only
branch, and a re-run of the same job passed unchanged:

> First `check` run failed on `test/studio/watch.test.ts:238` ("says so on the
> status") expecting no conflicts and getting one for `tables/orders.md`.

That is the **same test and the same case** the dbmd-25 agent named, and this
item''s original scope said to say whether it is Windows-only because CI would
then never catch a regression. **It is not Windows-only.** Both platforms, three
sightings, two of them on the identical test name.

## What the failure actually says, which narrows it

The assertion expects **no conflicts** and gets one for `tables/orders.md`. So the
test is not merely late; something produced a real conflict where the scenario
expected none. Given ADR 0019''s design, a conflict means a write was refused
because the file changed on disk after the studio read it.

Two candidates, and the item should distinguish them rather than assume:

- The **test** creates the conflict itself, by writing a fixture file at a moment
  the running studio can see, and usually finishes first.
- The **watcher** reports a change that is really the writer''s own save, which
  would be a product defect and a much more serious one, because a studio that
  conflicts with itself refuses a user''s work for no reason.

dbmd-19/23 has since landed and moved `isFileName` into `src/model/paths.ts`, and
dbmd-48 has landed and changed what a revision counts. Neither is likely to be
the cause, but both touch this area, so **reproduce against current `main`**
rather than against a remembered failure.

## Note on the environment

This is now the third distinct agent to report it and none has reproduced it
deliberately. It fails perhaps one run in ten. Do not conclude it is fixed
because a suite went green; that is what it does.

title: A stale page still overwrites a hand edit, and ADR 0019 says otherwise
description:
﻿The data loss dbmd-33 closed is still open, from the other side.

Found by a hunting pass and **reproduced by the orchestrator on `main`**. ADR
0019 opens with this exact two-step scenario and says it is fixed. It is not.
That makes it a stated invariant that is untrue, which this project treats as
worse than an absent one, so correcting the record is part of this item.

## The reproduction, on merged code

    page holds : id, email, display_name, created_at
    server sees: id, hand_added, email, display_name, created_at
    PATCH status 200
    disk now   : id, email, display_name, created_at
    conflicts  : []

1. The page loads and holds a model.
2. A person adds a column in their editor. **No studio write is pending.**
3. The stale page changes a column type, which sends the whole `columns` array
   it still holds.

The hand-added column is gone. The write succeeded. Nothing was reported.

## Why the existing guard does not catch it, and why review missed it

`absorb()` in `src/studio/edits.ts` freezes the baseline **only for files with a
pending edit**. With nothing pending it adopts the fresh read, so by the time the
`PATCH` arrives the server''s baseline already matches disk and the write is
correctly allowed. The server is not wrong. **The stale party is the browser**,
and it holds no baseline at all: `src/studio/client/main.ts` polls only after its
own write, with a comment saying that noticing a change on disk is dbmd-33''s job.

`WireStatus.revision` is documented in `src/studio/wire.ts` as "the client''s cue
to re-fetch and redraw" and **nothing in `src/studio/client/` reads it**.

The orchestrator''s review of dbmd-33 verified the guard with a **`layout`** patch,
which carries no column list, so nothing could be lost. The destructive case
needs a `columns` patch from a stale client. A narrow verification passed and a
wider one would not have.

## What has to be true when this is done

- **The client cannot silently overwrite a model it has not seen.** Either it
  reads `revision` and refuses or reloads, or `PATCH` carries a token the server
  checks, or both. `PATCH /api/table/:name` currently carries nothing and
  replaces `columns` wholesale.
- **`git checkout` must survive**, because ADR 0004, the status line and the
  inspector''s rename copy all name it as the undo. The hunting pass showed a
  checkout being reverted by the next inspector edit.
- **A refusal has to be visible.** `conflicts` is served on every status response
  and rendered nowhere; `showStatus` handles `writeError`, `pendingWrite` and
  `lastWrite` only. Today the studio never mentions a conflict in either
  direction. That was filed as a known follow-up and it is not separable from
  this: a guard nobody can see is half a guard.
- **ADR 0019 has to be corrected**, by amendment rather than edit, per the
  convention this repository has settled on. Its framing that "the data-loss half
  is server-side and complete, the visible half is a follow-up" is the thing that
  was wrong. The client''s staleness check is part of the data-loss guard, not
  part of the presentation.
- `dbmd studio --help` promises more than holds: "editing a file in your editor
  is the same feature seen from the other side ... rather than writing over your
  work."

## Watch out for

- The existing write-time refusal is **correct and necessary** and must stay. It
  catches the case it was built for; the orchestrator re-verified that a hand
  edit landing inside the debounce is still refused with the edit intact. This
  item adds the missing half rather than replacing anything.
- Do not fix it by making the client poll aggressively. The debounce and the
  `only` write set exist so the studio touches as little as possible, and a page
  that re-fetches constantly will fight both.
- Do not adopt the hand edit into the page silently while the user is typing in
  the inspector. Losing a half-typed field is a smaller loss than a column, and
  still a loss.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave nine, 2026-09-07

Branch: `studio/48-the-page-is-not-the-truth`. **ADR number 0025 is yours**, and
this one needs a record: you are deciding how a page relates to a model it does
not own. Do not take a different number; 0023 and 0024 are handed out.

### dbmd-48 and dbmd-39 are batched, because they are one seam

Both are the client acting on a model it has not checked. Fixing one without the
other means doing the same thinking twice and shipping half a guarantee.

**dbmd-48, the data loss.** Reproduced by the orchestrator on `main`:

```
page holds : id, email, display_name, created_at
server sees: id, hand_added, email, display_name, created_at
PATCH status 200
disk now   : id, email, display_name, created_at
conflicts  : []
```

A person adds a column in their editor with no studio write pending. The watcher
notices, the server re-reads, and correctly adopts it. Then the stale page
changes a type, sending the whole `columns` array it still holds. The column is
gone, the write succeeded, nothing was reported.

**dbmd-39, the half-applied rename.** A rename is several requests. When one of
the files it must edit has changed on disk, that file is correctly refused and
**the rest of the rename still happens**, leaving a model pointing at a table
that no longer exists, with no diagnostic, because a dangling ref is the
validator's business rather than the reader's.

The shared cause: **a `PATCH` is answered `200` when the edit is accepted, and
the refusal only comes into existence later, at the debounced flush.** The client
cannot abort on something that has not happened yet.

### What is already there and correct

- **The server's write-time refusal works and must stay.** A hand edit landing
  inside the debounce is refused with the edit intact; the orchestrator verified
  that separately. This item adds the missing half rather than replacing it.
- `WireStatus.revision` is documented in `src/studio/wire.ts` as "the client's
  cue to re-fetch and redraw" and **nothing in `src/studio/client/` reads it**.
  The write-side `revision` in `write.ts` is an unrelated private counter.
- `conflicts` is on every status response and **rendered nowhere**. `showStatus`
  in `main.ts` handles `writeError`, `pendingWrite` and `lastWrite` only.
- `Canvas.show` replaces everything and is re-callable. `main.ts` deliberately
  does not adopt the model from its status poll, with a comment saying that is
  this item's job.
- The dbmd-38 agent noted that `create` and `remove` both go through the same
  reload path, so they should inherit whatever you build rather than need their
  own fix. Check that.

### The decision, which is the ADR

The item names two routes and you may find a third: the client reads `revision`
and refuses or reloads, or `PATCH` carries a token the server checks, or both.

Whichever you choose, three things have to be true:

- **A page cannot silently overwrite a model it has not seen.**
- **A refusal is visible.** A guard nobody can see is half a guard, and today the
  studio never mentions a conflict in either direction.
- **`git checkout` survives.** ADR 0004, the status line and the rename
  confirmation all name it as the undo, and a hunting pass watched it be
  reverted by the next inspector edit.

### Watch out for

- **Do not fix it by polling hard.** The debounce and the `only` write set exist
  so the studio touches as little as possible, and a page that re-fetches
  constantly fights both.
- **Do not adopt a change into the page while somebody is typing in the
  inspector.** Losing a half-typed field is a smaller loss than a column and
  still a loss. Say what you do about that case.
- **ADR 0019 has to be amended, not edited.** Its framing that "the data-loss
  half is server-side and complete, the visible half is a follow-up" is the
  thing that was wrong: the client's staleness check is part of the data-loss
  guard. Amending rather than editing is this repository's convention and both
  ADR 0003 and ADR 0006 have examples.
- `dbmd studio --help` promises "editing a file in your editor is the same
  feature seen from the other side ... rather than writing over your work",
  which is currently untrue.

### Evidence bar

**Reproduce both defects on `main` first**, so each fix has a before. Then on
your branch:

- The column case, exactly as quoted above, driven through the API.
- **The same thing in a real browser**, because the API path is not what a person
  does: page open, add a column in an editor, then change a type in the panel.
- The rename case: rename a table while one of the files it must edit has
  changed on disk. Show what the model looks like afterwards and what the page
  said.
- `git checkout` under a running studio, then an edit, and show the checkout
  survives.
- A refusal, and **what the page displays when it happens**. Paste the text.
- Show that `create` and `remove` inherit it rather than bypassing it.
- The browser console, and that a normal editing session is not noticeably
  chattier than before.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: A rename can half-apply, and nothing says so
description:
﻿A rename can half-apply, and nothing says so.

Found by the dbmd-33 agent, on merged code, when the orchestrator asked it to
re-check the rename against its new conflict detection rather than assume.

## What happens

Rename `customers` to `clients` in the inspector while `tables/addresses.md`,
which refs it, is saved by hand in an editor at the wrong moment:

    conflicts:  ["tables/addresses.md"]      correct, and the hand edit survives
    tables now: addresses, clients, ...      customers is gone
    still ref `customers`: ["addresses"]     pointing at a table that no longer exists
    diagnostics: []

The model is left inconsistent, and **`diagnostics: []` is the part that makes
it dangerous**. A dangling ref is a cross-object fact, which ADR 0017 makes the
validator''s business rather than the reader''s, so the studio says nothing at
all. The page looks fine.

## Why it is a property of the design rather than a bug in the rename

`renameTable` issues its steps as separate requests. **The write is debounced,
so a `PATCH` is answered `200` when the edit is accepted, and the refusal only
comes into existence at the flush.** The client cannot abort on something that
has not happened yet: `await writer.settle(name)` waits for the write and then
never looks at `status.conflicts`.

So every multi-step edit through the panel has this shape. Rename is simply the
only one today that spans files.

ADR 0019 records it as a consequence, with the two ways out named:

- **A client that reads `conflicts` after each step and stops.** Smaller, keeps
  the server as it is, and leaves the earlier steps applied, so it has to say
  what it did and what it did not.
- **A rename endpoint the server can refuse as one thing.** Bigger, and the only
  version that is actually atomic. `writeModel` already takes an `only` set, so
  the writer can be told the whole group.

## Scope

- Decide which. Say why, and if it is the first, say what the user is told about
  the half that landed.
- Whichever it is, **the user has to learn that the rename did not complete**,
  at the time, not at the next `dbmd check`.
- Consider whether the studio should surface validator diagnostics at all. It
  runs the validator in the page already (dbmd-32), so the dangling ref is
  computable the instant it exists; it is simply not shown. That may be the
  cheapest half of the fix and it helps every other case too.

## Watch out for

- ADR 0016 already records that a rename failing between its steps leaves both
  files, with `git checkout` as the undo. This item is the narrower and worse
  case: the rename **succeeds** at every step it is allowed to take, and the
  result is a model nothing complains about.
- Do not make the rename synchronous by removing the debounce. The debounce is
  what makes a drag one write rather than sixty, and ADR 0013 pays for it.
- `dbmd check` is being built now and will catch this after the fact. That is
  worth having and is not a fix: the point is that the person who did it should
  find out while they are still looking at the screen.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
﻿## Correction from the dbmd-48 agent, 2026-09-07

This item says the studio does not surface validator diagnostics. **It does.**
`showDiagnostics` in `src/studio/client/main.ts` merges `validate()` over the
page''s own copy of the model, so a dangling ref appears in the footer as soon as
it exists.

That premise was written before dbmd-32 landed the inspector, which is where the
in-page validation came from.

**It does not change what this item is about.** The half-applied rename left the
model pointing at a table that no longer existed, and the problem was that the
rename kept going after one of its steps was refused, not that nothing said so
afterwards. The fix is that it stops, which dbmd-48 has now built.

title: An edge points at a table, not at the column it is about
description:
﻿The arrows point at tables, not at the columns they are actually about.

Owner, on seeing the canvas for the first time:

> the arrows need to point to the columns that they''re related to, and they
> need to stay there. Uh, whenever you move stuff around, you''ll see that the
> arrows move as well. They''re... it''s really table to table references right
> now rather than actually going to the, um, column.

## Confirmed in the merged code

`between()` in `src/studio/client/edges.ts` takes `centreOf(from)` and
`centreOf(to)`, so both endpoints are box centres. `EdgeSpec` already carries
`from.column` and `to.column` and they are used only for the hover `<title>`.
The geometry never sees them.

So an edge from `orders.customer_id` to `customers.id` is drawn between two
rectangles, and which columns it is about is invisible unless you hover.

## What it has to do

- **Leave the source box at the row of the referencing column, and arrive at the
  row of the target column.** A model with two refs from one table to another,
  on different columns, must show two edges leaving from two different rows.
- **Stay attached while the box moves.** The owner named this specifically. An
  anchor computed once at load and not recomputed on drag is the failure mode.
- Keep working when the column is not visible: a tall table, a scrolled box, or
  a collapsed one later. Clamping to the nearest visible edge of the box is a
  reasonable answer; silently reverting to the centre is not, because it looks
  correct and is not.

## Watch out for

- **The row position is a client-side measurement, not a model fact.** It comes
  from the rendered DOM, so it changes with zoom, with fonts, and when a column
  is added or removed. Whatever computes it has to run on the same pass that
  moves the boxes, or the arrows will lag the drag by a frame and look loose.
- `dbmd-31` already learned that an edge''s sideways offset must be a property of
  the **pair** and not of the direction it is read in, or the two legs of a
  mutual reference cancel and draw as one line. Anchoring to rows changes those
  endpoints; do not undo that fix while moving them. There is a comment at the
  line saying why.
- The fan offset exists so two relationships between the same pair do not
  overlap. Once each edge starts at its own row, some of that separation comes
  free and some does not. Two refs on the *same* column pair still need it.
- `edges.ts` has a test comparing path midpoints rather than path strings,
  because two different strings can describe the same line. Keep that property.

## Evidence bar

**Drive it in a browser and show the picture.** A screenshot where the anchors
are visibly at the right rows, on a model with at least two refs between one
pair of tables on different columns.

Then drag both boxes, at zoom 1 and at some zoom that is not 1, and show the
arrows still landing on the correct rows afterwards rather than near them.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave seven, 2026-09-06

Branch: `studio/37-edges-to-columns`. **ADR number 0018 is yours** if the
anchoring deserves a record. Do not take a different one; 0016 and 0019 are
handed to agents working right now.

### This is the owner's first complaint on seeing the studio

Quoted, because the wording carries what actually annoys:

> the arrows need to point to the columns that they're related to, and they need
> to stay there. Uh, whenever you move stuff around, you'll see that the arrows
> move as well. They're... it's really table to table references right now
> rather than actually going to the, um, column.

and `centreOf(to)`. `EdgeSpec` already carries `from.column` and `to.column` and
they feed only the hover `<title>`; the geometry never sees them.

**"They need to stay there" is the harder half.** An anchor computed once at load
and not recomputed while a box moves is the failure that looks like success right
up until somebody drags something.

### What dbmd-31 left you, and what you must not undo

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0015-*` first. Two things in `edges.ts` are
load-bearing and were paid for:

- **The sideways offset is a property of the pair, not of the direction the edge
  is read in.** Taking it from the edge's own direction flips it on the return
  leg of a mutual reference, the two shifts cancel, and the one pair the offset
  exists for draws as a single line. There is a comment at the line. That bug
  shipped and was found by looking at a screenshot, not by a test.
- **The test compares path midpoints, not path strings**, because `M a C … b` and
  `M b C … a` differ in every character while being the same line. Keep that
  property when you change the endpoints.

The fan offset still matters after your change. Two refs on the *same* pair of
columns still overlap; what you buy is separation for refs on *different*
columns, which is most of them.

### The measurement problem, which is the actual engineering

A column's row position is **not a model fact**. It comes from the rendered DOM
and moves with zoom, with fonts, and whenever a column is added or removed.

- Compute it on the same pass that moves the boxes. A frame's lag reads as the
  arrows being loose, and "loose" is exactly what the owner is objecting to.
- **Another agent is building the inspector right now**, which adds and removes
  columns from a live table. Rows will change under you at runtime. Whatever you
  build must recompute rather than cache across a model change; say in the PR
  body what triggers a recompute.
- Decide what happens when the row cannot be pointed at: a very tall table, a
  scrolled box. Clamping to the nearest visible edge of the box is a reasonable
  answer. **Silently falling back to the centre is not**, because that is the
  current bug wearing a disguise.

### Scope

Edges only. Not the inspector, not notes and groups, not visual polish. The
owner was explicit that appearance comes later:

> and then we'll work on making the visuals better

So make them correct, not pretty.

Keep out of the inspector's way: it owns the side panel and the editing. You own
`edges.ts` and whatever minimum it takes to learn where a column row is. Say
loudly in the PR body what you changed about how a box renders, because that is
the seam between the two of you.

### Evidence bar

The owner asked whether agents are actually driving this rather than asserting
it. So drive it, in a real browser, with `playwright-cli`.

- A model with **two refs between the same pair of tables on different columns**,
  screenshotted, with both arrows visibly leaving and arriving at the right rows.
  Build that fixture if `examples/shop` does not have one.
- **Drag both boxes and screenshot again.** The arrows must still be on the right
  rows, not near them.
- **Do it at a zoom that is not 1.** dbmd-31 proved the coordinate conversion is
  exactly invertible at every zoom step, so if anchoring drifts under zoom it is
  your arithmetic and not the geometry module's.
- Show a mutual reference still drawing as two distinguishable arrows. That is
  the regression you are most likely to cause.
- Show what happens for a column that cannot be pointed at.
- Paste the browser console.

Stop any server you start, by its own process. Do not kill node globally: two
other agents are working on this machine.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: A column cannot be declared unique
description:
A column cannot be declared unique, and the fact ends up only in prose.

Found by the dbmd-61 agent writing `examples/shop` by hand. It is the worst of
the eleven findings that item produced, and it is the one that contradicts ADR
0003 outright.

## What happens now

`indexes` takes `name` and `columns` and nothing else. `unique: true` is an
`unknown-key` warning. Four indexes in `examples/shop` are unique in the
business — a customer email, a product SKU, and the two handheld idempotency
keys that the entire `warehouse` group note is about — and every one of them is
recorded in a prose sentence like:

> `customers_email_key` is a unique index; the format cannot say so yet, so this
> comment is the only place that fact is written down.

**A load-bearing fact recorded only in a comment is precisely the failure ADR
0003 exists to prevent.** The example model in this repository currently
demonstrates the gap to every reader.

## Why it is more urgent than it looks

An import from Postgres or SQL Server cannot round-trip its own unique
constraints. Both engines report them; the introspection contract can carry
them; the markdown cannot receive them. So `dbmd import` silently drops a
constraint the database actually enforces, and `dbmd check`'s existing warning
about a `ref` whose target is neither unique nor a primary key can never be
anything but noise, because nothing can ever declare a target unique.

## Scope

- `unique: true` on an index entry, read, written and validated.
- Decide whether a single-column shorthand on the column itself is worth it.
  The argument against is that it puts the same fact in two places; the argument
  for is that `unique` on a column is how every person writing this by hand
  expects to say it. Pick one and record why.
- Update `examples/shop` to use it and delete the four apologetic sentences.
- The `ref` target warning in the validator becomes meaningful; check it.

## Related gaps, deliberately in scope to *decide* rather than build

`check` constraints and `on delete` behaviour on a `ref` are the same shape of
gap, named by the same agent. They may be worth doing here or worth their own
item, but they should not be discovered a third time. Say which.

## Watch out for

- This changes the format, so it touches the reader, the writer and the
  validator together, and it cannot be dispatched alongside work in any of them.
- ADR 0003 or ADR 0005 needs an appended section, not an edit.

comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave three, 2026-09-06

**dbmd-14 and dbmd-16 are batched into this one branch.** They touch the same
files, both migrate `examples/shop`, and both must land before dbmd-41 or an
import writes models at scale against a format that is still moving. Doing them
separately means migrating the example twice and reviewing the same files twice.
Work them as one change with two decisions in it.

Branch: `format/14-unique-and-nullable`. Read dbmd-16 in full as well as this
item; both descriptions are the brief and both name arguments against, which you
are expected to answer rather than skip.

**ADR number 0011 is yours** if you want a new record. Do not take a different
one and do not take "the next free number": it is handed out, checked against
`main` and every open branch, and `npm run check` fails a collision. Both items
ask for an *appended section* on ADR 0003 rather than an edit, and appending may
well be enough on its own. If it is, say so and leave 0011 unused.

### The two decisions, which are the actual work

Neither item tells you the answer. Both tell you what the arguments are and ask
you to pick one and record why. A pull request that implements the obvious thing
without answering the question in its item is not done.

- dbmd-14: whether a single-column `unique: true` shorthand on the column itself
  is worth it alongside the index entry. Same fact in two places, against the way
  every hand-author expects to say it.
- dbmd-16: whether the key becomes `nullable:`, `required:`, or stays. The item
  argues for the rename and then argues against itself honestly. Also decide what
  the old key does: a diagnostic naming the new key costs almost nothing and is
  kinder than a silent unknown-key warning.

dbmd-14 also asks you to **say something about `check` constraints and `on
delete` behaviour on a ref** without necessarily building them. They are the same
shape of gap, found by the same agent, and the point is that they are not
discovered a third time. Either do them here or say plainly why they are their
own item, and the orchestrator will file it.

### What this must not touch

`src/import/` is being changed by another agent in this wave for a different
reason. Stay out of it. If you believe the introspection contract has to change
for unique constraints, stop and say so on this item rather than reaching across.

### Evidence bar

The mechanical gate is the price of admission, not evidence. Beyond
`npm run check`:

- **Drive the round trip, not just the unit tests.** Read `examples/shop` with
  the new format, write it back, and paste the `git diff` of the model directory.
  Empty is the answer that proves canonicality survived the change.
- **Paste the diagnostic** a model using the old key now produces, as text, as a
  user would see it.
- **Show the four apologetic sentences deleted** from `examples/shop`. That gap
  is currently demonstrated to every reader of this repository and closing it
  visibly is half the value of the item.
- Say in the PR body which way you decided both questions and the sentence that
  made you decide, not just what you implemented.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: Canonical writer, and prove the round trip
description:
Write a model back to disk in a canonical form, and prove it round-trips.

This is the item the whole format stands on. If it is wrong, every studio save
produces a diff nobody can review, and the tool has failed at its only job.

## Scope

- `src/model/write.ts`: a function returning a file's full text for any kind
  (table, note, group), and `writeModel(dir, model)` writing each object to its
  own file in the right directory. ADR 0005 has the layout.
- Canonical means fixed: key order, indentation, quoting style, where blank
  lines go, and a single trailing newline. Two people producing the same model
  produce byte-identical files.
- The prose body is written back exactly as it was read.
- Group membership is written on the member and never on the group, and group
  geometry is never written at all because it is computed. If the writer emits
  either, the merge story in ADR 0005 is broken.

## The two properties to hold

1. Parsing a serialised model gives back an equal model, for every model.
2. Serialising a parsed file gives back identical bytes, for every canonical
   file.

The second only holds for canonical input, and that is the point: a hand-written
file normalises on the first save and then never moves again. Write a test that
reads a deliberately untidy fixture, saves it twice, and asserts the second save
changed nothing.

## Watch out for

- A write that is not atomic loses a file. The studio writes on every drag.
  Write to a temporary file in the same directory and rename over the target: a
  partial write on a crash is a corrupted model, and the developer has git as
  their undo, which will not have the file yet.
- Never write a file that failed to parse. A model carrying a diagnostic for a
  table must leave that table's file alone rather than serialise whatever half
  model it managed to build.
- Do not write files you did not change. Writing all forty tables when one moved
  makes `git status` useless and destroys the reviewability the format exists
  for. Compare the rendered text with what is on disk and skip if equal. This
  matters most for a group drag, which moves every member at once: only the
  members that actually moved get written.
- YAML emitters love to reflow, fold long strings, and drop quotes they think
  are unnecessary. Any of those turn a stable file into a churning one. If the
  library fights you, emit the frontmatter yourself: it is a fixed set of keys.

## Evidence bar

Show the actual `git diff` from changing one column's type in a ten-table
fixture. It must be one line. Then show the diff from adding one table to a
group: it must be one line, in that table's file, and the group file must be
untouched. Paste both in the pull request.

## Out of scope

Validation (dbmd-12). The studio's calls to this (dbmd-30).
close_reason: Merged in PR #10. Round trip verified against examples/shop, real hand-written prose: four lines across three of twelve files, second save a no-op, every body byte-identical. Sent back once for an opt-in parse guard that silently deleted two columns on the default call path; the fix makes that call not compile.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

Round-tripped `examples/shop` myself, because it is the only real hand-written
prose in the repository and a fixture built alongside the writer proves less.

Read, save, save again. Result matches the report exactly: **four lines changed
across three of twelve files**, all `default:` single-quote to double-quote, and
the second save wrote nothing. Every prose body, every `layout`, `"'GB'"`,
`now()`, key order, indentation and flow style came back byte-identical. That is
property 2 demonstrated on real content, and the normalise-once-then-stable
behaviour the format depends on.

Hand-emitting the frontmatter was the right call and the reasoning holds: the
alternative leaves the library's defaults, and its next release's defaults, in
the path of every file in every user's repository. Reading still goes through
`yaml`, so there is one parser and one place that knows what `null:` means.

## Code

**One defect, and it is the item's own hard rule.** The brief said: *never write
a file that failed to parse.* The report says that is implemented and describes
it unconditionally. It is implemented, but only when the caller opts in, and the
default is destructive.

`writeModel(dir, model)` is a legal call against the published signature —
`diagnostics` lives in an optional third `options` argument. Called that way over
`test/fixtures/model/`, it wrote `tables/coerced.md`, a file carrying three
error diagnostics:

```
-  - name: null
-    type: text
-  - name: flag
-    type: true
   - name: created_at
     type: timestamptz
-    default: 0
-    unqiue: true
```

Two columns and a default silently deleted. Called as
`writeModel(dir, model, { diagnostics: r.diagnostics })` the same file is
skipped with `reason: 'diagnostic'` and is byte-identical afterwards. So the
guard works; it just is not on unless you know to ask.

Why this is worth sending back rather than noting: **the studio calls this on
every drag.** One caller that forgets the option turns a recoverable broken file
into silent column deletion, and the user's undo is git, which will show a diff
that looks like a legitimate edit. This is also the one failure mode where being
wrong is unrecoverable rather than annoying — everything else the writer does
can be reverted by reading the file back.

The fix is a shape change, not a bug fix. Make the safe path the only path:
take the whole `ReadResult`, or make `diagnostics` required, or have the model
itself carry which objects were built from a file the reader could not fully
read. Any of those, and the destructive call should stop compiling.

Everything else in the code is right. The temp-file-plus-rename with the dot
prefix and no `.md` suffix, so the reader ignores it twice over, is careful. The
rename-mocking test that inspects the world at the instant of rename, and
asserts the temp holds the complete new text while the target holds the complete
old one, is a real test of atomicity rather than a test that a rename happened.

## Architecture

`src/model/paths.ts` holding the kind-to-directory map that the reader and
writer must agree on exactly, with `read.ts` importing it rather than keeping a
second copy, is the right move and prevents the drift that dbmd-13 already
exists to fix elsewhere.

ADR 0010 argues the never-delete decision rather than leaving it silent, which
matters: "not in the model" and "removed" being indistinguishable is a real
hazard and it is now written down where the next person meets it.

The four assumptions are all sound. Dropping a table layout's `w`/`h` follows
ADR 0005, refusing an object whose name is not a file name rather than escaping
the directory is right, and frontmatter always being LF while the body stays
verbatim is the only choice that lets two machines produce the same bytes.

## Verdict

Send back for the opt-in guard. Everything else is ready to land.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Follow-up: the fix, and one thing it found that I did not ask for

Verified each claim rather than reading them.

**The destructive call no longer compiles.** I wrote the old call into a scratch
file and ran `tsc`:

```
error TS2554: Expected 2 arguments, but got 3.
```

**The careless call is now safe.** `writeModel(dir, model)`, the shortest call
the signature allows, over `test/fixtures/model/`: `tables/coerced.md` is skipped
with `reason: 'incomplete'` and is byte-identical afterwards. That is the exact
case that silently deleted two columns and a default an hour ago.

**`complete` is required on both `CanvasObject` and `Model`.** Not optional, so
an importer or a test building a model from scratch has to say `complete: true`
out loud. Every construction site in the repo had to be edited, which is the
cost and is also the reason it cannot be got by omission.

**The round trip is unchanged**: four lines across three of twelve files on
`examples/shop`, second save writes nothing.

**And the part I did not ask for.** Choosing the per-object field over a
required argument meant `complete` could be set from the *phase boundary* rather
than by matching diagnostic paths, and that draws a line path-matching could not.
`tables/shipments.md` declares `group: shipping` with no such group file. That is
an error, but everything the file says did reach the object, so saving it loses
nothing — and it is now correctly written rather than blocked. The flags read
`coerced=false shipments=true orders=true`, which is the distinction that
actually matters: not "did this file produce an error" but "does the object hold
everything the file does".

That is a better answer than the one I asked for, and it came from taking the
harder of the three options rather than the cheapest.

Renaming the skip reason `'diagnostic'` to `'incomplete'` follows from it and is
the right name: it describes the object rather than the event.

## Verdict

Merge.

title: Model types and the reader
description:
Read a `db-model/` directory into a typed model in memory.

## The directory, per ADR 0005

```
db-model/
  _model.md          name, engine, prose about the model as a whole
  tables/*.md        kind: table
  notes/*.md         kind: note
  groups/*.md        kind: group
```

The directory decides the kind. The `kind:` key in the frontmatter is a
cross-check, and a file whose `kind` disagrees with its directory is a
diagnostic, never a silent reinterpretation.

## Scope

- `src/model/types.ts`: `Model`, `Table`, `Column`, `Index`, `Ref`, `Note`,
  `Group`. Exact shapes are yours; ADR 0003 and ADR 0005 have the fields.
- `src/model/read.ts`: `readModel(dir)` returns the model plus a list of
  diagnostics. It does not throw on a bad file; a bad file is a diagnostic with
  a path and a line, because the studio has to show that rather than crash.
- Two computed indexes, built once here because the studio, the validator and
  the exporter all want them: which tables point at a given table, and which
  tables are in a given group. Group membership is declared by the member with
  a `group` key and is never stored on the group.
- The markdown body after the frontmatter is kept as one opaque string, exactly
  as read, newline for newline. It is never parsed as markdown. For a note the
  body is the note.

## Watch out for

- YAML will silently do the wrong thing and look right. A key named `null` is a
  real key and depending on the parser it can arrive as a boolean. A column
  default of a quoted SQL string must survive with its quotes intact rather than
  arriving as a bare word. Pick a YAML parser that lets you see the raw scalar
  and its style, and write a test for both of those exact cases before you write
  anything else.
- YAML 1.1 booleans. A column typed `y` or `no` is unusual but `on` and `off`
  are not, and neither is a table named `on`. Every place a string is expected,
  assert it is a string and diagnose rather than coerce.
- CRLF. This repository normalises to LF on checkout and developers are on
  Windows. The body string must not gain or lose a carriage return on the way
  through, or every save produces a whole-file diff. There is a `.gitattributes`
  doing half of this; do not rely on it doing the other half.
- A frontmatter block that is absent, empty, or unterminated are three different
  diagnostics, and a file with no frontmatter at all is a plain markdown file
  that happens to be in the directory. Decide what that is and say so in code.
- A group key naming a group file that does not exist is a diagnostic, not a
  reason to invent the group.

## Evidence bar

A fixture directory with at least: a table with a composite primary key, a
column whose default is a quoted SQL string, a column named `null`, a table
whose prose body contains a fenced code block with three dashes inside it, a
file with broken YAML, a note, a group with two members, and a file in the wrong
directory for its kind. Report what `readModel` returned for the broken ones,
not that it did not throw.

## Out of scope

Writing (dbmd-11). Validating references (dbmd-12).
close_reason: Merged in PR #5. Reader verified against an orchestrator-written adversarial fixture, not the PR's own: null key, quoted SQL default, YAML-boolean-shaped names, byte-exact CRLF body through a fence containing three dashes, and the group not invented.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Dispatched 2026-08-25, stopped by the owner before it reported.

What it left in its worktree: `yaml@^2.9.0` added to package.json and installed.
No commits, no source files, no tests. Nothing worth preserving, and nothing was
merged or pushed. `main` is untouched.

Not resumed and not finished by the orchestrator. The item is open and
unchanged, and the next dispatch starts clean.

One real finding came out of it anyway: agent worktrees are created at
`.claude/worktrees/` inside the repository, so every one of them shows up as
untracked in `git status` on `main`. Fixed separately.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

Drove the reader myself against a fixture I wrote, not the one in the PR, built
specifically to break the four claims this item stands on. Compiled `dist` and
called `readModel` directly.

- `null: false` arrives as `nullable: false`. The key named `null` survived.
- `default: "'pending'"` arrives as the nine characters `'pending'`, quotes
  intact. `default: "false"` arrives as the string `false`, not a boolean.
- A column named `on` arrives as the string `on`.
- `ref: other.id` resolves to `{ table: 'other', column: 'id' }`.
- `group: nope`, naming a group with no file, is kept on the table, produces
  `group-unknown`, and `groupMembers` has no `nope` key. The group is not
  invented, which is the ADR 0005 property.
- The body round-trips byte for byte. My fixture used CRLF throughout, a fenced
  SQL block containing a line of three dashes, trailing spaces, and no final
  newline. `onDisk.endsWith(body)` is true, the carriage returns are still
  there, and the fence did not terminate the frontmatter.

Line numbers are honest: `group: nope` is on line 20 of my file and the
diagnostic says 20. A missing `_model.md` warns with no line rather than a
fabricated one.

That is the item's central claim and it holds.

## Code

Read the reader. The kind dispatch, the field reader and the diagnostic
plumbing are one shape each rather than three, which is what keeps a 980-line
file legible. Reading map keys from the scalar's source text whenever a plain
scalar did not resolve to a string is a good single rule: it makes `null:`,
`on:` and a quoted `"null":` all behave, instead of three special cases.

Not storing the quoting style is right, and the PR gives the reason: ADR 0003
has the writer emit a canonical style, so remembering the input's style would
be remembering something the writer is going to discard.

**One defect, and it is one byte.** `test/model/read.test.ts` contains a literal
NUL at offset 1241, inside `customers?.body ?? '<NUL>'`, which was meant to be
`''`. Consequences, in order of how much they matter:

1. **Git classifies the file as binary.** `git diff --stat` reports
   `Bin 0 -> 16788 bytes`, so the largest test file in the pull request cannot
   be reviewed as a diff, now or in any future change to it. In a repository
   whose entire premise is that the diff is the review, that is the finding.
2. The assertion still behaves acceptably: if `customers` were undefined,
   `endsWith('\0')` is false and the test fails loudly.

CI is green and will stay green, which is exactly why this needed reading
rather than trusting.

## Architecture

ADR 0008 is a real record: it states the rule (diagnose, never coerce), names
what it costs, and its assumptions are the kind that would otherwise be
invisible, particularly the file name being the identity with `table:` as a
cross-check.

No entropy added. `src/import/`, `src/index.ts` and the concurrent agent's
surface were left alone as briefed. `package.json` gained exactly one
dependency with one transitive, and the PR says what it buys and what was
considered instead.

The report that YAML 1.1 booleans are unreachable through frontmatter is
reported as a finding rather than claimed as a fix, and the string assertions
are still in place regardless. That is the right way round.

## Verdict

Send back for the one byte. Everything else is ready to land.

title: The model on disk
description:
The model on disk, as ADR 0003 describes it: one markdown file per table under
`db-model/`, YAML frontmatter for structure, free markdown for the prose that
explains why the table exists.

Everything else in this project reads and writes through this layer. The CLI,
the studio and the importer are all clients of it, so getting the round-trip
right here is what stops every one of them producing noisy diffs.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0003-markdown-on-disk-is-the-model.md` before
opening any child of this epic. It carries the four requirements the format
exists to satisfy and the rejected alternatives, so an agent that skips it will
re-argue a settled question in a pull request.
close_reason: All eleven children closed. The format holds tables, columns, indexes, notes and groups, and dbmd-45 settled where the model-not-migration line sits.

title: Nothing looks at what a merge did to main, and it has been red seven times
design:
`merge-pr.mjs` refuses to merge a pull request whose checks are red, stale or
behind. That is the prevention, and it works. **There is no detection on the
result**, and the result is the one thing a bypass cannot avoid producing.

What that costs, measured on 2026-09-07: `check.yml` has 100 runs on `main` and
**four of them failed**. Every one of those was a merge that had reported green
on the branch and went red on the default branch minutes later. Nobody noticed
any of the four, including me, because a merge ends with the merge and nothing
looks at what it triggered. Two of the four were a race the flush repair (#44)
had already fixed by the time I read them, which is the good case: main was red
for the length of the next merge and healed on its own. Two are live, and they
are dbmd-056.

The gap is small and specific. After `merge-pr.mjs` merges, it knows the commit
it just put on `main`. Nothing waits for that commit's run, and nothing reports
it. A merge that leaves the default branch red is exactly the event the merge
gate exists to prevent, and it currently produces no signal at all.

## Watch out for

- **Do not make this block the merge.** The run starts after the merge, so
  waiting for it turns every merge into a several-minute stall, and a merge that
  cannot be undone by waiting is a merge that should not wait. The output is a
  report, not a gate.
- **A re-run erases the record.** `gh run rerun --failed` updates the run in
  place, so the run listing understates how often `main` has been red. Anything
  that counts historical failures from `gh run list` is reading a floor, not a
  rate. Say so wherever the number is printed.
- **Three workflows run on `main`**, not one: `check.yml`, `model.yml` and
  `provenance.yml`. Only the first has ever failed there, which is not a reason
  to look at only the first.
- **`check-main-provenance.mjs` is the shape to copy**, not to extend. It reads
  the finished state of `main` from the GitHub API and reports rather than
  prevents, which is the same job on a different property. It also fails
  transiently right after a merge because it calls the API per commit, so
  whatever this becomes should tolerate a run that has not appeared yet rather
  than calling its absence a failure.
notes:
Demonstrated on the change that filed it. PR #137's whole subject was that a red build on main goes unnoticed. Its own post-merge run, 34152213762 on 85cac58c, went red on the watcher debounce flake at 18:35 UTC, and I did not notice for about an hour. Nothing looked at it, including the person who had just written the sentence.

Two things this adds to the item. First, the counting is worse than filed: main has 140 check runs and seven of them failed, not four; I read the newest 100 as a census. Whatever this becomes should never take a count from a windowed listing without comparing the window to the total. Second, and more useful for the design: the signal has to arrive without being asked for. A report you have to go and read is the thing that already exists and it is exactly what failed here twice in one afternoon.

title: A test in the merge gate is flaky, and I hit it on a documentation-only branch
description:
Observed on 2026-09-07 on pull request #132, which changes **three markdown files
and nothing else**.

```
FAIL test/studio/watch.test.ts > the watcher, counted at the callback
     > turns a burst of separate changes into one wake-up
AssertionError: expected 2 to be 1
```

`verify (24)` failed. `verify (22)` passed on the same commit. Re-running the
failed jobs with no change at all: **both green**.

## Why this matters more than one red run

`check.yml` is the merge gate. A ruleset on `main` requires it green with an
empty bypass list, so this test can refuse any pull request in the repository,
including ones that cannot possibly have caused it. **A gate that fails at random
teaches everybody to press re-run**, and the next time it catches something real
it gets re-run too.

There is a note in `verified.md` about exactly this shape: *a matrix doubles the
chance of seeing a flake and dresses it as the version-specific break the matrix
was added to find.* This is that, and the note was written before this happened.
The failing leg was read rather than assumed: the assertion is about coalescing a
burst, not about anything Node 24 does differently.

## What the test is asserting

That several file changes arriving together wake the watcher **once**. It saw
two wake-ups. That is a timing race between the burst and the debounce window,
and a shared CI runner is exactly where the burst stops arriving together.

## What a fix must not be

- **Do not delete the assertion.** Coalescing is real behaviour and it was
  verified by hand: a `git checkout` that rewrote every table file in
  `examples/shop` moved the studio's revision by one, not eight. Something should
  hold that.
- **Do not just raise a timeout.** That is the change that makes a flake rarer
  and unfixed, and the next person meets it with less context than you have.
- **Do not make the test pass by loosening it to "one or two".** That asserts
  nothing: two wake-ups from one burst is the failure.

The honest options are to make the burst deterministic, which probably means
driving the debounce clock rather than the filesystem, or to move the assertion
somewhere the timing is owned rather than observed. Say which, and say what it
costs.

## Watch out for

- **Reproduce it before fixing it.** A flake that has been seen once and fixed by
  reasoning is a flake that comes back. Run the test in a loop, on both Node
  versions, under load, and say how often it failed before and after.
- `test/studio/watch.test.ts` already carries the corrected story of dbmd-c8p, an
  item whose premise about this watcher turned out to be backwards because the
  test harness handed every case a freshly attached directory. Read that comment
  first: this file has been wrong about its own timing before.
notes:
## Three occurrences, not two, and one of them was on `main`

Searched all 100 `check.yml` runs from 2026-09-07. Every one of these is
`verify (24)`, `the watcher, counted at the callback > turns a burst of separate
changes into one wake-up`, `AssertionError: expected 2 to be 1`.

| when | branch |
| --- | --- |
| 12:52 | **`main`** |
| 16:09 | `tooling/86c-a-check-that-reads-lines` |
| 16:36 | `docs/what-was-checked-and-what-was-got-wrong` |

**The 12:52 one was a red build on the default branch.** Nobody noticed it,
including me, because the merge that triggered it had already succeeded and
nothing looks at a post-merge run.

Two of the three are still in the run listing. The third is mine and it is gone,
because I re-ran the failed jobs and a re-run updates the conclusion in place.
**So the visible rate is 2 in 100 and the floor is 3 in 100**, and the difference
is one person pressing re-run once.

## Against the idle rate

**28 runs of `test/studio/watch.test.ts` on this machine, quiet, 64% memory: 28
passes.** Two batches, 8 then 20. So it does not reproduce without contention,
and roughly 3% in CI against 0 in 28 locally is the shape of the thing: a race
that a shared runner loses and a quiet laptop does not.

That is the before-rate the fix needs to beat, and it has to be taken under load
rather than at idle, or it will read as fixed when nothing changed.

## Still always the same leg, and still not proof

All three on `verify (24)`, none on `verify (22)`. `verified.md` carries the
warning this runs into: a matrix doubles the chance of seeing a flake and
dresses it as the version-specific break the matrix was added to find. Three
samples on one leg is consistent with a Node 24 difference and equally
consistent with the two legs racing on one runner and 24 losing more often.
Read the failing leg rather than the shape of the failure.
## Four red builds on main, not one, and the Node 24 pattern does not survive them

Swept every workflow rather than the one test. On `main`: `check.yml` 100 runs,
**4 failed**; `model.yml` 100 runs, 0 failed; `provenance.yml` 100 runs, 0
failed. So the 12:52 build was not a lone miss.

 run         | UTC   | commit   | leg | what failed
-------------|-------|----------|-----|-------------------------------------------------
 34097917141 | 07:55 | 83651eb4 |  22 | PATCH: carries a unique index through a patch
 34098266297 | 08:00 | 7255471d |  24 | 3 tests, server.test.ts and watch.test.ts
 34118140833 | 11:44 | fdbf0ce9 |  22 | checkout is noticed, undone version not written back
 34124239676 | 12:52 | 2a5c2471 |  24 | the burst-into-one-wake-up debounce

**Two of the four are already fixed.** 83651eb and 7255471 merged at 02:55 and
03:00 local, and the flush repair merged at 03:01 as 60f0279 (#44). Before it,
`flush` was a 400ms sleep and a `GET` that was called a fence and was not one,
so a snapshot taken after it read the file before the write landed. Every
assertion in those two builds has that shape: `expected [] to deeply equal
['tables/orders.md']`, a written-files list that was empty because nothing had
been written yet. Neither is evidence of a live problem and neither should be
counted against the rate.

**Two are live, both in `test/studio/watch.test.ts`, and they are different
tests on different legs.**

- `the watcher, counted at the callback > turns a burst of separate changes
  into one wake-up`, on **verify (24)**: `expected 2 to be 1`.
- `git checkout, which ADR 0004 says is the undo > is noticed, and the undone
  version is not written back`, on **verify (22)**: the file held the committed
  layout `{ x: 480, y: 340 }`, so the patch to `{ x: 500, y: 500 }` never
  landed. The test waits for the watcher to notice the checkout, then patches
  and flushes; a second watcher event arriving between the patch and the flush
  marks the file stale and the write is refused as a conflict. The test asserts
  nothing about conflicts, so a refused write reads as a wrong layout.

## What that does to the Node 24 hypothesis

The note above says all three occurrences were on `verify (24)` and warns that
three samples on one leg is equally consistent with the two legs racing on one
runner. **The fourth is on `verify (22)`.** A Node 24 difference does not
explain a Node 22 failure, and both failures are the same shape: the watcher
delivering more events than the test assumed. Drop the version hypothesis and
treat the leg as noise.

## The general problem, which is bigger than this test

Nothing looks at a post-merge run. All four of these went red on the default
branch after the merge had already reported green, and in every case the
orchestrator had moved on. `merge-pr.mjs` refuses a red or stale PR, which is
the prevention; there is no detection on the result. Filed separately.

## This flake can fail the owner's first release, and the release page does not say so

`release.yml` has no test step of its own on purpose: `npm publish` runs
`prepublishOnly`, which is `npm run check`, which runs the whole vitest suite
including `test/studio/watch.test.ts`. So **the one command the owner has left
to run is the command this flake sits in.** A tag push that loses the race
prints a test failure and publishes nothing.

It is recoverable, and nobody has written down how. The tag is fine and the
version comparison passed; only the publish job failed, so re-running that job
publishes. The workflow's own error text tells a person to delete the tag and
tag again, which is the right advice for a version mismatch and the wrong
advice here.

Two consequences:

- This is a reason to fix the flake before the first release rather than after,
  which is a stronger claim than the one this item was filed with.
- Whatever fixes it should also leave `release.yml` saying what a red publish
  means, because the two failures look identical to somebody reading a red tick
  and only one of them is about their tag.

The registry name is clear, checked on 2026-09-07: `dbmd` returns 404, and so do
`db-md`, `db_md`, `dbMd` and `dbmd.js`, so npm's too-similar rule has nothing to
catch on either. The first publish will not fail for the boring reason.

Raised P2 to P1. Not because the test matters more than it did, but because the publish the owner has been asked to trigger runs it, and a lost race there costs them a failed release rather than a re-run on a branch.
## Correction: seven red builds on main, not four, and one of them is mine

The census two notes up is wrong and the error is mine. I ran
`gh run list --limit 100` against a branch with **140 runs**, so the window cut
off everything before about 07:00 UTC, and I reported the window as a census.
Then a seventh happened while I was writing about the first four.

Every failed `check.yml` run on `main`, taken with the limit above the run
count. Times are UTC; local is five hours behind.

 run         | UTC   | commit   | leg | what failed
-------------|-------|----------|-----|-------------------------------------------------
 34075103319 | 02:05 | 3395a0df |     | PATCH: changes a column type and writes exactly that one file
 34080447829 | 03:40 | dd12379f |     | the same
 34097917141 | 07:55 | 83651eb4 |  22 | PATCH: carries a unique index through a patch
 34098266297 | 08:00 | 7255471d |  24 | 3 tests, server.test.ts and watch.test.ts
 34118140833 | 11:44 | fdbf0ce9 |  22 | checkout is noticed, undone version not written back
 34124239676 | 12:52 | 2a5c2471 |  24 | the burst-into-one-wake-up debounce
 34152213762 | 18:35 | 85cac58c |  24 | the burst-into-one-wake-up debounce again

**Four are the flush race, not two.** All four predate `60f0279` (#44), which
landed at 03:01 local, and every assertion in them has that shape: a
written-files list that was empty or wrong because the snapshot was taken before
the write landed. None is evidence of a live problem.

**Three are live, not two.** The debounce case has now failed four times
counting branches: 12:52 and 18:35 on `main`, 16:09 on
`tooling/86c-a-check-that-reads-lines`, 16:36 on a docs branch of mine whose
record I erased by re-running. The checkout case has failed once, on
`verify (22)`.

## The seventh is the one worth reading twice

`85cac58c` is **my own merge of #137**, and #137 was the pull request whose
entire subject was that red builds on `main` go unnoticed. Its post-merge run
went red on the same flake it was reporting, and I did not notice, because
nothing looks at a post-merge run and because I had just finished writing that
sentence. That is `dbmd-rjd`, demonstrated on the change that filed it.

## Reproduced under contention, on this machine, 27 failures against 28 idle passes

The note above says it does not reproduce at idle and that any before-and-after
rate has to be taken under load. It reproduces easily under load, and the recipe
is one sentence: **run the suite while another copy of the suite is running.**

Measured 2026-09-07, running `npm run check` in the main checkout while an agent
ran its own check in a worktree:

 what                    | idle          | under contention
-------------------------|---------------|------------------
 `watch.test.ts` runs    | 28 passes/28  | see below
 failed tests            | 0             | **27**
 failed test files       | 0             | 5
 wall clock              | fast          | 127.83s
 summed test time        |               | 538.92s
 node processes on the box |             | 147, 96 of them this project's
 memory used             | 64%           | 75%, 7.8 GB free

## Timeouts are a third symptom and the diagnosis has to cover them

Every failure visible in the captured output was `Error: Test timed out in
5000ms`, not an assertion. Two by name:

- `git checkout, which ADR 0004 says is the undo > is noticed, and the undone
  version is not written back`, `watch.test.ts:781`. In CI this one failed with
  a wrong layout rather than a timeout.
- `a rename while one of the files it must edit changes on disk > runs to the
  end when nothing changes underneath it`, `watch.test.ts:1167`. **This test has
  not appeared in any CI failure**, so contention reaches further than the CI
  record shows.

So the same file produces at least three symptoms: `expected 2 to be 1`, a
layout that never landed, and a hang past five seconds. A fix that explains the
first two and not the third is probably incomplete, and the CI census undercounts
the affected surface because a runner is less contended than this box was.

## And the framing this corrects

"It fails in CI and not locally" invited a hypothesis about the runner, then
about the Node version. Both were wrong. It is contention, it is reproducible on
demand, and the reproduction costs one extra terminal.

**Five test files failed, not one.** The captured output was a `tail -30` so the
other three are not named here. Anyone re-running this should capture the whole
output rather than a tail, which is the same mistake as reading a windowed run
listing as a census.

## Correction: my diagnosis of the checkout case was wrong, and the agent has the counter-example

A note above says the checkout failure happens because "a second watcher event
arriving between the patch and the flush marks the file stale so the write is
refused as a conflict". **That is wrong and it cannot happen.** `Edits.absorb`
freezes the baseline for a file with unwritten edits, and a test that forces
exactly that reload passes, with the write landing and no conflict. I wrote it
as a reading of the test rather than as a reproduction, and it read plausibly
because the symptom fits.

**The real cause, reproduced deterministically:** `writeFile` truncates before
it writes. A wake-up landing inside the checkout reads an **empty** file. The
studio does the right thing and carries the last good version forward as
`complete: false`, but that still moves the revision, so the test's
`until(revision > written.revision)` is satisfied by a state on the *way to* the
checkout rather than by the checkout. The next patch then hits an incomplete
object, is refused 409, and the flush writes nothing. What a reader sees is the
committed layout where the patched one should be.

So the shape I described, "the watcher delivers more events than the test
assumed", is right for the burst case and wrong for this one. This one is about
*which* event the test decided to wait for.

## And the timeouts are not this race

My note above put the timeouts in with the two assertion failures and asked for
a diagnosis covering all three. **That was the wrong ask.** The measurement:

 case                                                    | under load
---------------------------------------------------------|-----------
 `runs to the end when nothing changes underneath it`     | failed 35/48
 `turns a burst of separate changes into one wake-up`     | failed 0/48

The first contains no `until`, no watcher wait and no sleep. It is ten HTTP
round trips and five flushes, so it cannot lose a watcher-event race. It ran out
of its budget because the machine was oversubscribed, which my own numbers said:
127 seconds of wall clock against 539 seconds of test time. Capacity, not a
race, and the two have opposite signatures under the same load.

## The one real defect my contention run did expose

**`until` in both studio test files had a 5000ms deadline, exactly equal to
vitest's default `testTimeout`, and vitest's clock starts first.** So no `until`
in these files has ever been able to report what it was waiting for: the test
dies at the framework's deadline a moment before the helper would have said
`timed out waiting for the watcher to notice a checkout`. That is why my
contention run produced bare timeouts and line numbers instead of named waits,
and it is why the CI record has been harder to read than it needed to be.

That is a diagnosis fix rather than a timing fix, and it is worth having on its
own regardless of what happens to the two flaky cases.

## Closed by #144. What was fixed, what was not, and what was never a defect.

**Fixed: both flaky cases, and neither by waiting longer.**

- The burst case was the test's assumption. `ModelWatcher` promises one wake-up
  per burst, where a burst is events no further apart than the window. Two
  changes further apart are two bursts and are owed a wake-up each; answering
  one would swallow the second change. The case saved two files and expected one
  wake-up without ever controlling the gap. `expected 2 to be 1` was the right
  answer to a question it did not mean to ask. The debounce is now a `Burst`
  class driven directly, so the cases that count wake-ups make their bursts
  instead of hoping the operating system delivers one.
- The checkout case was waiting on the wrong event. `writeFile` truncates before
  it writes, so a wake-up inside a checkout reads an empty file; the studio
  correctly carries the last good version forward as `complete: false`, and that
  still moves the revision, so `revision > written.revision` was satisfied on
  the way to the checkout. The patch then hit an incomplete object, was refused
  409, and the flush wrote nothing. It now waits for the studio to be serving
  what the file says, and asserts the patch returned 200 so a refusal reports as
  a refusal.

**No behaviour changed, so ADR 0057 is still free.** The watcher change is an
extraction: same trailing timer, same interval, same `unref`, same
`attachKinds` then `onChange` order. I checked that line by line rather than
from the summary.

**Verified independently.** I branched from the change, put the old wait back
into the new deterministic case and nothing else, and got `expected 409 to be
200`. Then restored and ran the file as delivered: 38 passed.

## What has a measured rate and what does not

 assertion                  | idle | 10 spinners | 5 suites + 10 spinners
----------------------------|------|-------------|-----------------------
 old `wakes === 1`          | 0/25 | 0/60        | 1/80
 new `wakes <= 2`           | 0/25 | 0/60        | 0/80
 driven `calls === 1`       | 0/25 | 0/60        | 0/80

**The burst half has a before-and-after. The checkout half does not**, because
it did not reproduce naturally in 80 runs on either wait, which is consistent
with one sighting in a hundred CI runs. Its evidence is the deterministic
reproduction instead, and saying so is better than inventing a rate.

## The timeouts were never this item

My contention run produced 27 failures and I asked for a diagnosis covering all
three symptoms. That was wrong. `runs to the end when nothing changes underneath
it` has no wait, no watcher poll and no sleep, so it cannot lose a race; it
failed 35 times in 48 under load while the burst case failed 0 in 48. Opposite
signatures, and one of them is capacity. A machine running five copies of the
suite makes tests miss a five second budget, and that is the machine.

## The finding worth more than the fix

**Both `until` helpers used a 5000ms deadline against vitest's 5000ms default,
and vitest's clock starts first.** So no `until` in either studio test file has
ever been able to say what it was waiting for: the framework gives up a moment
before the helper would have named the wait. Every timeout in the CI record for
these files has been less informative than it needed to be. Now 4000ms, and
documented as a diagnosis fix rather than a timing one, because it buys nothing
against any race.
close_reason: Closed

title: Say prominently that this was vibe coded with b-fac, and that it is a personal tool
description:
Asked for by the owner on 2026-09-07, in their words:

> Add to the repo a prominent "This was 100% vibe coded using b-fac" and link to
> the b-fac repository. Lets also convey that I created this as a tool for
> personal use.

## What that means concretely

- **The sentence is theirs and it is quoted above.** "100% vibe coded using
  b-fac" is the wording they chose. Do not soften it, do not hedge it into
  "developed with the assistance of", and do not explain what vibe coding is.
- **The link is `https://github.com/BlakeHastings/b-fac`**, taken from the
  plugin's own manifest rather than guessed. MIT, by the same author.
- **Prominent** means the README, near the top, where somebody who lands on the
  repository sees it before they see the feature list. Not a footnote and not
  only in `AGENTS.md`.
- **A personal tool** is the other half and it changes what a reader expects.
  Somebody who arrives at a public repository assumes it wants users, issues and
  pull requests. This one was built by one person for their own use. Saying so
  sets the right expectation about support, stability and scope, and it is the
  honest frame for everything else on the page.

## Where else it may belong

Decide and say which you chose. Candidates: `README.md` near the top,
`AGENTS.md`, and the npm package description, since the package is about to be
publishable and `package.json`'s `description` is what a stranger reads first on
the registry. **The README is not optional; the others are a judgement call.**

## Watch out for

- **`README.md` now has a test behind part of it.** ADR 0056 and
  `test/docs/readme.test.ts` define three fence tags and require every block in
  the `dbmd import` walkthrough to carry one. Adding prose above that section is
  fine; adding a fenced block anywhere near it is not, unless it is tagged.
- **`scripts/check-commands.mjs` asserts the README documents all seven
  commands.** Do not disturb the entries it reads.
- **Do not add a badge.** Nothing in this repository has one and a badge is a
  claim that needs a service behind it.
- The tone of the rest of the README is plain and technical. The new lines
  should read like the page they are on, and the owner's sentence should be
  quoted rather than paraphrased into that tone.

## Evidence bar

- The rendered README, from the top, pasted or screenshotted, so the word
  "prominent" can be judged rather than asserted.
- The link, followed, resolving.
- Every place you added it, listed, with what each says.
- `npm run check` green, including the README test.
notes:
## What the page looks like today, so the brief is about the real thing

`README.md` opens with the title, one line of positioning, a paragraph of what
the format is, and then a screenshot section. **The natural place is between the
one-line positioning and the paragraph**, or immediately after the paragraph and
before the picture. Anything below the screenshot is not prominent.

The package's own description is:

> "Model your database in markdown, edit it in a local web view, commit the
> result."

That is what a stranger reads first on the registry, and the package becomes
publishable the moment the owner pushes a tag. **A personal-tool note belongs
there too**, if it can be said in a clause rather than a sentence, because npm
truncates.

`package.json` already carries `homepage` and `repository` pointing at this
project. The b-fac link is a different thing and goes in the prose.

## The two things not to get wrong

- **The sentence is the owner's.** "100% vibe coded using b-fac". Quote it.
- **`https://github.com/BlakeHastings/b-fac`** is the repository, taken from the
  plugin manifest in `~/.claude/plugins/cache/b-fac/b-fac/0.38.0/`, which names
  it as both `homepage` and `repository`, MIT, same author. Follow it before you
  paste it.
close_reason: Landed as PR #133, and it is the owner's own request. Their sentence is verbatim and first, above the screenshot, which is the definition of prominent on that page. The second paragraph is the better half: first person, in their voice, saying what the consequence is rather than apologising, so a stranger arriving at a public repository knows there is no release cadence and that issues may sit. Three places, each judged and listed: the README near the top, AGENTS.md where it is scope rather than attribution, and package.json's description as a leading clause so npm's truncation cannot cut the note off. The b-fac link was taken from the plugin manifest and followed before it was pasted.

title: dbmd import has no input path, because dbmd query does not exist
description:
`dbmd import` landed on 2026-09-07 and works. **A user cannot get it anything to
import without reading the TypeScript.**

The tool's own error messages send them to a command it then rejects:

```
$ echo '{"hello":"world"}' | dbmd import --dir /tmp/x
error $.dbmdIntrospection [import/missing-field] this file has no `dbmdIntrospection`
  version, so it is not an introspection file dbmd produced; run `dbmd query` and
  import the JSON it prints

$ dbmd query
dbmd: unknown command "query". Expected one of: init, import, check, studio, export.
```

`docs/import-format.md` opens by saying the file is "produced by running
`dbmd query --engine X` themselves". ADR 0007 describes `dbmd query --engine X`
and `dbmd import` as the two callers that resolve through the provider registry.
`AGENTS.md` describes `dbmd query, which prints the SQL`. Four error messages in
`src/import/contract.ts` name it.

**None of it exists, and there was no backlog item for it.** The SQL is real and
proven against live databases in containers, but it lives in
`INTROSPECTION_QUERY` inside `src/import/providers/*.ts`, reachable only through
`introspectionQuery()` on the provider interface, which nothing calls.

So the argument this project is built on, that a database becomes markdown
becomes a picture you can drag, has a missing first step for everybody who is
not reading the source.

## Scope

`dbmd query --engine <id>` prints the introspection SQL for that engine on
stdout, and with no `--engine` says which engines there are.

## Watch out for

- **stdout is the whole point.** The output is meant to be piped into a database
  client or redirected to a file, so narration goes to stderr and nothing
  prompts. ADR 0006 and ADR 0011, and the gate fails the build on a stray write.
- **This is the one command with no model directory.** Do not make it take one,
  and do not have it default to `db-model` out of symmetry with the others.
- **`--engine` is required here and optional on `import`**, which is not an
  inconsistency: import reads the engine out of the file, and there is no file
  yet. Say so in the help rather than leaving a reader to notice.
- **The provider registry already resolves engines**, and dbmd-44 proved the seam
