title: An empty name passes dbmd check with no problems
description:
﻿An empty name is not a name, and nothing says so.

Found by a hunting pass over the whole journey, confirmed by the orchestrator
against the merged `dbmd check`.

## What happens

This file passes with `exit 0`:

    columns:
      - name: id
        type: uuid
        pk: true
      - name: ""
        type: ""
    indexes:
      - name: ""
        columns: []

    $ dbmd check empty-model
    empty-model: 1 table, 0 notes, 0 groups, no problems.
    exit=0

**"no problems" is wrong**, and it is wrong in the place a team trusts most: a
model that means nothing passes CI.

## Why it matters more than it reads

**This is not a hand-written curiosity. It is what the studio writes.** One click
of *Add column* puts `- name: "" / type: ""` on disk immediately, and one click
of *Add index* puts `- name: "" / columns: []`. That is the normal first step of
adding a column, so any model edited in the page passes through this state.

The inspector already says so in its own words, *"this column has no name, and
will be written as an empty one"* and *"this index has no name. this index names
no columns"*, so **the page and the validator disagree about the same file**. The
page is right.

`docs/format.md` says `name` is required on a column and that an index''s
`columns` must be columns of its table. Neither claim is enforced for the empty
case: `field-missing` fires when a key is absent and an empty string is present,
and `index-column-unknown` fires the moment you type a real-but-wrong column name
but has nothing to say about an empty list.

## Scope

- Decide the severity, and it is a real decision. An error is defensible because
  the format says the key is required. A warning is defensible because a
  half-typed column is the normal state of a model somebody is editing, and a
  studio that turns the footer red on every *Add column* click teaches people to
  ignore it. **Say which and why.**
- Whatever it is, `dbmd check` must not say "no problems" about that file.
- Cover the empty cases the same way for a table name, a column name, a column
  type, an index name and an empty `columns` list.
- Check whether a whitespace-only name behaves the same as an empty one. It
  should.

## Watch out for

- **`docs/format.md` has a row for every diagnostic code and a test that fails if
  a code has no row.** A new code changes that page in the same commit.
- The page's own messages already exist and are good. If a new diagnostic
  duplicates them, prefer making the page show the diagnostic to having two
  sentences about one fact, which is the entropy this project keeps filing items
  about.
- Do not make the studio refuse to add a column. Writing the empty row is how the
  interface works and it is fine; what is missing is anything saying the model is
  not finished.

title: The studio can stop passing only and nothing fails
description:
﻿The studio can stop passing `only` and every test stays green.

Found by the dbmd-36 agent and confirmed by the orchestrator, who found it is
worse than reported.

## What was measured

Remove the option from the studio''s write and run everything:

    - const result = await writeModel(this.dir, this.model, { only: this.writing })
    + const result = await writeModel(this.dir, this.model)

    $ npm run test
     Test Files  23 passed (23)
          Tests  502 passed (502)

**Nothing fails.** The dbmd-36 agent believed the property was still gated by
`only leaves a neighbour that is not canonical exactly as it was` in
`test/model/write.test.ts`. That test guards `writeModel`''s parameter, which is
a different claim from **the studio passing it**.

## Why the guard stopped guarding

`only` exists because of a defect found by driving the studio during the dbmd-30
review: a single edit rewrote four neighbouring files, because the writer
canonicalises everything it is handed and a hand-written model is rarely
canonical. Dragging one box reformatted three files nobody touched. ADR 0013
records it.

The studio test that pins "writes exactly that one file" runs against
`examples/shop`. **`examples/shop` became byte-canonical when dbmd-14 landed**,
so there is no longer any difference between writing one file and writing the
whole model: the other seven produce no bytes either way.

The guard did not break. The world moved under it, months of commits later, in a
change that had nothing to do with the studio.

## Scope

- Give the studio''s "writes exactly one file" assertion a fixture that is **not**
  byte-canonical, so the difference is observable again. `test/fixtures/untidy`
  exists for this shape of question.
- **Verify by removing `{ only: this.writing }` and watching the suite go red.**
  That is the acceptance test for this item and it is the only one that matters.
  Restore it afterwards.
- Look for the same rot elsewhere: any assertion whose fixture is canonical and
  whose subject is about *not* rewriting things. This is a pattern, not one test.

## Watch out for

- **Do not change `examples/shop`.** It is byte-canonical on purpose, it is the
  example every reader meets, and dbmd-14 spent a diff making it so.
- Do not delete the existing studio assertion. It still catches a PATCH that
  changes a second file, which is worth having. It has simply stopped catching
  the narrower thing it was written for, and the fix is another fixture rather
  than fewer tests.
- The general lesson is worth a sentence somewhere durable: **a test whose
  fixture is "clean" can quietly stop distinguishing "wrote a little" from "wrote
  everything".** Wherever that belongs, it is not a new document.
close_reason: PR #44 merged: verified by mutation, removing { only: this.writing } now fails two tests including a data-loss case.

title: Create and delete a table from the canvas
description:
﻿Create and delete a table from the canvas.

Owner: *"you need to build out the ability to edit these tables, add tables, add
columns, remove columns, group. All those things are important."*

Editing a table''s contents is dbmd-32 and groups are dbmd-34. **Adding and
removing whole tables had no item**, which is how it went missing: the server
grew the routes and nothing in the page ever calls them.

## What exists already

`POST /api/table` and `DELETE /api/table/:name` are live and reviewed. They
refuse an unsafe name, they write through the same debounced path as everything
else, and they were driven with `curl` during the dbmd-30 review. **No part of
the page has ever called either of them.**

So this item is mostly the interface, and the interface is the part nobody has
tested.

## Scope

- **Create a table.** Somewhere obvious on the canvas, a new table appears where
  it was asked for rather than at the origin, with a sensible starting shape and
  a name the user then edits.
- **Delete a table.** With a confirmation that says what it will cost, because
  the file goes away. Say whether anything refs it *before* deleting, not after:
  a delete that silently dangles three refs in other files is a bad diff to
  discover in review.
- The new table appears with a `layout`, since it was placed by pointing at a
  spot on a canvas, and that is the one piece of information the server cannot
  invent.

## Watch out for

- **A name is a file name.** `src/studio/safe-path.ts` refuses names the writer
  and the filesystem cannot take, and it answers over HTTP with a message. Show
  the user that message rather than a generic failure; it is a good message.
- **Two tables whose names differ only in case are one file on Windows and two
  on Linux.** `docs/format.md` has the measurement. Creating `Orders` next to
  `orders` is a real hazard and the interface is where it can be caught.
- Deleting is the only destructive action in this tool. `git checkout` is the
  undo and the status line already says so, but that only helps if the file was
  committed. Be sure the confirmation is honest about that.
- Do not build a rename here. Renaming a table has to update every ref pointing
  at it, in other files, and dbmd-32 owns that with its own warning about
  saying so before doing it.

## Evidence bar

Not `curl`. **Do it with the pointer, in a browser, as a user would**, and paste
the `git diff` and `git status` after each action:

- Create a table by pointing at a spot, and show the new file, its `layout`, and
  that nothing else in the model changed.
- Try to create one with a name the writer will not take, and paste the message
  the page showed you.
- Delete a table that nothing refs, and show the file gone and no other file
  touched.
- Delete a table that something **does** ref, and show what the interface told
  you before it happened.

title: A studio test can see the writer's temp file, and CI goes red at random
description:
﻿`test/studio/server.test.ts` is flaky: it can see the writer''s temp file.

Observed once in CI on the merge commit for dbmd-13 (PR #18), run 34075103319.
The same commit passed on a re-run, so `main` was never actually broken, but an
intermittently red gate is corrosive in a way a slow one is not: people learn to
re-run rather than to read.

## What happened

    FAIL test/studio/server.test.ts > PATCH /api/table/:name
         > changes a column type and writes exactly that one file
    AssertionError: expected [ Array(1) ] to deeply equal [ 'tables/orders.md' ]
    +   "tables/.orders.md.77f4e0f3-b8dc-45fc-87b7-b7849d626440.tmp"

The test lists the model directory to assert which files a PATCH touched, and it
listed it while the writer was between creating its temp file and renaming it
over the target.

## Why the product is fine and the test is not

The writer writes to `.<name>.<uuid>.tmp` and renames, which is what makes a save
atomic: a reader never sees half a file. The temp name **starts with a dot**, and
`docs/format.md` says files whose name starts with `.` are skipped, so `readModel`
never picks one up. The design is right.

The test applies no such rule to its own directory listing, so it sees a file the
product deliberately ignores. **This is a test bug, not a writer bug**, and the
fix should not change the writer.

## Scope

- Make the assertion ignore what the reader ignores. Filtering dotfiles out of the
  listing is the smallest honest fix and it matches the documented rule.
- Check whether any sibling assertion in the same file lists a directory the same
  way. One flake found by chance usually has quiet relatives.
- Consider whether the rule "a model directory listing skips dotfiles" wants to be
  one function the tests and the reader share, rather than a convention each
  applies separately. That is the entropy question, and the answer may legitimately
  be no for a two-line filter.

## Watch out for

- **Do not make the test wait or retry.** The race is real and a sleep hides it
  while making the suite slower and the next race harder to see. The assertion is
  simply asking the wrong question.
- Do not widen the assertion to "at least one file changed". The test is valuable
  precisely because it pins that a PATCH writes **exactly** one file, which is the
  property ADR 0013''s `only` option exists to protect.
- It reproduces rarely. Judge the fix by reading it rather than by the suite going
  green once, which it did anyway.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eight, 2026-09-06

Branch: `studio/36-snapshot-skips-dotfiles`. **No ADR.** This is a test asking the
wrong question; deciding nothing. 0020, 0021 and 0022 are handed to agents
working right now, so do not take a number.

This is a small item and the brief is longer than the fix will be. That is
deliberate: the value is in fixing it the right way rather than the quick way.

### What was observed

CI went red once on a merge commit and green on a re-run of the same commit:

```
FAIL test/studio/server.test.ts > PATCH /api/table/:name
     > changes a column type and writes exactly that one file
AssertionError: expected [ Array(1) ] to deeply equal [ 'tables/orders.md' ]
+   "tables/.orders.md.77f4e0f3-b8dc-45fc-87b7-b7849d626440.tmp"
```

`main` was never broken. **An intermittently red gate is corrosive in a way a
slow one is not**: people learn to re-run rather than to read, and then a real
failure gets re-run too.

### Where it actually is

Not in the test file. `snapshot` in `test/model/fixtures.ts` walks the model
directory and returns every file it finds, with no filter. `test/studio/server.test.ts`
diffs two snapshots to assert which files a PATCH touched, and can catch the
writer between creating `.<name>.<uuid>.tmp` and renaming it over the target.

**The product is right and the test is wrong.** The writer's temp name starts
with a dot, `docs/format.md` documents that files whose name starts with `.` are
skipped, and `readModel` honours that. The test applies no such rule to its own
listing, so it sees a file the tool deliberately ignores.

### The fix, and the two ways to get it wrong

Make the listing ignore what the reader ignores. That is the smallest honest
change and it matches a documented rule.

- **Do not add a wait or a retry.** The race is real; sleeping hides it, slows
  the suite, and makes the next race harder to see. The assertion is simply
  asking the wrong question.
- **Do not widen the assertion to "at least one file changed".** That test is
  valuable precisely because it pins that a PATCH writes *exactly* one file,
  which is the property ADR 0013's `only` option exists to protect. Weakening it
  would delete the reason it is there.

### Two things worth doing while you are in it

- **Check for quiet relatives.** `snapshot` is shared. Any other assertion built
  on a directory listing has the same hole, whether or not it has been unlucky
  yet.
- **Decide whether "a model directory listing skips dotfiles" should be one
  function** the reader and the tests share, rather than a rule each applies
  separately. The answer may legitimately be no for a two-line filter; say which
  and why. This project has been bitten twice by one idea spelled two ways, so
  it is worth a sentence either way.

### Watch out for

- Three other agents are working: in `src/cli/`, in `src/studio/client/`, and in
  `src/import/` plus `src/model/`. You should need none of those. If your change
  reaches beyond `test/`, stop and say why.
- `.beads/`, `.git/` and `node_modules/` are not the target here. The rule is
  about a model directory, and a model directory is what `snapshot` walks.

### Evidence bar

A flake that reproduces rarely cannot be judged by the suite going green once,
because it did that anyway.

- **Reproduce it deliberately.** Force the ordering, or call `snapshot` against a
  directory that contains a file named like the writer's temp file, and show the
  old assertion failing and the new one passing.
- Show the assertion still fails when it should: make a PATCH touch two files, or
  otherwise break the property, and show the test catching it. A gate nobody has
  seen fail is indistinguishable from one with nothing to catch.
- Say what you found when you looked for relatives, even if the answer is none.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: unique in the format, isUnique in the contract
description:
The format says `unique` and the contract says `isUnique`, and the argument that
settled the other key says they should match.

Found in review of dbmd-14 and dbmd-16, by applying that pull request's own
reasoning to the other half of its own diff.

## What happened

dbmd-16 renamed the markdown key `null:` to `nullable:`, and one of the two
arguments that settled it was that `Column.nullable` in `src/import/contract.ts`
is already spelled that way, so the rename **makes the markdown key and the
introspection field the same word** and a trip between a database and a file
stops being a negation somebody has to get right. That argument is recorded in
the appendix to ADR 0003 and it is a good one.

dbmd-14, in the same pull request, added `unique: true` to an index entry. The
contract calls the same fact `Index.isUnique`, and it also carries
`Index.isUniqueConstraint` for the narrower thing Postgres and SQL Server both
distinguish. So the same reasoning applied to the same pull request produced two
different answers, and nobody noticed because the two halves were argued
separately.

## Why it is worth an item rather than a shrug

`dbmd-41` is the code that translates one into the other. It is the only place
the mismatch costs anything, and it is exactly the place where a mismatch turns
into a bug: `isUnique` and `isUniqueConstraint` are two fields and `unique` is
one, so the mapping is a decision and not a rename.

Doing it after dbmd-41 is a migration of written models. Doing it before is a
key nobody has typed yet.

## Scope, which is to decide and possibly to do nothing

- Decide whether the markdown key stays `unique`, or the contract field becomes
  `unique`, or they are deliberately different and the reason is written down.
  **Deliberately different is a legitimate answer**: the contract is a wire
  format produced by an engine, the markdown is written by a person, and
  `isUnique` reads like a boolean accessor in a way a frontmatter key should not.
  If that is the answer, it belongs in the ADR 0003 appendix beside the argument
  that appears to contradict it, or the next reader will file this again.
- Decide what the markdown does with `isUniqueConstraint`. A unique *constraint*
  and a unique *index* are not the same object in either engine, and the format
  currently cannot tell them apart. That may be fine and it may not.

## Watch out for

- This touches `src/model/types.ts` and `src/import/contract.ts` together, so it
  collides with reader, writer and provider work at once. It is small, and being
  small is the argument for doing it in a gap rather than for doing it late.
- Do not reopen the dbmd-14 decision that uniqueness lives on an index and never
  on a column. That was argued from the constraint having a name the engine
  prints, and nothing here disturbs it.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:

right. `Column.nullable` is that word in both places.

`unique` is not. The contract has `Index.isUnique` and `Index.isUniqueConstraint`.
So the same reasoning applied to the same pull request gave two answers, and
nobody noticed because the two halves were argued separately.

**"Deliberately different" is a legitimate answer** and you should consider it
properly: the contract is a wire format an engine produces, the markdown is
written by a person, and `isUnique` reads like a boolean accessor in a way a
frontmatter key should not. If that is your answer, it belongs in the ADR 0003
appendix **beside** the argument that appears to contradict it, or the next
reader files this again.

Also decide what the markdown does about `isUniqueConstraint`. A unique
constraint and a unique index are different objects in both engines and the
format cannot currently tell them apart. dbmd-44 confirmed SQL Server reports
both, distinctly.

### dbmd-23: `writeModel` throws where it should skip

`isFileName` refuses the empty string, `.`, `..`, and anything with a slash, and
an object failing it is skipped as `unsafe-name`. That is the right shape: a
problem with the model becomes a `WriteSkip` the caller can report.

A name containing `:` passes that check and then fails at the filesystem, so
`writeModel` throws `EINVAL`. **That puts a model problem on the exception path**,
where the caller gets no object name and cannot say which table caused it.

The studio survives only because `src/studio/safe-path.ts` refuses `:` first, at
the HTTP boundary. **So the guard protecting the writer belongs to one of its two
callers, and dbmd-41 is the third caller with no boundary of its own**: an
importer takes names from a catalogue, and a name a catalogue accepts is not
automatically a file name. dbmd-44 imported a table literally called
`Ledger [Entry]`.

Decide where the rule lives. Duplicating `safe-path.ts` into the writer is two
spellings of one fact, which is the entropy this whole item is about.

### Watch out for

- **`docs/format.md` is executable**: fenced blocks tagged `dbmd:` must read and
  validate clean, `dbmd-error:` blocks must produce exactly the codes they name,
  and a test asserts every diagnostic code has a row. A new code or a renamed key
  changes that page in the same commit.
- **A renamed markdown key is a format change.** If `unique` moves,
  `examples/shop` moves with it, the way `null:` did, and the old spelling wants
  a `superseded-key` diagnostic rather than silence. ADR 0003's appendix has the
  precedent and the reasoning for making it an error rather than an alias.
- `docs/import-format.md` describes the contract and has no per-code test
  (dbmd-46). Update it anyway.
- One agent is working in `src/studio/`. Stay out of it. If your `safe-path`
  decision implies a studio change, **say so and do not make it**.

### Evidence bar

- **The two-spellings question answered in one sentence** in the ADR, whichever
  way it goes, with the consequence for dbmd-41 stated.
- If a key moved: `examples/shop` migrated, the old spelling diagnosed, and the
  round trip byte-identical.
- **A table named `a:b` written through `writeModel`**, showing a `WriteSkip`
  rather than a thrown error, with the object named.
- The same for whatever else the filesystem refuses that `isFileName` currently
  lets through. dbmd-44's `Ledger [Entry]` is a real name from a real catalogue.
- `examples/shop` silent from the reader and the validator, before and after.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: Wire dbmd studio into the CLI
description:
Wire `dbmd studio` into the CLI, and make `npm run studio` real.

Split out of dbmd-30 by the orchestrator at dispatch, because dbmd-30 and
dbmd-20 both wanted to own `src/cli.ts` and were dispatched in the same wave.
dbmd-30 builds the server as a module with a programmatic entry point and is
explicitly told not to create or edit the CLI. This item is the one-file join
once both have landed.

## Scope

- `dbmd studio [--port N] [--no-open]` as a subcommand of the entry point
  dbmd-20 built, calling the server dbmd-30 exported.
- The `studio` script in package.json, so that `npm run studio -- --port 0`
  works. `docs/process/working-an-issue.md` already instructs agents to run
  exactly that command and it does not exist, which is an invariant standing
  ahead of its code.
- `--help` for the subcommand, consistent with whatever dbmd-20 established.

## Watch out for

- Do not re-litigate the server's shape or the CLI's argument parsing. Both
  were decided in their own items and this is the join, not a third opinion.
- `--port 0` is the default and the printed URL is the only way a caller
  learns the real port. Do not swallow that line.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave six, 2026-09-06

Branch: `cli/35-studio-command`. **ADR number 0016 is yours** in the unlikely
event this needs one. It probably does not: this item is a join between two
decisions already recorded, ADR 0012 and ADR 0013, and inventing a third would be
the failure mode rather than the deliverable. Do not take a different number:
0015 and 0017 are handed to agents working right now.

### Both halves exist and neither is yours to redesign

This item was split out of dbmd-30 at dispatch, because dbmd-30 and dbmd-20 would
otherwise have both owned `src/cli.ts` in the same wave. Both have landed. You
are the join.

- **The server**: `startStudio` from `src/studio/index.ts`. Read ADR 0013 and the
  server's own header comment, which document four security layers. Do not
  weaken any of them and do not add a flag that could.
- **The command line**: `src/cli/main.ts` holds a `COMMANDS` array, and
  `src/cli/command.ts` defines what a command is. A new subcommand is a `Command`
  and one line in that array. `--help` for it, the root usage listing, and both
  unknown-thing messages then work without you writing them.
- **The output contract**: `src/cli/output.ts` is now the **only** module in
  `src/` allowed to write, landed as dbmd-70, with a gate that fails the build on
  a bare `console.log` anywhere. A command takes an `Output` and its last line is
  `return out.report({ code, text, json })`.

Read all three before writing anything. The whole value of this item is that it
adds no fifth opinion.

### The specific thing that makes this more than plumbing

`startStudio` writes the bound URL to stderr itself, and **`--port 0` is the
default**, so the printed line is the only way anybody learns the real port. Do
not swallow it, do not print a second one, and do not decide the port is
uninteresting because you passed it in.

The server installs **no signal handler**, deliberately, because that is a
caller's decision. Your subcommand should call `close()` on interrupt: there may
be a debounced write that has not fired, and that write is somebody's work.
`close()` flushes it and then stops listening. Getting this wrong loses data
quietly, which is the same failure the studio's own watcher item is about.

### The invariant this item makes true

`docs/process/working-an-issue.md` tells every agent to run
`npm run studio -- --port 0` and that script does not exist. It has been telling
them that since before the studio did. **That is an invariant standing ahead of
its code and you are the item that closes it**, so the `studio` script in
`package.json` is not a nicety here, it is half the point.

Check the wording in that process doc still describes what your command actually
does, and correct it if it does not.

### Scope

`dbmd studio [--port N] [--no-open]`, the `studio` script, and `--help`. Nothing
else. The canvas is somebody else's item and is being written right now.

**Another agent is in `src/studio/client/` at this moment.** Stay out of
`src/studio/` entirely if you can; you are consuming its public entry point, not
editing it. If you genuinely need a change there, keep it to a line and flag it
prominently.

### Watch out for

- **`--no-open` has to actually not open a browser**, and the default has to
  actually open one. This is the flag most likely to be wired backwards and least
  likely to be caught by a test, because a test will pass `--no-open` every time.
  Drive both.
- `--port` takes a number, and a non-number is a usage error with exit 2, which
  the entry point already has a shape for.
- Everything through `out.report`. The gate will tell you, but it is quicker to
  know.

### Evidence bar

From an installed tarball, not from the source tree, because `bin` and the
packaged `files` list are exactly what a source run hides:

- `npx dbmd studio` in a directory with a model, and **paste the URL line it
  printed**, plus proof something answered on that port.
- `npx dbmd studio --port 0` twice at once and show two different ports. That is
  the property several agent worktrees depend on.
- **Show `--no-open` not opening a browser and the default opening one.** Say how
  you observed it rather than asserting it.
- Interrupt it and show the process exits without leaving the port bound.
- `npm run studio -- --port 0` working, from the repository.
- A bad `--port` value, with its message and exit code.

Stop every server you start, by its own process. **Do not kill node globally**:
two other agents are working on this machine right now.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: An expression index is indistinguishable from a column
description:
An expression index looks exactly like a column with a strange name.

Found by driving dbmd-43's shipped query against a live Postgres during review.

## What happens

`create index entry_lower_code on public.entry (lower(ledger_code))` comes back
from the provider as:

```json
{"name":"entry_lower_code","columns":[{"name":"lower(ledger_code)"}],"isUnique":false}
```

Nothing in that distinguishes it from an index on a column literally named
`lower(ledger_code)`, which is a legal Postgres identifier.

## Why it has to be settled before dbmd-41

The markdown format's `indexes` entry takes `columns: [name, ...]`, and those
names are validated against the table's real columns. An imported expression
index therefore either produces a dangling-column diagnostic on every import
that has one, or the validator has to be loosened in a way that stops it
catching real typos. Both are bad and both are avoidable by deciding now.

Expression indexes are common: `lower(email)`, `date_trunc('day', created_at)`,
and every functional index anyone has added for a case-insensitive lookup.

## Scope, which is to decide and then do the small thing

The contract change is likely one discriminated field on an index column, along
the lines of a column reference or an expression, rather than a bare name. Both
engines have the concept: Postgres has functional indexes, SQL Server has
computed-column indexes and both have filtered or partial indexes whose
predicate is already carried separately as `filterExpression`.

Then decide what the **markdown** does with it, which is the harder half and the
reason this is not just a contract tweak:

- carry the expression as an opaque string in the index entry, and have the
  validator skip validating it
- refuse to import expression indexes and diagnose them, which is honest and
  loses information
- something else

## Watch out for

- `filterExpression` already exists on `Index` and is exactly the precedent for
  carrying engine-native SQL as an opaque string. Look at why that was
  acceptable before inventing a different answer here.
- This touches `src/import/contract.ts`, so it cannot run alongside provider
  work, and it touches the markdown format, so it cannot run alongside reader or
  writer work either.
- Whatever is decided, `docs/import-format.md` is the contract and has to say it.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## `check` constraints belong to this item, from the dbmd-14 review

dbmd-14 was asked to say something about `check` constraints and `on delete`
behaviour rather than build them, so that neither is discovered a third time. Its
answer was that they are two questions and not one, and the reasoning holds:

- **`check` is this item's question.** A check constraint is engine-native SQL
  that dbmd can neither parse nor compare, which is exactly the problem an
  expression index poses. Whatever this item decides about how opaque engine text
  lives in the markdown — carried as a string the validator skips, refused and
  diagnosed, or something else — is the same decision for both. Deciding it twice
  would be how the two answers end up different.
- **`on delete` is not.** It is a fact about what the engine *does*, which puts it
  against ADR 0003's model-not-migration line rather than against the opaque-text
  question. Filed separately as **dbmd-45**.

`Table.checkConstraints` already exists in `src/import/contract.ts` and both
providers populate it, so this is the familiar shape: the wire carries it and the
markdown cannot receive it.

Whichever agent takes this item should decide `check` in the same breath as
expression indexes, or say explicitly why they are different after all. Do not
leave it unmentioned: that is the outcome this note exists to prevent.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eight, 2026-09-06

Branch: `import/18-expression-indexes`. **ADR number 0022 is yours.** This one
probably does need a record: you are deciding how engine-native SQL lives in a
format that deliberately does not understand SQL. Do not take a different number;
0019, 0020 and 0021 are handed to agents working right now.

### Why this is the item that unblocks the import journey

`dbmd-41`, the actual import, is blocked on you and on two smaller things. It
cannot start until the format can receive what the providers already produce.

Found by driving the Postgres provider against a live database:
`create index entry_lower_code on public.entry (lower(ledger_code))` comes back
as a column named `lower(ledger_code)`, which is indistinguishable from an index
on a column literally called that. Both are legal.

### The precedent to read before inventing anything

**`filterExpression` already exists on `Index` in `src/import/contract.ts` and
carries engine-native SQL as an opaque string.** Your item names it as the
precedent and it is the right one. Go and read why that was acceptable, and
either follow it or say what makes this different. Inventing a second, unlike
answer to the same question is how a format gets two spellings for one idea,
which is the entropy this project keeps filing items about.

### The harder half is the markdown, not the contract

The contract change is likely one discriminated field on an index column: a
column reference or an expression, rather than a bare name. That part is
mechanical.

What the **markdown** does is the decision, and your item lists the candidates:

- carry the expression as an opaque string in the index entry, with the validator
  skipping it
- refuse to import expression indexes and diagnose them, which is honest and
  loses information
- something better

Whichever you choose, **the validator now exists** (`src/model/validate.ts`,
landed today) and it has a rule that an index may only name columns its table
has. That rule is exactly what an expression index breaks, so your change has to
say what happens to it. Both engines have the concept; SQL Server has computed
columns and both have filtered indexes.

### Watch out for

- **`docs/format.md` is executable.** Every fenced block tagged `dbmd:` is
  assembled into a model that must read *and now validate* with zero
  diagnostics, and every block tagged `dbmd-error:` must produce exactly the
  codes it names. There is also a test asserting every diagnostic code has a row
  in the page. **If you add a code or change what an index may contain, that page
  changes in the same commit**, and it will tell you.
- `docs/import-format.md` is the contract's own page and has no such test.
  dbmd-46 is filed for that. Update the page anyway; your item says the contract
  has to say it.
- **dbmd-19 is filed and not yours**: the markdown says `unique` and the contract
  says `isUnique`, and the same argument that settled the nullability key gives
  the opposite answer there. Do not fix it, but do not make it worse either. If
  your discriminated field needs a name, notice that this project has just been
  bitten by naming the same idea two ways.
- **`check` constraints are the same question**, and there is a note on this item
  saying so from the dbmd-14 review. They are engine-native SQL the tool can
  neither parse nor compare, exactly like an expression. Decide them in the same
  breath or say explicitly why they are different after all. Do not leave it
  unmentioned; that note exists to stop this being discovered a third time.

### Scope

The contract, the markdown format, the validator's index rule, and the two docs.
**Not the import itself**, which is dbmd-41. Not the SQL Server provider, which
is dbmd-44 and is sequenced after you precisely because the contract is moving.

Stay out of `src/cli/` and `src/studio/`: agents are working in both.

### Evidence bar

- **Round-trip a real expression index.** Take the shape the Postgres provider
  actually produces for `lower(ledger_code)`, put it through the contract, into
  the markdown, and back. Paste each stage.
- **Show it is distinguishable from a column with a strange name.** A table with
  a real column called `lower(ledger_code)` and an index on an expression of the
  same text must not collapse into one thing. That is the entire item.
- Show the validator's index rule doing the right thing for both.
- Show what a hand-author writes, since `docs/format.md` is written for somebody
  with a text editor and no tooling.
- Say in the PR body what you decided about `check` constraints, and why.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: null: false reads backwards
description:
`null: false` reads backwards, and it is a naming choice rather than a YAML trap.

The dbmd-61 agent typed it about forty times writing `examples/shop` and stopped
to re-check its direction on ten of those. That is a 25 percent hesitation rate
on the single most common key in the format, measured by someone doing the work
rather than imagining it.

## The argument

ADR 0003 files this under "YAML brings YAML's traps" and says a key named `null`
needs care because a parser may hand it back as a boolean. All true. But the
trap only exists because we named the key `null`. Nothing about YAML forces it.

The reader's own type already calls the field `nullable`. `nullable: false`
parses with no special case at all, needs no paragraph in the ADR, and would
delete `NULL_KEY` and its comment from `src/model/read.ts`. `required: true` is
the other candidate and reads the way people speak.

So this is the rare change that removes a documented trap, removes code, and
removes a paragraph of ADR, rather than trading one problem for another.

## The argument against, which is real

`null: false` mirrors SQL's `NOT NULL` and is what an importer sees coming out
of a database. Somebody reading a schema all day may prefer it. And the reader's
handling already works, so this is churn on something that is not broken.

Counter: it works because of a special case that exists only to support the
name, and the person who has to think is the one writing the model, not the one
reading the importer's output.

## Scope

Decide, then do it properly or close this with the reasoning recorded.

If it changes: reader, writer, validator, `examples/shop`, the fixtures, and an
appended section on ADR 0003. Decide whether `null:` stays readable as an alias
for one release or is simply an error with a message naming the new key. A
diagnostic that says "use `nullable`" costs almost nothing and is kinder than a
silent unknown-key warning.

## Watch out for

- Touches the reader, the writer, the validator and every fixture at once, so it
  cannot run alongside work in any of them.
- **Do this before anything writes a model at scale**, which means before
  `dbmd import` lands. Afterwards it is a migration rather than a rename.

title: Write the format down, for a person with no tooling
description:
Write the format down, from the hand-author's complaints rather than from the ADRs.

There is no format reference. ADR 0003 and ADR 0005 are decision records: they
argue for choices and are not a document you can write a model against. The
dbmd-61 agent could only write `examples/shop` correctly because it read
`src/model/read.ts` first, which is not a thing a user can be asked to do.

## The specific things that are true and written nowhere

Each of these cost the hand-author real time. All were reported.

1. **`_model.md` needs `kind: model`.** Neither ADR shows `_model.md` with
   frontmatter at all, and `model` is not one of the three kinds listed
   anywhere. `checkKind(ctx, fields, 'model')` in the reader is the only place
   it exists. A person following the ADRs gets `kind-missing` on the first line
   of the first file they write and has nothing to look it up in.
2. **The `default:` quoting rule.** `now()` bare, `"'GB'"` double-then-single for
   a SQL string literal, `'1'` and `'false'` quoted because the reader rejects a
   number or boolean. The ADR demonstrates only the string-literal case, and the
   `250` case is the one people hit first.
3. **A composite primary key's column order is the file's line order**, so
   reordering the `columns` list for readability silently changes the key.
4. **Flow versus block style.** ADR 0003's own example mixes them. dbmd-11 is
   settling what the writer emits; this documents it.
5. **Prettier will edit a model's prose.** It rewrote `*style*` to `_style_`
   inside a body on its first run. Any user keeping a `db-model/` in a repo that
   runs prettier over everything gets their prose quietly edited, and with
   `proseWrap` set to anything but `preserve` it gets reflowed, which turns
   every save into a whole-file diff. **This is advice we owe every user**, and
   probably a `.prettierignore` entry in whatever `dbmd init` writes.

## Scope

`docs/format.md`: the reference. Every key, what it means, what is required,
what the diagnostics are when you get it wrong, and the five things above
stated plainly. Written for somebody writing a model by hand with no tooling,
because that is a real user and currently an unserved one.

Link it from the README and from `dbmd init`'s output.

## Watch out for

- **Do not write this from the ADRs.** They are the reasoning, not the
  reference, and rewriting them as documentation reproduces the gaps that made
  this item necessary. Write it from `src/model/read.ts`, from
  `examples/shop`, and from the list above.
- Do not restate ADR reasoning. Link to it. A reference that argues is a
  reference nobody finishes.
- It goes stale the moment the format changes, so say what holds it true:
  ideally the examples in it are themselves parsed by a test.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave four, 2026-09-06

Branch: `dx/15-format-reference`. **ADR number 0014 is yours** in the unlikely
event this needs one. It probably does not: a reference documents decisions
already taken rather than taking new ones. If writing it makes you want to change
the format, that is a finding to report, not a thing to do here.

### Why this item is worth more today than it was yesterday

**The format settled this morning and it settled against you.** dbmd-14 and
dbmd-16 merged a few hours ago and changed two of the things you have to
document, so start from `main` and not from anything you remember:

- A column says `nullable: false`. The key `null:` is **retired and is a hard
  error**, not a warning and not an alias, with a `superseded-key` diagnostic
  naming the replacement.
- An index entry takes `unique: true`. A `unique:` key on a *column* is also a
  hard error, and the diagnostic tells the author which `indexes:` entry to write
  instead. The reasoning, which the reference should carry in a sentence, is that
  a unique constraint has a name and that name is what the engine prints when the
  constraint fires.
- The appendix to ADR 0003 has both arguments in full. `examples/shop` is migrated
  and is byte-canonical, so it is a trustworthy source of truth for what the
  writer emits.

Anything you write from memory of the old format will be wrong in a way that is
worse than the gap this item exists to close.

### The item's five complaints are the spine

They came from an agent writing `examples/shop` by hand and losing time to each
one. Do not lose them in a tidy reference organised by key. Every one of the five
is a thing a reader hits and cannot look up:

1. `_model.md` needs `kind: model`, and nothing outside the reader says so.
2. The `default:` quoting rule, including the `250` case that people hit before
   the string-literal case the ADR demonstrates.
3. A composite primary key's column order is the file's line order, so reordering
   for readability silently changes the key. This one is a data-loss footgun in a
   document about a text format.
4. Flow versus block style, which the writer now settles.
5. Prettier will edit a model's prose, and did, rewriting emphasis inside a body.

**Number five is advice this project owes every user** and it is not only a
documentation item. `dbmd init` landed this morning; the item suggests the
scaffold should write a `.prettierignore`. Decide whether it should. If yes, that
is a small change to `src/cli/init.ts` and it is in scope. If no, say why, and the
reference carries the warning instead. This repository's own `.prettierignore`
already holds `examples/` for exactly this reason, with the incident in the
comment, so the precedent is on disk.

### Write it for the person who has no tooling

That is the item's title and it is the whole test. The reader has a text editor
and a model to write. They cannot run `dbmd check`, because it does not exist yet.
They should never need to open `src/model/read.ts`, which is the only reason the
last person got it right.

Verify what you write against the reader rather than against your reading of the
reader. Every claim in the document is checkable by writing a small model and
reading it; where a claim is subtle, the check is cheap and the mistake is
expensive.

### Watch out for

- `docs/` is deliberately not formatted by prettier: prose is human-owned.
- Two agents are working in `src/cli/` and `src/studio/` right now. Stay in
  `docs/`, plus `src/cli/init.ts` only if you decide the scaffold writes a
  `.prettierignore`, and say so loudly in the pull request if you touch it.

### Evidence bar

Documentation is verified by being used, not by being read.

- **Write a model against your own document and nothing else.** Not by copying
  `examples/shop`. A few tables, a note, a group, a composite key, a ref, and at
  least one `default:` of each shape the quoting rule covers. Then read it with
  the built reader and paste the diagnostics. Zero is the result you want, and any
  non-zero is a bug in your document rather than in the model you wrote.
- Paste that model's frontmatter in the report so the next reader can see what a
  correct file looks like when written by somebody following only the reference.
- List anything true of the format that you could not find a home for. A reference
  with a known gap named in the pull request is worth more than one that quietly
  has the same gap.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: One Diagnostic type, not two
description:
Two `Diagnostic` types, converged independently, now a parallel source of truth.

Found by the dbmd-10 agent reviewing its own rebase against dbmd-40's merged
work, which is the entropy question review lens 3 asks and the reason it is
asked.

## What is there now

`src/model/types.ts` and `src/import/diagnostics.ts` each define `Diagnostic`,
a `DiagnosticCode`, a `'error' | 'warning'` severity, and a code-unit sort
(`compareDiagnostics` / `byText` against `compareCodeUnits` / `sortDiagnostics`).
Two agents working in parallel, neither able to see the other, arrived at nearly
the same shape. That they converged is evidence the shape is right. That there
are two of them is the problem.

## The real divergences

- **`path` means different things.** In the model reader it is a filesystem path
  relative to the model directory, with an optional 1-based `line`. In the
  import contract it is a JSONPath rooted at `$`, with no line, because its input
  is a JSON document with no lines to point at. Both are correct for their own
  input, and `dbmd check --json` will eventually emit both.
- **Message style.** The import convention is one sentence with no trailing full
  stop. Several model messages end with one.

## Why this is worth an item rather than a refactor in passing

ADR 0006 makes diagnostic structure a public contract, because `--json` exposes
it. Unifying after that ships is a breaking change; unifying before it costs
nothing. So this wants doing before dbmd-21 (`dbmd check`), and dbmd-21 is what
would otherwise be forced to reconcile them at the point of printing.

## Watch out for

- **Do not force one `path` to mean the other.** A JSONPath and a file path with
  a line number are genuinely different things. The likely answer is a common
  `Diagnostic` with a discriminated location, not a lowest common denominator
  string that loses the line number.
- The severity type and the sort are the parts that should simply be shared.
  Two sorts that agree today will not agree forever.
- This touches `src/model/` and `src/import/` at once, so it cannot be
  dispatched alongside work in either.

## Evidence bar

One `Diagnostic` type imported by both. Show the `--json` shape a mixed run

title: The output contract, built once and enforced
description:
The output contract, built once and enforced.

ADR 0006's four rules, made into code that other commands cannot get wrong by
accident. Do this before there are four commands rather than after.

## Scope

- `src/cli/output.ts`: one place that owns writing. Data goes to stdout,
  narration goes to stderr, and a command that wants to print does it through
  here rather than through `console.log`.
- Colour on when stdout is a TTY, off otherwise, off when `NO_COLOR` is set in
  the environment, and `--no-color` to override the detection. No colour library:
  this is a handful of escape codes.
- `--json` handled once: same exit codes as the text form, JSON on stdout,
  nothing else on stdout.
- A deterministic sort helper, used by everything that emits a list.
- A lint rule or a test that fails on a bare `console.log` outside this module.
  That is the part that makes the contract hold in six months.

## Watch out for

- `console.log` writes to stdout and `console.error` writes to stderr, and it is
  extremely easy to narrate to stdout by habit. That single mistake breaks every
  pipe and every agent, and it is invisible in a terminal because both look the
  same on screen. The test is the only thing that catches it.
- Exit codes with `--json` are the classic bug: the command prints valid JSON
  describing three errors and exits 0 because printing worked.
- Windows terminals and escape codes. Verify colour detection on Windows and in
  a piped context on Windows, not just in one shell that happens to work.
- Do not add a `--quiet`. If narration is on stderr, quiet is `2>/dev/null` and
  the flag is a symptom of rule 1 having been broken somewhere.

## Evidence bar

For one real command, paste four runs: at a TTY, piped to `cat`, with `--json`
piped to a JSON parser, and with `NO_COLOR` set. Show the exit code in the
failing case for both the text and the JSON forms.

title: An example model that is the demo, the fixture and the test data
description:
An example model that is the demo, the fixture, and the test data.

One realistic model, committed, that does three jobs at once. That is the point:
three copies of a sample schema drift apart, and the one that goes stale is
always the one in the README.

## Scope

- `examples/shop/` : a small commerce model with maybe eight tables, real
  relationships, at least one composite primary key, one grouping box, and two
  sticky notes that say something a schema cannot.
- The prose in it is written properly. This is the file people will read to
  understand what the prose is for, so a table documented with "the orders
  table" teaches exactly the wrong lesson.
- `npm run dev` opens the studio on it, and the test suite uses it as a fixture.

## Watch out for

- It has to stay valid. Wire `dbmd check` on `examples/shop` into `npm run check`
  as soon as `dbmd check` exists, or this rots within a month.
- Resist making it big. Eight tables that each earn their place beats thirty that
  demonstrate a feature list, and the diagram has to be legible in a screenshot.
- Do not use a real company's schema, and do not use anything that looks like
  personal data.

## Watch out for the ordering

This is worth doing early even though the format is not finished, because it is
the fastest way to find out that the format is annoying to write by hand. If
writing this by hand is unpleasant, that is a finding about ADR 0003 and it
should be reported rather than worked around.
close_reason: Merged in PR #8. Verified by breaking the model myself to prove the rot test fails, and by reading the prose in the files the agent did not showcase. Its eleven hand-authoring findings are filed as dbmd-14, dbmd-15, dbmd-16, dbmd-17 and comments on dbmd-41.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

Drove it rather than reading the report. `readModel('examples/shop')` returns
zero diagnostics, eight tables, two notes, and `warehouse` with exactly
`[shipments, stock_movements]` computed from the members.

**I did not take the claim that the rot test works.** I broke the model myself,
changing `ref: customers.id` to `ref: custmoers.id` in `orders.md`, and ran the
suite: 1 failed, 15 passed. Restored, 16 passed. The guard against this example
going stale is real and not decorative, which matters more than usual because
this file is the thing that rots first in every project that has one.

## Code

I read the prose in the files the report did **not** put in front of me, which
is the only honest way to review a writing deliverable. `products.md` and the
group file are as good as the two that were showcased. From the group:

> Treat this box as a warning rather than a label. It is not a bounded context
> and it is not a module. It is the part of the model where the network is a
> participant.

That is the feature working. A grouping box that says "Orders area" is worth
nothing; that one changes what a reader does next. `products.md` explaining that
a product is a coffee at a bag size, and why there is deliberately no variants
table, is the kind of thing no introspection can recover and no diagram tool has
a place to put.

The two out-of-scope edits are both correct and both carry their reason in a
comment. `examples/` in `.prettierignore` is not tidying: prettier rewrote
`*style*` to `_style_` inside a body, which is a live contradiction of ADR 0003's
byte-for-byte guarantee, and the comment says so.

## Architecture

No new decisions, and none were needed.

The 500-character floor on body length is a good instinct honestly labelled: it
cannot tell good prose from bad, and it can tell that somebody gutted it.

**The findings list is worth more than the model.** Eleven of them, from the
first person to write this format by hand in bulk, which is exactly what this
item was for. Several are real format defects, and the most important is #1:
there is no way to say an index is unique. Four indexes in this model are unique
in the business and the fact is recorded only in prose, which is precisely the
failure ADR 0003 exists to prevent. Every one is being filed rather than
absorbed into this pull request.

## Verdict

Merge. The prose is the deliverable and it is the standard for everything after
it.

title: CONTRIBUTING and the path from clone to a running studio
description:
CONTRIBUTING.md, and the path from clone to a running studio.

## Scope

- `CONTRIBUTING.md`: prerequisites, `npm ci`, `npm run check`, and the one
  command that puts a real model on screen. Then the reading order for anyone
  about to change something: AGENTS.md, the decision records, and which ADR
  covers the area they are touching.
- A `npm run dev` script that starts the studio on the example model with an
  OS-assigned port, so a contributor's first successful command produces a
  picture rather than a passing test.
- Say plainly what this project will and will not accept. It does not generate
  DDL and does not connect to databases, and both of those are decisions rather
  than gaps, so a contributor should learn that before writing the PR.
- The decision-record habit, in three sentences: numbers are handed out, not
  taken, and `npm run check` fails a collision.

## Watch out for

- Do not document commands you have not run on a clean clone. The classic
  failure is instructions that work only because your machine already has
  something. Test from a fresh clone in a different directory.
- Windows. This is developed on Windows and most contributors will not be on it.
  Every command in the file has to work in both places or say which is which.
- Do not restate AGENTS.md. Link it. Two files describing the same conventions
  drift, and the one that drifts is always the one nobody runs.

## Evidence bar

Clone this repository into a fresh directory, follow your own file top to
bottom, and paste the terminal from the clone to the studio being open. If a
step needed something the file did not mention, that is the finding.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eight, 2026-09-06

Branch: `dx/60-contributing`. **No ADR unless something genuinely surprises you**,
and then it is 0023. Do not take a different number; 0020, 0021 and 0022 are
handed to agents working right now and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### Why this item is dispatchable while four other agents are mid-flight

Because it documents **how to work on this repository**, which is settled, rather
than **what the product does**, which is moving under you as you read this.

Four branches are in flight and three of them change what the product is. So:

- **Write about `npm ci`, `npm run check`, the reading order, the decision-record
  habit, and what this project will not accept.** All stable.
- **Do not write a feature tour.** A list of what `dbmd` can do today would be
  wrong within the hour. `README.md` is dbmd-51 and is deliberately not being
  dispatched yet for exactly this reason.

If you find yourself describing a command's behaviour rather than how to run the
repository, you have drifted into the other item.

### Two things the item asks for that have changed since it was written

Check both against the code rather than trusting the item:

1. **It asks for an `npm run dev` script.** `npm run studio` already exists and
   does what that describes: it builds, then opens the repository's own
   `examples/shop` with an OS-assigned port. **Do not add a second script that
   does the same thing under a different name.** Either the item is satisfied
   already, in which case say so and document the real command, or `dev` is a
   better name and `studio` should be renamed, in which case say why and change
   one thing rather than adding one. Two scripts for one job is the entropy this
   project keeps filing items about.

2. **`docs/format.md` now exists**, and it is the reference a person writing a
   model needs. The reading order in this file should point at it, and should be
   honest that `AGENTS.md` is for someone changing the code while `docs/format.md`
   is for someone writing a model.

### The three traps in the item, all real

- **Do not document a command you have not run on a clean clone**, in a different
  directory, from scratch. The classic failure is instructions that work only
  because your machine already has something. This is the whole evidence bar.
- **Windows.** This is developed on Windows and most contributors will not be.
  Every command has to work in both places or say which is which. There is a real
  case in this repository already: `docs/format.md` records that two file names
  differing only in case are one file here and two on Linux.
- **Do not restate `AGENTS.md`.** Link it. Two files describing the same
  conventions drift, and the one that drifts is always the one nobody runs.

### Worth saying because it is true and not obvious

The project **does not generate DDL and does not connect to a database** except
to read a JSON file a human produced by running a query themselves. Both are
decisions, recorded in ADR 0003 and ADR 0007, not gaps waiting to be filled. A
contributor should learn that before writing the pull request, not in review.

The decision-record habit is three sentences: numbers are handed out rather than
taken, `npm run check` fails a collision, and a record is appended to rather than
edited when it turns out to be wrong. That last part has happened twice this week
and both amendments are worth linking as examples.

### Evidence bar

**A clean clone, in a different directory, following only your file.**

- Clone, then run every command in the order you wrote them, and paste the
  terminal. If a step needs something your machine already had, that is the
  finding and it belongs in the file.
- Paste what the first successful command puts on screen. The item's point is
  that a contributor's first success should be a picture rather than a passing
  test.
- Say which commands you ran on Windows, since that is where you are, and which
  you are asserting rather than observing for other platforms. **Assert nothing
  you did not run**; say "not verified here" instead. This project sent a page
  back this week for a claim about Windows that was checkable and wrong.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: One CLI, three callers
description:
One CLI, three callers: a human, a pipeline, and an agent.

ADR 0006 is the contract. This epic is making it real and keeping it true.

The three callers want opposite things and a CLI designed for any one of them is
actively bad in the other two. A tool that prompts hangs a GitHub Actions job for
six hours. A tool whose output reorders between runs makes an agent think
something changed. A tool that mixes progress chatter into stdout cannot be
piped anywhere.

The rules are checkable rather than aspirational, which is the point: stdout is
data and stderr is narration, nothing ever prompts, everything that reports has
a JSON form, and the same input produces the same bytes.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0006-one-cli-three-callers.md` before opening
any child of this epic.
close_reason: Both children closed. The output contract is built once and enforced, and the CI recipe is pinned and run by this repository.

title: The repository a contributor can run
description:
The repository a contributor can understand and run.

This is an MIT-licensed open source project, which means the first experience
most people have of it is not the tool. It is this repository, arriving from a
link, on a machine that has nothing installed.

Two audiences, and they need different things:

- **Someone evaluating it.** They want to know what it is and whether it solves
  their problem, in under a minute, without cloning anything.
- **Someone contributing.** They want to get from clone to a running studio with
  a real model in front of them, in one command, and then to know where the
  decision they are about to argue with was already made.

The second one is what this epic is mostly about, because the first is the
README and that is dbmd-51.

The thing that makes this repository unusual is that it already writes its
decisions down. `docs/architecture/decisions/` is not overhead here, it is the
answer to most of what a new contributor will ask. What is missing is the path
that points them at it.
close_reason: All five children closed. A contributor can clone, run npm run check, and open the studio on the example.

title: Notes and groups on the canvas
description:
Notes and groups on the canvas.

The part that makes this a diagram rather than a schema dump. ADR 0005 has the
format and the reasoning; read it before you start, particularly the section on
why a group has no coordinates.

## Scope

**Notes.** Create, move, resize, edit, delete. The body is markdown and it is
rendered, not shown raw, but editing is a plain textarea. A colour from a small
fixed palette, named rather than a hex value, so a diff says `color: amber` and
not `color: "#fbbf24"`.

**Groups.** Create with a label and a colour. A table joins or leaves a group
from the inspector, which writes one line in that table's file. The group box is
drawn as the bounding box of its members plus padding, computed on every render
and never stored. Dragging the group's header moves every member, and each
member's own layout line is what changes.

Groups render behind everything and notes render in front of the tables, because
a note is a person talking and a group is a region.

## Watch out for

- **A group must never acquire coordinates.** The temptation is to cache the
  bounding box for performance and then to write it "just this once" when
  somebody resizes. That is the failure mode ADR 0005 exists to prevent, and it
  turns into a file that can disagree with reality.
- Dragging a group is a multi-file write. Flush all of it on pointerup as one
  batch, and write only the members that actually moved.
- An empty group has no bounding box. Render something rather than nothing, or a
  group whose last member left vanishes and the user thinks they deleted it.
- Removing a table from the canvas that is a group's only member leaves an empty
  group, which the validator warns about. Do not silently delete the group.
- A note resize writes `w` and `h`. Debounce it like everything else, and snap to
  something coarse, or a drag produces a diff for every pixel.
- Group colours and note colours have to be legible in both light and dark. Pick
  the palette once, in one place, and do not let each component invent a shade.

## Evidence bar

Build a fixture with six tables, put three of them in a group, add two notes.
Then, in the studio: drag the group, and paste the `git diff`, which must be
three `layout` lines in three table files and nothing in the group file. Drag
one table out of the group and paste the diff, which must be one line in one
file. Include a screenshot of the canvas with the group box and the notes on it.
close_reason: PR #55 merged: notes and groups draw, and dragging the group wrote both members' layout lines and nothing into the group file.

title: Watch the directory, survive a broken file
description:
Watch the model directory and reload, and show parse failures without dying.

This is what makes hand editing and studio editing the same feature seen from
two sides.

## Scope

- Watch the model directory. A file changing on disk updates the open studio.
- A file that fails to parse shows as an error on that table. The canvas keeps
  showing the last good version of it rather than emptying.
- Writes the studio itself made must not bounce back as an external change.

## Watch out for

- An editor saving a file produces several filesystem events, and often a
  temporary file and a rename rather than a write. Debounce and re-read from
  disk rather than trusting the event.
- The echo. The studio writes, the watcher fires, the studio reloads, and if the
  reload is not identical you have a loop that rewrites the file forever. Ignore
  a change whose content matches what you just wrote.
- `fs.watch` is not consistent across platforms and this project runs on
  Windows. Verify on Windows specifically, not on the assumption that it behaves
  like a mac.

## Evidence bar

With the studio open, edit a table file in an editor and confirm the canvas
updates. Then break the YAML in that file and paste a screenshot of what the
studio shows. Then fix it and confirm it recovers without a restart.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## The gap is silent data loss, not staleness. From the dbmd-30 review.

dbmd-30 landed the studio server and correctly scoped the watcher out to this
item. Reproduced during review, on the merged code, so that this item says what
it actually costs rather than describing it as freshness:

1. Start the studio on a model directory.
2. Edit one of its table files in a text editor and save. Any edit; it does not
   have to be broken.
3. Change that same table in the studio, or drag it.

The studio writes its in-memory version over the top. **The hand edit is gone,
there is no warning, no diagnostic, and no conflict.** The only recovery is
`git checkout`, which the studio's own status line already tells people is the
undo, and which only helps if the edit was committed.

The read-only half of the same gap is milder and is what the item currently
implies: a hand edit is invisible in the studio until something triggers a
re-read, so the page shows a model that is not on disk.

## Why this raises the item's priority rather than its scope

The tool's whole premise is that the markdown files are the model and a text
editor is a first-class way to work with them. ADR 0004 says the studio is a
local editor of files rather than an application with a database. A studio that
silently discards what the editor wrote contradicts that premise in the one
workflow the product exists to support: edit the model, commit the diff, open a
pull request.

It is also the failure a user cannot diagnose. Nothing is logged, the studio
looks correct, and the file simply reverts.

## What the fix has to cover, beyond watching

The item is not finished by adding a watcher, because a watcher introduces the
race rather than removing it. At minimum:

- A change on disk to a file the session has pending, unwritten edits for. Both
  versions are real work and one of them is about to lose.
- A change on disk to a file the session edited earlier and has already written.
- A file that becomes unparseable while the studio is running, which is the
  ordinary state of a file halfway through being typed. It must not be treated
  as a deletion, and the studio must not write over it.
- Whether the answer is "refuse and tell the user" or "reload and discard the
  studio's pending edit". Refusing is safer and more annoying. Say which and why.

`src/studio/edits.ts` names the seam and the ADR 0013 header says where a watcher
would attach. The debounce window is where the race lives: a write can be pending
for a few hundred milliseconds while a file changes underneath it.

## Watch out for

- Editor save behaviour is not one behaviour. Many editors write a temporary file
  and rename over the target, so a naive watcher sees a delete followed by a
  create, and some see several events for one save. Debounce the watcher too.
- Do not make the studio re-read the whole model on every event. The point of
  dbmd-30's `writeModel` `only` option was that touching files nobody edited is
  itself the bug.

title: The inspector: columns, indexes, prose
description:
The inspector: edit a table's columns, indexes and prose.

## Scope

- Selecting a table opens a side panel.
- Edit the table name, and add, remove, reorder and edit columns: name, type,
  nullability, primary key, default, and `ref`.
- Add and remove indexes.
- Edit the markdown body in a plain textarea. It is text, not a rich editor.
- Every change writes through, debounced, like everything else.

## Watch out for

- Renaming a table must update every `ref` that points at it, or the rename
  silently breaks the model. That touches other files, which means other diffs;
  say so in the interface before doing it rather than after.
- A textarea will happily give you carriage returns on Windows. The body must
  reach disk with the same line endings it left with, or every prose edit is a
  whole-file diff.
- Typing in a field must not write a file per keystroke. Debounce, and do not
  reformat the field under the user's cursor while they are still in it.
- Removing a column that another table refs is a real decision. Warn, name the
  tables, and let it happen: this is a modelling tool and a broken ref is a
  diagnostic, not something to prevent.

## Evidence bar

Rename a table that two other tables point at, and paste the resulting
`git diff` across all three files. Then edit a prose body and show that the diff
is only the lines you typed.

title: The canvas: boxes, edges, pan, zoom, drag
description:
The canvas: table boxes, relationship edges, pan, zoom and drag.

## Scope

- Each table is an absolutely positioned element listing its columns, with the
  primary key and foreign keys marked.
- Each `ref` is an edge on one SVG overlay behind the boxes.
- Pan and zoom are a CSS transform on the container. Drag moves a box and writes
  the new `layout` through to disk, debounced.
- Positions come from `layout` in the frontmatter. A table without one is placed
  on a deterministic grid rather than at random.

## Watch out for

- Dragging with a CSS transform in play is the classic source of the box that
  jumps on mousedown or drifts from the cursor at zoom levels other than 1.
  Convert screen coordinates to model coordinates once, in one function, and use
  it everywhere. Test at zoom 0.5 and 2, not just at 1.
- Use pointer events, not mouse events, and capture the pointer. Without capture
  a fast drag that leaves the window leaves a box stuck to the cursor.
- Debounce writes, but flush on pointerup. A drag that ends and then never gets
  written because the tab lost focus is the one bug that makes a developer stop
  trusting write-through.
- Edges to and from the same pair of tables overlap. Two straight lines on top
  of each other read as one relationship, which is wrong in a way nobody
  notices. Offset them or curve them.

## Evidence bar

Open a fixture model with at least ten tables, drag three boxes, and paste the
`git diff`. It must touch exactly three files, one line each. Include a
screenshot of the canvas.

## Out of scope

Auto layout, multi-select and a minimap are all deliberately not in the MVP.
ADR 0004 says when to revisit that.

title: The studio server
description:
The studio server: loopback, ephemeral port, and it edits files.

## Scope

- `dbmd studio [--port N] [--no-open]`. Default port 0, meaning the OS picks;
  print the URL it actually bound to. Bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
- Serves the client bundle, built by esbuild as part of `npm run build`.
- `GET /api/model` returns the model plus diagnostics.
- `PATCH /api/table/:name` applies an edit and writes through, debounced a few
  hundred milliseconds so a drag is one write rather than sixty.
- `POST /api/table` and `DELETE /api/table/:name` for adding and removing.
- Every response says when the last write to disk landed, so the client can show
  it rather than guess.

## Watch out for

- Never write outside the model directory. A table renamed to `../../etc/x` is a
  path traversal, and this server writes files on behalf of a web page. Resolve
  every path and assert it is still inside the model root before writing. This
  is the one security property this tool has and it is worth a test that tries.
- Bind to loopback explicitly. `server.listen(port)` alone listens on all
  interfaces, and this is somebody's laptop on a coffee shop network.
- Never write a file that failed to parse, and never write a file you did not
  change (dbmd-11 has both).
- `--port 0` is not a nicety. Several agent worktrees run this at once, and a
  fixed default makes them collide silently with whichever started first.
- Do not add an HTTP framework. `node:http` serves four routes and a static
  directory in under a hundred lines, and install time is a feature here.

## Evidence bar

Start it, `curl` the model endpoint, `PATCH` a column type, and show the
resulting `git diff` in the model directory. Then attempt a traversal write and
paste the refusal.

## Out of scope

The canvas (dbmd-31), the inspector (dbmd-32), the watcher (dbmd-33).
