title: dbmd check
description:
`dbmd check`: validate the model, print diagnostics, exit non-zero on error.

The command a team puts in CI so the model in the repository cannot drift into
something that does not parse.

## Scope

- Reads the model, runs `validate`, prints diagnostics grouped by file.
- Exit 0 when there are no errors, 1 when there are. `--strict` makes warnings
  errors.
- Plain text by default. `--json` emits the diagnostics as JSON for anyone
  wiring it into something else.

## Watch out for

- A parse failure is an error, not a crash. `dbmd check` on a repository with
  one broken file must report that file and still report on all the rest.
- Exit codes are the whole contract in CI. Test them, and test that `--json`
  still exits non-zero rather than exiting 0 because printing succeeded.

## Evidence bar

Run it in a directory with one broken file and one dangling ref, and paste both
the output and the exit code you actually observed.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eight, 2026-09-06

Branch: `cli/21-check`. **ADR number 0020 is yours** if this needs one. It may
not: every piece you need was decided elsewhere and this is the item that joins
them. Do not take a different number; 0019, 0021 and 0022 are handed to agents
working right now and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### Everything this item was waiting for has landed

This was blocked on four items and all four are in. Read them in the code, not
in the backlog:

- **`src/model/validate.ts`** (dbmd-12) returns diagnostics for the model as a
  whole: dangling refs, duplicate names, an index naming a column that does not
  exist, a table with no primary key, a ref whose target is not unique, an empty
  group. Nine rules, each with a severity.
- **`src/diagnostics.ts`** (dbmd-13) is the one diagnostic type. A location is a
  discriminated union: `{ in: 'file', path, line? }` or
  `{ in: 'document', jsonPath }`. `locationText` prints either, and a consumer
  that only prints needs no conditional. **The type is a type alias rather than
  an interface and that is load-bearing**: an interface cannot be handed to
  `report({ json })`, and there is a comment and a test protecting it.
- **`src/cli/output.ts`** (dbmd-70) is the only module allowed to write. A
  command takes an `Output` and returns `out.report({ code, text, json })`, so
  the exit code, the prose and the payload come out of one value. `--json` is
  handled once, colour precedence is decided, and there is a gate that fails the
  build on a bare `console.log` anywhere in `src/`.
- **`src/cli/main.ts`** (dbmd-20) has a `COMMANDS` array. A new command is a
  `Command` and one line in it; `--help`, the root listing and both
  unknown-thing messages then work without you writing them.

**So the shape of this command already exists.** If you find yourself inventing
an envelope, a sort, or a way to print a location, stop and go and find the one
that landed.

### The part that is actually yours

Three things, and they are all about the contract rather than the plumbing:

1. **Grouping by file, readably.** `locationText` gives you the location; what a
   person reads down the left of their terminal is your decision. A run over a
   model with problems in four files should be scannable without counting.
2. **The exit code policy.** Errors fail, warnings print, `--strict` promotes.
   The validator gives you severities; the policy is this command's, and dbmd-12
   deliberately left it here. Write down where the boundary is.
3. **A broken file must not stop the run.** The item is explicit: `dbmd check`
   on a repository with one unparseable file reports that file *and still reports
   on every other one*. The reader already behaves this way, per ADR 0008; do not
   undo it by treating a read diagnostic as fatal.

### Watch out for

- **The classic bug is exiting 0 because printing succeeded.** `--json` must exit
  non-zero when there are errors, exactly like the text form. dbmd-70's `report`
  makes this hard to get wrong; prove it anyway, because this is the whole
  contract in CI and the item says so.
- ADR 0006 makes your JSON shape **public API the moment this ships**. dbmd-13
  chose the diagnostic shape deliberately so you would not have to; use it as it
  is and change nothing about it. If you believe it needs to change, stop and say
  so rather than reshaping it at the point of printing.
- A reader diagnostic and a validator diagnostic are the same type and belong in
  one sorted list. They are already comparable by one comparator.
- One invalid file can produce forty diagnostics, all true, because a broken flow
  sequence swallows the rest of the document. **dbmd-24 is filed for that and it
  is not yours.** If your output makes it unbearable, say so in the PR body.

### Scope

`dbmd check` and nothing else. `dbmd export` is dbmd-22 and is blocked on this.
Do not touch `src/studio/` or `src/model/`: agents are working in both.

### Evidence bar

The item sets it and you are held to it. **From an installed tarball, not from
the source tree.**

Build a model directory with, in one run: one file that does not parse, one
dangling ref, one table with no primary key, and one empty group. Then paste,
as text:

- The full text output, so a reader can judge whether it is scannable.
- The exit code, observed rather than assumed.
- The same run with `--json`, piped through a JSON parser, **and its exit code**.
- The same run with `--strict`, and its exit code, showing a warning promoted.
- A clean model, showing exit 0 and what it prints. `examples/shop` is silent
  from both the reader and the validator, so it is the right one to use.
- The broken-file run again, showing that problems in the *other* files are still
  reported. That is the claim the item cares about most.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: CLI entry point and dbmd init
description:
The CLI entry point, and `dbmd init`.

## Scope

- `src/cli.ts` with a shebang, wired as the package `bin` named `dbmd`.
- Argument parsing with no dependency: the surface is four commands and a
  handful of flags, and `parseArgs` from `node:util` is in the standard library.
- `dbmd init [dir]` creates the model directory with `_model.md` and one example
  table demonstrating the format, including prose and a `ref`. It refuses to
  overwrite an existing non-empty directory.
- `--help` on the root and on each command. `--version` from package.json.
- Unknown command and unknown flag both exit non-zero with a message naming what
  was expected.

## Watch out for

- `npx` runs this on Windows. Path handling goes through `node:path`, and the
  shebang plus the `bin` mapping is what makes it run at all. Test from a
  `npm pack` tarball rather than from the source tree: the source tree hides a
  missing `files` entry, and that failure only appears for your users.
- The example model `init` writes is the first thing every user reads. It is
  documentation, not a fixture. Make it a small, real-looking schema.

## Evidence bar

`npm pack`, install the tarball into an empty temporary directory, run
`npx dbmd init` there, and paste the files it produced. Not `node src/cli.ts`.

## Out of scope

`check`, `export` and `studio` are their own items.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave three, 2026-09-06

Branch: `cli/20-entry-point-and-init`. **ADR number 0012 is yours** if the CLI's
shape deserves a record. Do not take a different one and do not take "the next
free number": numbers are handed out here and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### The relay that matters most

**The frontmatter format is changing under you in this same wave.** Another agent
is settling how a column is declared unique and is probably renaming the key that
says a column is not nullable. You cannot see that branch and it will land near
yours.

So: **`dbmd init` must generate its example model with `writeModel` from
`src/model/`, not by hand-writing YAML into a template string.** If you
hand-write frontmatter you will encode a format that is about to be wrong, your
tests will assert it, and the rebase will be a real one instead of a trivial one.
This is also just the better design, which is why it is an instruction rather
than a warning.

### Scope discipline

- The item's scope is the entry point, `dbmd init`, `--help`, `--version`, and
  non-zero exits with useful messages. `check`, `export` and `studio` are other
  items and are out of scope.
- **Do not invent the output contract.** dbmd-70 builds ADR 0006's four rules
  into code that other commands cannot get wrong, and it is deliberately
  sequenced after you. Obey ADR 0006 (stdout is data, stderr is narration,
  nothing prompts, output is deterministic) but keep the plumbing minimal and do
  not build a framework for it. If you find yourself designing the shape all four
  commands will share, stop: that is dbmd-70's job and it is easier to do once
  there is one caller than to undo a guess.
- **dbmd-35 will wire `dbmd studio` into whatever you build**, after this wave.
  Leave the subcommand table extensible and say in the PR body how a new
  subcommand is added. Do not add a `studio` command yourself; the server does
  not exist on `main`.
- `parseArgs` from `node:util` is in the standard library and the item says to
  use it. No argument-parsing dependency. Install time is a feature and any new
  dependency needs a line in the PR saying what it replaces or makes possible.

### Evidence bar, which the item already sets and which you are held to

`npm pack`, install the tarball into an empty temporary directory, run
`npx dbmd init` there, and paste the files it produced. **Not `node src/cli.ts`.**
The source tree hides a missing `files` entry and a broken `bin` mapping, and
that failure appears only for users.

Note that `package.json` is currently `"private": true` with no `files` and no
`bin`. Getting the tarball to work is part of this item. If it forces a decision
that belongs to dbmd-50 (publishable package, verified from a tarball) instead,
say so on the item rather than quietly doing dbmd-50.

Also paste: `--help` at the root and for `init`, the exit code and message for an
unknown command, and the refusal when `init` is pointed at a non-empty directory.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: Validation with actionable diagnostics
description:
Validate a model and produce diagnostics a human can act on.

## Scope

`src/model/validate.ts`: a `validate(model)` returning diagnostics, each with a
severity, a message, the file path and, where it can be known honestly, a line
number.

The rules for the MVP:

- every ref resolves to a table and a column that exist
- no two tables share a name; no two columns in a table share a name
- no two indexes in a table share a name
- an index names only columns that exist in its table
- a table with no primary key is a warning, not an error
- a ref whose target is neither unique nor a primary key is a warning: it is
  usually a typo and occasionally deliberate
- a group key naming a group that does not exist is an error
- a group with no members is a warning: an empty group is almost always a rename
  that went wrong
- a file whose kind disagrees with its directory is an error

## Watch out for

- A line number that is wrong is worse than no line number. If you cannot derive
  one honestly from the parse, omit it. Do not guess by searching the file for
  the column name: a column named `id` appears forty times.
- Warnings must not fail `dbmd check` by default, or nobody will put it in CI.
  Errors fail; warnings print. `--strict` promotes warnings, and that flag is
  what a team opts into.
- Diagnostics are output, so ADR 0006 applies: they sort deterministically, and
  the JSON shape is a contract before it is a convenience.

## Evidence bar

Run it against a fixture with a dangling ref, a duplicate column, a missing
primary key, an empty group and a misfiled note, and paste the exact terminal
output. It should be readable without the file open beside it.

## Out of scope

The `dbmd check` command that wraps this (dbmd-21).

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
﻿## Diagnostic volume, from the dbmd-30 review

One invalid file produced **41 diagnostics**, 40 of them distinct, during review
of the studio server. The cause is not duplication: an unterminated flow sequence
swallows the rest of the document, so the YAML parser reports a genuine and
different complaint on nearly every remaining line.

    frontmatter-invalid|4|Implicit keys of flow sequence pairs need to be on a single line
    frontmatter-invalid|5|Block collections are not allowed within flow collections
    frontmatter-invalid|5|Implicit keys need to be on a single line
    frontmatter-invalid|6|Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings
    ... 36 more

Every line is true and the first one is the only one worth reading. The other 40
are the parser describing the wreckage after the mistake rather than the mistake.

This is now user-visible in two places rather than hypothetical: the studio shows
diagnostics in a panel, and `dbmd check` is this item's downstream consumer.
Forty lines of parser vocabulary is not an actionable diagnostic, and "actionable"
is this item's title.

Worth deciding here rather than in each caller:

- Whether a file caps its diagnostics, and at what number. One syntax error per
  file may be all that is ever useful, since the second is usually a consequence
  of the first.
- Whether a `frontmatter-invalid` from the parser is reported verbatim or
  translated. The parser's wording assumes the reader knows YAML's flow and block
  collections, and the person writing a model has been told they are writing
  frontmatter.
- Whether the cap belongs in the reader or in the presentation. Putting it in the
  reader means the studio and the CLI cannot disagree about it, which is the same
  argument ADR 0006 makes about output.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave six, 2026-09-06

Branch: `format/12-validation`. **ADR number 0017 is yours** if this needs a
record. Do not take a different one: 0015 and 0016 are handed to agents working
right now and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### Almost everything this item assumed has now landed

The item was written before any of it existed. Read it for the rules, not for the
surroundings, and read these first:

- **`src/diagnostics.ts` is the one diagnostic type**, landed an hour ago as
  dbmd-13. A location is a discriminated union: `{ in: 'file', path, line? }` or
  `{ in: 'document', jsonPath }`. Yours are all `in: 'file'`. The type is a type
  alias rather than an interface **and that is load-bearing**; there is a comment
  saying why. Do not add a second diagnostic type. That item exists because
  somebody did.
- **`src/cli/output.ts` is the only module allowed to write**, landed as dbmd-70,
  with a gate that fails the build on a bare `console.log` anywhere in `src/`.
  You will meet it. The answer is never an exemption.
- **`docs/format.md` has a row for every diagnostic code**, with a test that
  reads the union out of the source and fails if a code has no row. **If you add
  a code, that page changes in the same commit.** The test will tell you, but you
  should know before it does.
- ADR 0008 says the reader diagnoses rather than guesses. This item is that same
  principle applied to the model as a whole rather than to one file.

### The three things in this item that are judgement rather than typing

The rule list is the easy half. These are not:

1. **A line number that is wrong is worse than none.** The item says do not guess
   by searching the file for a column name, because a column named `id` appears
   forty times. Most of your rules are *about the model* rather than about a
   file, so for several of them the honest answer is a path with no line. Take
   the honest answer. `line` is optional in the type for exactly this reason.
2. **Warnings must not fail the check by default**, or nobody puts it in CI, and
   a linter nobody runs is worse than none. Errors fail, warnings print,
   `--strict` promotes and is what a team opts into. You are building the
   `validate` function rather than the command, so what you owe dbmd-21 is a
   result it can apply that policy to, not the policy itself.
3. **The ref-target warning is now meaningful and was not when this was
   written.** dbmd-14 made `unique: true` sayable on an index, so "a ref whose
   target is neither unique nor a primary key" can finally be computed rather
   than always being noise. That rule is the one to get right; it is the reason
   several other things in the backlog were sequenced behind this.

### The finding already on this item

Read the comment on this item about diagnostic volume before you start. One
invalid file produced 41 diagnostics, 40 of them distinct, because a broken flow
sequence swallows the rest of the document and the YAML parser reports every
line. Every line was true and only the first was worth reading.

Decide whether a cap belongs in the reader, in your validator, or in the
presentation, and say why. Putting it where the studio and the CLI cannot
disagree about it is the same argument ADR 0006 makes about output. **This is in
scope to decide. It is not compulsory to build**, if you conclude it belongs to
whoever prints rather than to whoever produces.

### Scope

`src/model/validate.ts` and its tests. **Not `dbmd check`**, which is dbmd-21 and
is blocked on you. Do not add a command.

Stay out of `src/cli/` and `src/studio/`: agents are working in both right now.
If a rule forces a change to `src/model/read.ts`, keep it small and say so.

### Evidence bar

- **Build a model that breaks every rule you implemented**, one violation each,
  and paste the full diagnostic list as a user would see it. That list is the
  product: if reading it does not tell somebody what to go and fix, the rules are
  right and the messages are not.
- **Show a clean model producing nothing.** `examples/shop` is byte-canonical and
  realistic and should be silent. If it is not, either you found a real problem
  in the example, which is a good outcome and worth saying loudly, or a rule is
  too eager.
- **Show the ref-target warning firing and not firing**: a ref to a column
  covered by a unique index, and a ref to one that is not. That pair is what
  proves dbmd-14 paid off.
- For each rule, say whether it produces a line number and why. A table of rule,
  severity, and whether a line is honest would be the most useful thing in the
  pull request.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: Owner: the name, and whether this is published to npm
description:
Owner decision: the name, and whether this gets published to npm.

`dbmd` is a working name, chosen because it is short, says what it does, and was
unclaimed on npm on 2026-08-24. Nothing depends on it being the final name yet,
and that stops being true the moment dbmd-50 lands and a README says it.

## What is needed

1. Is `dbmd` the name? If not, what is, and it should be checked on npm before
   it goes into files.
2. Is this published publicly to npm, or installed from a git URL inside your
   own projects? `npx` works from a git URL, so publishing is not required for
   the workflow to work.
3. If public: scoped (`@blakehastings/dbmd`) or unscoped?

## Recommendation

Keep `dbmd` and publish unscoped. It costs nothing to hold the name now, and
`npx dbmd studio` is the sentence the whole tool is trying to be. The cost of
being wrong is a rename before anyone depends on it, which is cheap.

## Meanwhile

Everything proceeds under the working name. The rename would touch package.json,
the bin name and the README, and nothing else, because no source file should
hardcode it.
close_reason: Answered: the name is dbmd, MIT licensed, public on GitHub. LICENSE and package metadata landed in the same pass.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Answered by the owner on 2026-08-24.

- The name is `dbmd`. It was free on npm when checked the same day.
- It goes on GitHub as an open source project, MIT licensed.
- Public repository, unscoped package.

Acted on in the same pass: LICENSE added, package.json carries the licence,
repository, homepage and bugs fields, and the repository was created and pushed.

Publishing to npm itself is still a separate step and has not happened. dbmd-50
is what makes the package correct enough for it.

title: The studio
description:
The local web editor, as ADR 0004 describes it: a view onto files, not a diagram
application that imports and exports them.

The files are the state. Every edit writes through to disk, there is no Save
button, and undo is `git checkout`. The client is vanilla TypeScript and SVG
bundled with esbuild; there is no UI framework and no diagram library, and ADR
0004 says why and when to revisit that.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0004-the-studio-is-a-local-editor-of-files.md`
before opening any child of this epic.
close_reason: All sixteen children closed. The canvas draws tables, notes and groups, edges anchor to columns, and every edit was driven in a browser.

title: The command line
description:
The command line surface. Four commands in the MVP:

- `dbmd init` scaffolds a model directory
- `dbmd check` validates and exits non-zero, for CI
- `dbmd studio` opens the local editor (epic dbmd-3)
- `dbmd export` writes a mermaid diagram other people can read on GitHub

The tool is run with `npx`, so start-up time and install size are features, not
afterthoughts. Anything that costs a dependency has to say what it buys.
close_reason: All three children closed. init, query, import, check, studio and export all exist and are driven by tests and by hand.

title: The one step of the publish path that has never run would blame the owner's tag
design:
`release.yml` has three steps between the tag and the upload: the version
comparison, the ancestry check, and `npm publish`. **The ancestry check has
never run**, because no tag has ever been pushed to this repository, and it is
the only thing in the whole of CI that depends on a remote-tracking ref
existing:

```bash
if ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "${GITHUB_SHA}" origin/main; then
```

Nothing else in `.github/workflows/` or `scripts/` referenced from CI reads
`origin/anything`. `check-setup.mjs` does, and it runs on a developer's machine
where the ref is there because a human cloned it.

Whether `actions/checkout@v7` with `fetch-depth: 0` creates
`refs/remotes/origin/main` **on a tag push** is the open question. The comment
above the step says it does and gives the right reason for `fetch-depth: 0`. I
have no evidence either way, and this repository has no run that would produce
any.

## The failure mode is safe, which is why this is not urgent

Measured locally on 2026-09-07:

 command                                              | exit
------------------------------------------------------|-----
 `git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/does-not-exist` | 128, `fatal: Not a valid object name`
 `git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/main`      | 1, when genuinely not an ancestor

A missing ref exits **128**, not 0. `if !` catches it, the step fails, and
nothing is published. So the guard cannot wrongly allow a publish because the
ref is absent. It errs closed.

## What it costs is the owner's afternoon

The message it prints is the same one it prints for a real off-main tag:

```
::error::<sha> is not an ancestor of origin/main
Nothing was published. A release is cut from a commit that went
through the check gate on a pull request; tag one on main instead.
```

**The owner would push a correct tag from `main` and be told their tag is not on
`main`.** They would go looking at their tag, their branch and their history,
and none of it would be wrong. This is the first release, it is the step they
have been asked to take, and a misleading error on it is expensive out of
proportion to the fix.

## The fix

Say which of the two things happened. Something like: verify the ref resolves
before comparing against it, and if it does not, fail with a message about the
checkout rather than about the tag, naming `fetch-depth` as the thing to look
at. Two lines and one extra message.

## Watch out for

- **Do not test this by pushing a tag.** `release.yml`'s own header says pushing
  tags is "the one step of this that no agent in this repository is allowed to
  take", and the reason is that a publish cannot be taken back. A tag whose
  version does not match `package.json` would fail at the earlier step and prove
  nothing about this one.
- **The order of the steps is load-bearing and should stay.** The version
  comparison runs first and is the cheap one. Moving a ref check before it would
  make the common mistake, a mismatched version, report as a checkout problem.
- **`npm publish` runs `prepublishOnly`**, which is the whole check suite. So the
  publish step takes minutes even when it is going to fail, and a failure there
  is not necessarily about the tag either. That is `dbmd-056`.
- **A `git fetch origin main` in the step would work and is the wrong fix**: it
  hides whether checkout did its job, and the next person to read the comment
  above the step would find it saying something the workflow no longer relies on.

title: The merge guard says a test catches its drift, and that test is in another repository
design:
`scripts/guard-merge.mjs` carries a region marked `BEGIN command reader` /
`END command reader`. Its comment says the region is "one reader carried in
three files", and that `scripts/command-reader.test.mjs` runs every copy over
one corpus so that a drift is a red test rather than a lucky reading.

**`scripts/command-reader.test.mjs` is not in this repository.** It is in b-fac,
and it reads three paths, all of them inside b-fac: that repository's own
`scripts/guard-merge.mjs`, `assets/guard-guest-writes.mjs` and
`assets/guard-merge.mjs`. Our copy is a fourth, installed from the third, and no
test anywhere has ever looked at it.

**It has drifted, and it is a generation behind.** Measured on 2026-09-07 by
lifting the region out of each file and dropping whole-line comments and blanks,
which is the same normalisation the b-fac test uses:

 copy                                  | significant lines
---------------------------------------|-------------------
 dbmd `scripts/guard-merge.mjs`        | 118
 b-fac `assets/guard-merge.mjs`        | 147
 b-fac `scripts/guard-merge.mjs`       | 147
 b-fac `assets/guard-guest-writes.mjs` | 147

The three b-fac copies are byte-identical to each other after that
normalisation. Ours matches none of them. The difference is structural rather
than cosmetic: ours pushes `segments` as arrays of tokens, theirs pushes
`{ tokens, substituted }` and tracks a substitution depth, so theirs can tell a
command the line runs itself from one inside `$(...)`.

**It is not a live hole today, and I checked rather than assuming.** I fed both
guards the same eight lines on stdin, which is safe because the guard only reads
a command and prints a verdict. They agreed on all eight, `gh pr merge 42`,
`echo $(gh pr merge 42)`, `echo "$(gh pr merge 42)"`, `x=$(gh pr merge 42)`, a
chained form, the `gh issue comment` false-positive case, and two pushes. The
newer machinery is `outerSegmentsOf`, and the asset's own comment says "nothing
in this file asks it yet", which is why the verdicts still match.

So what is wrong is the claim, not the behaviour. A comment in an installed
guard tells whoever reads it that a test is holding this, and nothing is. That
is the invariant-ahead-of-the-code failure, and b-fac's own test header
describes this exact shape as its worst case: the copy that mattered most "had
drifted so far that it was a generation behind, and nothing here noticed,
because nothing here looked."

## Watch out for

- **The comment is wrong twice over in an installed copy.** It calls the file it
  sits in "this asset", which is true in b-fac and false here, and it names a
  sibling test by a path that resolves in b-fac and not here. Both are artifacts
  of shipping a file whose comment describes the shipping repository. Whatever
  fixes this should not just refresh the region and leave the comment lying in a
  new way.
- **Do not copy the b-fac test in.** It compares three copies that live there. A
  useful check here compares our one copy against the asset we installed it
  from, and the asset is not in this repository either, so the check has to
  either vendor a hash or fetch. That is a design question, not a copy.
- **Refreshing the region is not free.** The newer reader changes what `read`
  returns, and every rule downstream of it reads that shape. Take the whole
  region and check the rules still compile against it rather than merging a diff
  hunk by hunk.
- **The eight-line agreement is evidence, not proof.** It says the forms I
  thought of agree. `dbmd-76x` is about the guard list and this is adjacent to
  it.
notes:
How this was found is itself filed as dbmd-9lm: the stale reference is a backticked bare path into scripts/, and check:commands reads an invocation rather than a path, so it scanned the file and saw nothing. ADR 0036's revisit condition asks for exactly that case to be written down. Fixing this item may delete the only reference dbmd-9lm's new shape would fire on, so the two want an order.
## Decided: refresh the region and fix the comment. Do not build a drift check here.

The item left "vendor a hash or fetch" open. Settling it, because it is a choice
between two reasonable implementations and that is not the owner's to make.

**A local check cannot detect the drift that actually happened.** Three options
and what each one catches:

 option                                  | catches a local edit | catches falling behind upstream
-----------------------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------
 vendor a hash of the region             | yes                  | **no**
 fetch the asset at check time           | yes                  | yes
 fix the comment, refresh the region     | no                   | no

The observed defect is the third column. Our copy did not drift because somebody
edited it here; it drifted because b-fac's moved and ours did not. A vendored
hash of our own region compares our file to our own expectation and would have
been green through the entire generation gap.

**Fetching is worse than the problem.** `npm run check` runs in `prepublishOnly`
and is what the owner's tag will run. Putting a network call to another
repository in it means a release that fails because GitHub is slow, and it makes
a check that is supposed to answer "is this tree good" answer "is this tree good
and is the internet up". `docs/ci.md` already argues this about `npx dbmd@latest`
in a CI job, in as many words: a moving dependency resolved at run time is a
supply chain decision made by accident.

**So: refresh the region from the current asset, and rewrite the comment to
describe an installed copy.** No new check. The detection this wants belongs
upstream, where the asset is authored and where all the copies are visible, and
that is b-fac #185, whose second option is to stamp a version into the region so
a host repo can compare one line without fetching anything.

## What that leaves for whoever does it

1. **Take the whole region**, not a hunk-by-hunk merge. The newer reader changes
   what `read` returns, from an array of token arrays to
   `{ tokens, substituted }` objects, and every rule downstream reads that
   shape. Copy `BEGIN command reader` to `END command reader` from
   `assets/guard-merge.mjs` wholesale and make the rules compile against it.
2. **Keep our rules.** ADR 0001 deleted a push rule from this repository's guard
   that ADR 0033 keeps in the shipped one. The region is the reader, not the
   verdicts, and b-fac's own test says asserting equal verdicts would be
   asserting a fiction. If refreshing the region changes what any command is
   allowed to do here, something has been taken that should not have been.
3. **The comment is the deliverable.** It currently calls the file it sits in
   "this asset" and names a test by a path that resolves only in b-fac. Both are
   false in an installed copy. Say instead what is true: this is a copy
   installed from a skill, the authority is upstream, nothing here checks it, and
   here is how to compare it by hand.
4. **Prove the refresh changed no verdict.** I fed both guards eight lines and
   they agreed on all eight, before any change. Feed them again after and get
   the same eight agreements, plus the forms the new reader exists for. That is
   the evidence the pull request needs, because a guard is not believed until it
   has been seen to fail, which is ADR 0034.

title: The check that proves the installed binary works never runs three of its seven commands
design:
`smoke-pack.mjs` packs the tarball, installs it elsewhere and drives the real
binary, which is the only check that looks at what a stranger downloads. It
drives every command's `--help` from the help listing, so a new command is
covered the day it lands. Beyond `--help` it drives **four of the seven**:
`init`, `check`, `check --strict` and `export --stdout`.

`query`, `import` and `refs` are never run. The function's own docstring names
the three it does drive and gives no reason for the three it does not, which
reads like a list that grew rather than a decision.

**Two of the three are cheap, and I drove both by hand on 2026-09-07 to be sure
before filing this.**

- `dbmd query --engine postgres` needs no model, no database and no credential.
  It printed 12,403 bytes of SQL on stdout with 270 bytes of narration on
  stderr, exit 0. That is the same shape as `export --stdout` and the same ADR
  0006 assertion: data on stdout, narration on stderr, seen on a real pair of
  descriptors in an installed binary.
- `dbmd refs accounts <model>` works against what `init` already scaffolded in
  that same function, because the scaffold ships `accounts` and `api_keys` with
  a ref between them. It printed 311 bytes on **stderr** and nothing on stdout,
  exit 0, naming `api_keys.account_id -> accounts.id` and calling it `required`.

`import` is the one that is genuinely hard: it needs JSON that only a real
database produces, and `query` prints the SQL rather than the result, so the two
do not chain without an engine. Leaving it out is defensible. Saying so is the
part that is missing.

**`query` is the pointed one.** Until 2026-09-07 it was named by four error
messages, the format page, ADR 0007 and `AGENTS.md` and did not exist. The tool
told people to run a command it then rejected. It would be the same shape again
for the check that proves the installed binary works to be the one place that
never runs it.

## Watch out for

- **Assert on what it said, not on the exit code.** Every existing case in that
  function says so and each one has a reason attached. `refs` narrates to
  stderr and puts nothing on stdout, so a stdout assertion on it would be wrong
  in the opposite direction from the `query` one.
- **`query` takes `--engine` and it is required**, unlike `import` where it is
  optional. The help explains why: the imported file says which engine produced
  it and here there is no file yet. A smoke that omits the flag tests the error
  path by accident.
- **Do not generate these from the help listing.** The listing is what covers
  `--help`; the point of this half is arguments only somebody who knows the
  command can supply, which is exactly what a generator cannot produce.
- **The scaffold is the fixture.** `refs` should ask about a table `init` wrote,
  so that the case keeps working if the scaffold changes and fails loudly if the
  scaffold stops having a ref in it, which would itself be worth knowing.
close_reason: Closed

title: The README's one picture shows a bug that was fixed today and misses a feature
description:
`README.md` opens by saying its screenshot is the whole product: *"One picture
and one file, and they are the same thing."* That picture,
`docs/media/studio-shipments.png`, was committed with dbmd-34 and the canvas has
changed three times since, twice today.

I rendered the same view on the current build and compared.

## Three ways it is stale, and the first is the bad one

- **It shows the truncated ref that dbmd-fnl.1 fixed this afternoon.** The
  picture has `customer_id  uuid -> customers...`,
  `shipping_address_id  uuid -> a...` and `subscription_id  uuid -> subsc...`.
  The current build puts the ref on its own line and none of them is cut. **So
  the page's headline image is a screenshot of a defect**, and it is the defect
  somebody would notice first, because the whole argument for this tool over a
  diagram is that a ref names a column.
- **The group label reads `Wr`.** dbmd-fnl.2 moved the notes this afternoon and
  it now reads `Written by the depot handheld` in full. The picture shows the
  note sitting over it.
- **The inspector has no referential-action controls.** The current panel shows
  `on delete: restrict` and `on update: unsaid` beside `order_id`. That feature
  landed with ADR 0046 and the picture predates it, so **the one screenshot of
  the editor does not show a thing the editor does.**

## What to do

Retake it, from `git archive HEAD examples/shop` so it is the shipped model
rather than a working tree, with `shipments` selected so the panel matches the
alt text. **Then check the alt text still describes the picture**, because it
names what is in it and two of those things have moved.

## Watch out for

- **The alt text is long and load-bearing.** It is the only description a
  screen reader gets of the thing the page calls the whole product. Update it
  rather than leaving it; a stale alt text is worse than a stale image because
  nobody sees it drift.
- **This is the third README item today** and the other two are in flight. The
  block below the picture is being corrected separately, and three paragraphs
  above it landed an hour ago at the owner's request. Coordinate rather than
  colliding.
- **`git archive HEAD`, not the working tree.** I filed a finding this afternoon
  built on a screenshot of somebody's uncommitted arrangement and had to correct
  it publicly. Render what ships.
- The image is 162 kB. Keep it in that range; a README that takes a second to
  load is a worse README.

title: A 500 from the studio carries an absolute path, which ADR 0006 forbids
description:
Found while dbmd-e6e was being driven, and reported as minor and pre-existing.
It is neither, because of which rule it breaks.

Issue a delete for a file the session has already absorbed as unreadable. `rm`
throws `EBUSY`, nothing catches it, and the studio answers **`500 internal`
carrying an absolute path**.

**ADR 0006 forbids an absolute path in output**, and a 500 body is output. The
reasoning there is that a path from somebody's machine in a message is a leak of
where they keep their files, and every other surface in this tool already
follows it: the reader's `messageOf` throws the system message away for exactly
this reason, and there is a test that reads the same input from two directories
and demands the same bytes.

## What a fix has to do

- **Turn it into a refusal with a code**, the way dbmd-e6e just turned the write
  path's `EBUSY` into `reason: unreadable` quoting the reader's own clause. A
  delete that cannot happen is the same shape as a write that cannot happen.
- **Say the relative path**, which is what every other message in the studio
  says.
- **Do not invent a cause.** `EBUSY` and `EACCES` should read the same, which is
  the rule dbmd-e6e settled.

## Watch out for

- The delete path already grew an `unreadable` refusal code in dbmd-e6e. This is
  the case that one does not cover: the session had already absorbed the file as
  unreadable, so the check that catches the first case has nothing to compare.
- **The test belongs at the seam**, with `node:fs/promises` mocked, not at a real
  Windows lock, because CI runs Linux. `test/studio/unreadable.test.ts` is the
  shape to copy and it is where this case belongs.
- ADR 0006 is the argument; do not restate it, point at it.
close_reason: Landed as PR #126. I reproduced it on main first rather than trusting the report: the delete of a locked table the session had absorbed as unreadable answered 500 with a home directory, a machine layout and a session id in the body. On the branch the identical gesture answers 409 unreadable with a relative path and the reader's own clause, the file survives, and an ordinary delete still deletes. The diagnosis is the good part: the unreadable refusal hangs off a comparison, and an unreadable file goes missing from both sides of it once anything re-reads, so the sides agree and the refusal has nothing to refuse. Asking the reader's diagnostics before the comparison does not depend on what the session absorbed.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
PR #126 on studio/062-a-500-does-not-name-a-machine.

The delete's refusal hung off the disk-versus-adopted comparison, and an
unreadable file is missing from both sides once any re-read has happened, so the
sides agreed and the rm threw. The reader is asked before the comparison now:
saidAbout answers from the read just taken and does not depend on what the
session absorbed, so a file-unreadable at that path refuses 409 unreadable with
the relative path whatever the comparison says, and a difference with no such
diagnostic is still conflicted.

The unhandled 500 prints errnoText rather than the borrowed system message, so
the body and the stderr line name no machine even for a throw no refusal could
predict (a file that reads fine and still will not unlink, which is what a shared
handle gives on Windows).

Before and after pasted in the PR, driven against a real exclusive lock on
Windows. Three tests added at the seam in test/studio/unreadable.test.ts with
node:fs/promises mocked; all three fail on main, the eight from #124 pass
unchanged. ADR 0019's dbmd-e6e amendment corrected in place by appending, so no
new decision number was taken. npm run check green.

title: A ref on the canvas stops saying which column it points at
description:
Measured on 2026-09-07 in a real browser, `examples/shop` at 1600x1000:

- **7 of 64 column rows overflow their box.** The worst, `uuid -> subscriptions.id`,
  by 61 pixels.
- What a person sees is `customer_id  uuid -> customers...`.
- The `span.type` that clips has **no `title` attribute**, so hovering recovers
  nothing. The full string is in the DOM and unreachable.

**This is information loss rather than a preference.** The argument for this tool
over a diagram is that a ref points at a *column*, and this is the view where it
stops saying which one. The inspector still has it, but the canvas is where
somebody is looking when they ask.

## Options, and the cost of each

- **A `title` on the row.** One attribute, works today, and a tooltip is not a
  thing anyone reads while scanning.
- **Let the box size to its content.** Honest, and it makes a table with long
  names much wider than its neighbours, which changes every layout somebody has
  already arranged.
- **Wrap the ref onto its own line** under the column name, so it always fits.
  Costs a taller row on every referencing column.
- **Elide the middle rather than the end**, `custom...id`, so the column name
  survives. Cheap and reads badly.

Decide it and say why in the pull request. **A `title` is worth doing whichever
one wins**, because it costs nothing and no other option makes the string
reachable by a person who is unsure.

## Watch out for

- **Do not change the box width rule without checking every layout in
  `examples/shop`.** Coordinates are written by the drag and a width change moves
  what overlaps what.
- **`.scene >` is the convention** and `npm run check:scenes` enforces it: a
  class name both the canvas and the inspector write must be anchored to one
  scene. Two scenes sharing a stylesheet broke this page twice in one day.
- The edges must still leave and arrive at the rows of the two columns and stay
  there when a box moves. If a row's height changes, that is the thing to
  re-check first, and it is the owner's original complaint.

## Evidence bar

- **The measurement again, after the change**: how many of the 64 rows still
  overflow, and by how much.
- **A screenshot before and after**, same model, same window size.
- **A drag, after the change**, showing the edges still meeting the right rows.
- `npm run check` green.
close_reason: Landed as PR #127. I re-took the measurement on the branch against git archive HEAD: 64 rows, zero overflowing cells, zero rows without a title, where before 7 were cut and the worst by 61 pixels with no title on any of them. Then I dragged a box and looked, because a number does not say whether it reads right. Every ref is complete on its own line, the edges land on the correct rows at the new heights, and ten boxes make zero overlapping pairs. Turning down the wider box was right: a layout coordinate is what somebody wrote by dragging boxes of a known width past each other.

title: Making the visuals better, which is the phase the owner named
description:
The owner's own words, after asking whether the functionality was validated by
actually driving it: **"and then we'll work on making the visuals better."**
The functional work is done and every other epic is closed, so this is the phase
they named and nobody has picked it up.

**This epic is mostly theirs.** Most of what follows is taste, and taste about a
picture is not derivable from a repository. What is in here is a measurement of
what the studio looks like today, with options and a recommendation each, so
that a conversation about it takes five minutes rather than starting from a
blank page.

Measured on 2026-09-07 against `examples/shop` at 1600x1000, fitted, in a real
browser. Numbers are from the DOM rather than from an impression.

## Two of these are not taste and are already dispatched

- **A ref target is clipped and there is no way to get it back.** 7 of 64 column
  rows overflow their box; the worst by 61 pixels. `customer_id uuid ->
  customers...` is what a person sees, and there is no `title` attribute, so
  hovering gives nothing. The whole argument for this tool is that a ref points
  at a column rather than at a table, and the primary view is where it stops
  saying which column.
- **CORRECTED 2026-09-07: the example hides nothing, and the measurement that
  said it did was taken against a tree that no longer exists.** The numbers
  above came from a working tree carrying four uncommitted `layout` edits of
  the owner's. Those edits are gone, `git diff HEAD -- examples/shop` is empty,
  and against the committed model the claim is false by arithmetic rather than
  by opinion: the note `the-copies-are-deliberate` occupies y 320 to 580 and
  `shipments` starts at y 640, so it begins 60 pixels below the note's bottom
  edge and cannot be covered at any box height. `stock_movements` clears the
  other note by 80 pixels the same way. The only two tables that could sit under
  a note are `order_items` and `products`, both at y 40, and whether they do
  depends on rendered height, which needs a browser to settle. **Nobody should
  act on the 28,457 figure.**

## What is yours, with a recommendation each

- **Notes render in front of everything and there is no way behind them.** If a
  note is placed over a box, nothing lets somebody un-choose that except
  dragging. Options: a send-to-back, translucency while dragging, or
  leaving it and fixing only the example. **Recommend leaving the behaviour and
  fixing the example**, because a note in front is usually what somebody wants
  and a z-order control is a second thing to learn.
- **An edge says nothing about what a delete does.** The model has carried `on
  delete` since today and `dbmd refs` prints it, but on the canvas a cascade and
  a restrict are the same pale grey line. Options: weight, colour, or a small
  marker at the child end. **Recommend a marker rather than colour**, because
  colour is the thing that stops working when somebody prints it or is
  colour-blind.
- **Every box looks equally important.** Eight tables, one size, one colour, no
  hierarchy. A person cannot see at a glance that `orders` is the centre of this
  model and `subscriptions` is off to one side. Options: size by column count,
  weight by how many refs point in, or nothing. **Recommend nothing without a
  reason**: automatic emphasis that is wrong is worse than none, and the model
  has no field that says what matters.
- **The canvas may be emptier than it needs to be after a fit.** Flagged as
  needing re-measurement for the same reason as the corrected bullet above: the
  original reading was taken against the owner's uncommitted layout. Re-measure
  against the committed model in a browser before treating this as a finding.

## Watch out for

- **Do not auto-layout.** ADR-level decision, repeated in several places: tables
  land on a grid and the drag is what writes the coordinates. Anything here that
  moves a box the developer placed is out of scope.
- **`.scene >` is the convention** and `npm run check:scenes` enforces it. Two
  scenes once shared a stylesheet and it broke the page twice in one day.
- Whatever changes, the edges must still leave and arrive at the rows of the two
  columns and stay on those rows when a box moves. That was the owner's first
  complaint and it is the half that is hard.
notes:
Grounded the one remaining observation rather than leaving it as an impression: neither src/studio/client/edges.ts nor canvas.ts mentions onDelete or onUpdate anywhere, so the edge renderer genuinely has no access to the referential action at the point it draws. That is a fact about the code rather than about a screenshot, and it is the one claim in this epic that did not come from looking at a picture.
Two of the four bullets were measured against the owner's uncommitted layout edits and are corrected in the description above rather than here, on purpose: a correction that sits below a false claim is read second, and this item exists to be read by the owner once. The shipments overlap is false by arithmetic and is now stated as such. The fit reading is marked as needing re-measurement rather than being replaced with a number I cannot currently verify. The two bullets that were never geometric, the edge that says nothing about a delete and every box looking equally important, are unaffected and their recommendations stand.

title: A file one folder too deep is read by nobody and reported by nobody
description:
Found by driving on 2026-09-07. **A model can lose two paragraphs of
hand-written prose and still call itself healthy.**

Move `examples/shop`'s two notes into `notes/archive/` and nothing else:

```
$ dbmd check shop
shop: 8 tables, 0 notes, 1 group, no problems.
$ echo $?
0
```

The files are there. Nothing read them and nothing said so. `0 notes` is the
only signal, and it is a number nobody checks against a memory of what the
model used to hold.

This is the shape gotchas.md already records from the junctioned-`tables/` bug:
*not a malformed model, a correct one the tool refused to read and then called
healthy.* Same class, one level down, and still open.

## It is worse for notes than for tables or groups, because nothing points at a note

- **`tables/billing/orders.md`** gives two `ref-table-unknown` errors saying
  there is no `tables/orders.md`. True, and it names the consequence rather than
  the cause: nothing says there is a file at `tables/billing/orders.md` that was
  not read.
- **`groups/old/warehouse.md`** gives `group-unknown` on the table that joined
  it. Same shape.
- **`notes/archive/*.md`** gives **nothing at all**, because a note is what
  nothing references. The prose simply is not in the model.

## The reader already has the vocabulary, one level up

A stray directory at the model root is a warning today:

```
scratch
    warning  `scratch/` is not a kind of object dbmd knows; its files are ignored (unknown-kind-directory)
```

So the asymmetry is the argument. `read.ts` warns about an unread directory
beside `tables/` and is silent about one inside it.

## Flat is deliberate, and that is not the question

`docs/format.md` line 1224 and ADR 0003 both say table files are flat. Neither
is being overturned. But that same sentence reads **"Subdirectories under
`tables/` are the way out and nobody has needed one yet"**, which is an
invitation to try one, and somebody with a hundred tables will. What they must
not get is silence.

## Watch out for

- **`docs/format.md` is executable.** A new diagnostic code needs a row in its
  per-code table, and a test asserts every `ModelDiagnosticCode` has one and that
  the counts match. Adding the code without the row fails the build, which is the
  gate working.
- **Do not start reading subdirectories.** That is a format change, it collides
  with the flat-file rule ADR 0003 argues for, and the item is a diagnostic.
- **A directory that is not there is not an error.** A model with no `notes/` at
  all is normal and must stay silent.
- Decide whether the warning names the directory or each unread file, and say
  why. Naming the files is more useful and more noise for a `.git` that somebody
  has somehow put in the wrong place.
- Check what the studio does with it, since it reads through the same reader and
  shows diagnostics in its own panel.
close_reason: Landed as PR #123. I drove the case myself: on main the notes-one-folder-deep model reported no problems at exit 0, and on the branch it is one error naming the directory, a real file as evidence and the fix, at exit 1. The three quiet cases stay quiet, including the documented opt-out of a dot-prefixed directory. The tables case shows the new cause beside both existing consequence errors rather than replacing them. The rule that decides the boundary is the good part: the claim belongs to the .md name rather than to the directory, which is ADR 0040's own sentence with a folder in front of it, so a subdirectory of images or a stray README stays nobody's business.

title: A file another program has open is reported as a file somebody else edited
description:
Found by driving the studio on Windows with a real exclusive lock, the kind an
editor, OneDrive, a backup agent or antivirus takes routinely. **No data is
lost and nothing gets stuck.** What is wrong is that the studio says something
it already knows to be false, in the same breath as saying the true thing.

## What happens

A studio page is open. Something else opens `tables/orders.md` with
`FileShare.None`. Edit that table in the page:

- `PATCH /api/table/orders` answers **200**.
- The flush reports a conflict, and this is its whole message:

  > `tables/orders.md` changed on disk after the studio read it, so writing over
  > it would lose that change. The studio has reloaded the file and dropped its
  > own edit to it; make the edit again if you still want it

- **The file did not change.** I diffed it against the original afterwards and it
  was byte-identical the entire time.
- **`make the edit again` is wrong advice.** The next edit fails identically
  until the lock clears, so a person who follows it loops.

Once the lock is released the next edit writes normally, so this is a wrong
sentence rather than a broken state.

## The studio already knows the real answer

At that same moment `/api/model` carries the truth in its diagnostics, and the
page shows it in the panel:

```
error  file-unreadable  cannot read the file: the file is in use (EBUSY)
```

So a person is looking at two messages two inches apart. One says the file is in
use by another program. The other says somebody edited it and their change would
be lost. Only one of them happened.

## Why it happens, which is a one-line conflation

`write()` in `src/studio/edits.ts` decides a refusal like this:

```ts
const disk = await readModel(this.dir)
const refused = [...this.writing].filter(
  (path) => renderOf(disk.model, path) !== renderOf(this.adopted.model, path),
)
```

`readModel` does not throw on a locked file. It returns a model with a
`file-unreadable` diagnostic and **that table missing**, so `renderOf` differs,
so the path takes the conflict branch. **"Absent because it could not be read"
and "present and different" are the same thing to that comparison**, and they
are opposite facts about somebody's disk.

## What a fix has to keep

- **The refusal itself is right.** Writing over a file the studio could not read
  is exactly what should not happen. Do not turn this into a write.
- **The recovery is right.** ADR 0004's rule that there is no state but the files
  is why the refused edit is dropped rather than held, and that argument does not
  change because the reason changed.
- The two answers should agree. The reader already distinguishes unreadable from
  changed; the writer is the layer that flattens them.

## Watch out for

- **Do not reach for a diagnostic code comparison alone.** A file can be
  unreadable for reasons other than a lock, and a message naming a lock when the
  cause was a permission change would be the same mistake with a different face.
  Say what the reader said.
- `EBUSY` is what Windows gives here. POSIX will not produce it for the same
  gesture, so any test has to be honest about which platform it proves.
- dbmd-c5g just rewrote the page's stale-edit sentence to be about a person.
  Whatever this says should sit beside that one without contradicting it.
notes: Not dispatched yet, and the reason is collision rather than doubt. It changes write() in src/studio/edits.ts, and dbmd-6yo is in that same file right now deciding what body a newly created table gets. Dispatch this once dbmd-6yo has landed. Nothing else is queued behind it.
close_reason: Landed as PR #124. I drove it on Windows with a real exclusive lock: the refusal now repeats the reader's own clause, names no cause, and carries reason: unreadable so the page switches on a code rather than on prose. The file was byte-identical by sha256 through the whole sequence, recovery landed once the lock cleared, and the genuine hand-edit case is word for word unchanged. The agent found the case I had missed: a drag sends several patches, so the one after the refused flush came back stale and put the changed-on-disk sentence over a conflicts entry saying the opposite. They fixed the heading above the list as well as the entry inside it.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text: Fixed on studio/e6e-a-locked-file-is-not-a-conflict, PR #124. The writer now asks the reader which refusal it is holding (file-unreadable at the path, or at the kind directory that would not list) and repeats what the reader said, naming no cause. WireConflict gained reason: changed | unreadable; the delete route raises a new 'unreadable' code; the page got a second sentence beside dbmd-c5g's and the summary line no longer claims every refusal was a change on disk. ADR 0019 amended by appending. Driven on Windows with a real FileShare.None lock: the file is byte-identical throughout, the recovery still lands once the lock clears, and the genuine hand-edit conflict still says the old sentence. Two follow-ups found and left alone: the carried-forward object still says 'did not parse' in the incomplete refusal, the canvas and the inspector, which needs the page to know why an object is incomplete; and nothing wakes the studio when a lock is released, because a release is not a filesystem event.

title: Publish dbmd to npm, and make every page that says it is unpublished true again
description:
The owner answered on 2026-09-07: "Yes let's publish to npm".

`package.json` carries `"private": true` on purpose and that line comes out.
`check:pack` already builds a tarball, installs it, starts the studio from it
and asks that studio for its page, its bundle and its model, so the package
being correct is proven. What is not proven is that `npx dbmd` resolves for a
stranger, and only a real publish proves that.

## The publish itself is the owner's hand on the trigger, not the loop's

Do not publish. Build the path and say exactly what the owner must do. A
workflow that publishes on a pushed tag is the shape: the token is a repository
secret only they can add, and a loop that can publish to a public registry is a
loop that can publish a mistake to a public registry.

## Four pages currently say the tool is not on npm, and all four become false

`README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/ci.md`. The last one is
the sharpest: it says the CI recipe does not run as written for exactly this
reason. A false claim in `AGENTS.md` is already why a CI recipe invented a
version number once, so this is the same failure with the sign flipped. Every
one of them moves in the commit that makes it false, or none of them do.

## Watch out for

- **Versioning.** The package has never been released, so the first version is
  a decision. Say which and why.
- **The `files` allowlist and the `bin` entry** decide what a stranger gets.
  `check:pack` is the thing that already tests this; extend it rather than
  trusting a listing.
- **The name was free as of 2026-09-07.** Confirm it still is before writing a
  page that assumes it.
close_reason: Landed as PR #118. I verified the finding the design rests on rather than taking it: npm publish --dry-run with private: true still set exits 0, prints the file listing and ends '+ dbmd@0.0.0' without ever mentioning private. So a dry run is not a rehearsal. I then set the line back on the branch and check:pack failed with exit 1 naming the reason, which is the layer that survives somebody re-adding it. Sent back once for an appended section on ADR 0024, which the repo's own rule requires and which also caught a second superseded paragraph I had not named. Nothing is published: the token and the tag are the owner's.

title: dbmd refs does not say which refs cascade, which is the question it exists for
description:
`dbmd refs` answers "what points at this table". ADR 0042 says why it exists:
**you ask it immediately before a delete.**

`on delete` landed after it, so nothing wired them together. The model now knows
which of those refs cascade and the command does not say.

```
$ dbmd refs orders examples/shop
  order_items.order_id -> orders.id  tables/order_items.md  key required

$ grep -A1 'ref: orders.id' examples/shop/tables/order_items.md
    ref: orders.id
    on delete: cascade
```

`--json` is the same: an incoming ref carries `from`, `to`, `path` and
`inPrimaryKey`, and nothing about the action.

So a person asks the tool what happens if they delete a row, and the tool tells
them which files reference it and **not which of them will lose rows.** That is
the difference between "three tables point here" and "three tables point here and
one of them empties when you delete".

## Why this is worth a P2 rather than a P4

The two marks `refs` already prints, `key` and `required`, exist because ADR 0042
argues that "three referrers" is not actionable and what you need is what to edit.
**`on delete` is the same argument one step further**: it is the difference
between retargeting a ref and losing rows, and it is now a fact the model holds.

## Scope

Carry the action into both forms. The prose has room beside `key` and
`required`; `--json` should carry it on the ref rather than as another mark,
because it is a value from a closed vocabulary rather than a flag.

## Watch out for

- **`on update` is the same fact and should arrive in the same breath.** ADR 0046
  refused to hold one clause and not the other, and the same reasoning applies to
  showing them.
- **Absent and `no action` are different facts** and a real catalogue reports
  both. ADR 0046 is explicit about that. Do not print `no action` where the file
  says nothing.
- **Do not make the marks longer than the answer.** Four marks on every line is a
  table nobody reads. Consider whether `no action` and a missing clause should
  both be silent, and say what you chose.
- **`refs` must still answer on a model that does not validate**, which is the
  gap it was built for: half way through a rename, `dbmd export` refuses and
  `refs` answers. Whatever you add must not need the validator.
- `src/cli/refs.ts` is the command; `Ref` in `src/model/types.ts` now holds both
  clauses.
close_reason: Landed as PR #117. Both clauses print beside the row that carries them and ride --json as omitted-when-absent siblings of path. I reproduced the mid-rename case myself: dbmd export refuses with 2 errors and dbmd refs answers with on delete: restrict on both surviving rows. I also mutated the source to hide 'no action', which is the alternative ADR 0049 refuses, and two tests failed including the mid-rename one, so the absent-is-not-no-action distinction is held by a test rather than by intent.

title: The validator's expression advice loops when the name is already the mapping spelling
description:
`index-column-unknown` teaches the expression spelling, which is right, and
**wraps whatever it was given**, which is wrong when what it was given is already
the mapping spelling.

Reproduced end to end:

```
columns: ["{ expression: lower(display_name) }"]
  error  ... write it as `{ expression: { expression: lower(display_name) } }`

columns: [{ expression: { expression: lower(display_name) } }]
  error  `expression` must be a string, but YAML read `{ expression: ... }` as a
         mapping; quote it
```

**Quote it and you get the first. Follow the first and you get the second.**
There is no exit inside the tool.

## Why a person lands there

Found by the dbmd-vdh agent, and it is the likeliest path rather than a contrived
one. The studio's panel prints a held expression key as
`{ expression: lower(email) }` in a read-only row and puts an editable field
directly beneath it, so the shortest route from "I want one of those" to a
keystroke is to copy the line above. ADR 0047 records why the panel will not
learn to write these, and PR #110 fixed the studio half: the row now says the
field holds the mapping spelling. **The validator still gives the looping
advice**, and it is what a person editing a file by hand meets.

## Scope

When the unknown column name is itself the mapping spelling, say the quotes are
the problem rather than offering another wrapper. Something like: this is a
quoted string, so it is a column name; remove the quotes.

## Watch out for

- **Do not stop teaching the spelling.** The message is one of the best in the
  tool for the ordinary case, where somebody typed `lower(email)`, and dbmd-vdh's
  whole argument rests on the validator still judging column names.
- **Do not guess.** A column genuinely called `{ expression: x }` is legal and
  reachable, and the file escapes it by quoting the scalar. ADR 0022 and ADR 0026
  both refuse to guess about names, and ADR 0047 refuses it one level up. Saying
  what it looks like is not guessing; rewriting it would be.
- **`docs/format.md` needs a look in the same breath.** It calls the panel's
  read-only row "temporary" and tells readers to wait for it to go away. ADR 0047
  makes it the decision rather than a waiting room.
- The message and its wrapper live in `src/model/validate.ts`.
close_reason: PR #114 merged: the advice now says remove the quotes, following it arrives, and the ordinary case is byte-identical.

title: The truncation message is wrong for both engines, and its test breaks on a reflow
description:
Two halves, both surfaced by dbmd-pqd and both left alone because they sat in
another branch's files.

## The message

`src/cli/import.ts` still tells everyone the same thing when `JSON.parse` fails:

> The usual cause is a paste that stopped early.

That was written when truncation was the likeliest arrival. It is now wrong for
**both** documented routes, and wrong in the same direction:

- **sqlcmd** appends `(1 rows affected)`, so the file is too **long** and the
  failure is at the end.
- **psql** without `-t` writes a header and a rule of dashes, so the file is too
  long **and the failure is at the front**, before any of the JSON has been read.

dbmd-4cp and dbmd-pqd each answered this in their own engine's comment block,
which is where a user who has just run the command is looking. The shared
message still sends everybody hunting a truncation.

The position `dbmd import` already prints separates the cases: a failure at
position 0 is not a paste that stopped early.

## The test

`test/import/sqlserver.test.ts` asserts that prose **raw**, with `/stopped
early/`. So rewrapping the paragraph turns the build red, which teaches people
not to improve the paragraph.

dbmd-pqd's own guards assert against the block with markers stripped and
whitespace flattened, so a reflow is not a red build and a deletion is. **That is
the shape to copy.**

## Watch out for

- **Do not lose the truncation advice.** It is still right for a copy out of a
  grid, which is the route the SQL Server block spends most of its length warning
  about. The message needs to name more than one cause, or to use the position it
  already has to choose between them.
- **A message that names a cause it cannot know is worse than one that names
  none.** If the position does not distinguish the cases reliably, say so and
  give the shape of a correct file instead, which is what dbmd-pqd's block
  settled on for clients it could not test.
- Both engines' comment blocks now answer this locally. Whatever the shared
  message becomes, it must not contradict them.
close_reason: PR #100 merged: four cases decided from the file's shape, because two of the three real shapes carry no position at all. The reflow/delete pair verified both ways.

title: Nothing notices a command that exists and is not documented
description:
`check:commands` fails the build when documentation names a command that does not
exist. **Nothing checks the other direction**, and the other direction went wrong
twice today.

When `dbmd query` shipped, `README.md` kept a heading reading **"The five
commands"** over five entries while the CLI had six, and kept a sentence saying
that printing the introspection query from dbmd is "still open work", which had
just stopped being true. Both survived every check in the gate and were found by
an agent building an unrelated command.

The same thing will happen the next time a command lands. It already happened
twice: `dbmd import` left the README saying the import path was unfinished, and
`dbmd query` left it undercounting.

## Scope

Fail the build when a command in the CLI registry has no entry in `README.md`.
The registry is the authority, the way it already is for `check:commands`.

## Watch out for

- **The count in a heading is the fragile part**, and it is what actually broke.
  Consider whether the check should read the heading, or whether the heading
  should stop carrying a number. **A heading that cannot go stale is better than
  a check that notices it has**, and that may be the whole fix.
- **Do not require a section per command in every document.** `AGENTS.md` names
  the commands in a sentence and `docs/ci.md` names two of them on purpose.
  `README.md` is the one that promises to document them all, and it should be the
  only file this applies to unless you can say why.
- **`check:commands` is the model to follow**, including its treatment of the
  hypothetical marker and its habit of naming exclusions in an ADR rather than
  leaving them quiet. Read `scripts/check-commands.mjs` before writing a second
  scanner; the two may want to be one.
- **Prove it fails** in `test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts`, by adding a
  command to the registry in a scratch copy without documenting it. ADR 0034.
- The gate is long already. Say what this adds.
close_reason: PR #93 merged: the heading stopped counting and the entries got a check. Distance is what goes stale, which is why the rule is README-only.

title: The Postgres query says nothing about how to save its result, and the obvious way fails
description:
dbmd-4cp fixed the SQL Server recipe, which was wrong. **The Postgres one is not
wrong; it is absent, and the obvious command fails.**

`dbmd query --engine postgres` says only "Save that value to a file." Run the
obvious thing and `dbmd import` refuses:

```
$ psql -U postgres -f query.sql -o out.json
$ dbmd import --file out.json --dir out
dbmd: out.json is not JSON: Unexpected token 'd', ..."          dbmd_intro"... is not valid JSON
```

Verified on `postgres:16`. psql's default output is a header row of dashes, the
value padded into a fixed-width column, and a `(1 row)` footer. Adding `-t -A`
produces a file that imports first try and passes `dbmd check --strict`, also
verified.

So the asymmetry between the two engines is **not** "SQL Server ships a fragile
command and Postgres is safe". It is "SQL Server ships a command that can be
wrong and Postgres ships none", and both users hit the same class of failure. The
SQL Server user at least had something to correct.

## Scope

Give the Postgres query the same treatment: name the routes and give the
invocation that works. ADR 0041 states the position that applies here and calls
this change owed.

## Watch out for

- **`-t -A` is the pair that matters**, and say why: `-t` drops the header and
  footer, `-A` stops the padding. Either alone leaves a file that fails.
- **The message a user gets is misleading in the same way it was for SQL
  Server.** "The usual cause is a paste that stopped early" is what they see, and
  the file is too long rather than too short. dbmd-4cp rewrote that sentence for
  the SQL Server block; check whether the general message needs the same care.
- **Do not add a `SET`-style statement to the query.** dbmd-4cp established why
  for SQL Server: `test/import/sqlserver.test.ts` asserts a forbidden keyword
  list, the query's own comment claims it contains nothing of the kind, and a
  second statement breaks clients that run the statement under the cursor.
  Whatever the Postgres equivalent is, the recipe is the place to fix it.
- **The pgAdmin and DBeaver routes are the ones most people use** and are not
  testable from here. Say which you tested and do not turn "probably fine" into a
  result. dbmd-4cp left the SSMS routes untested and said so.
- **Nothing in the SQL may change.** dbmd-4cp's check was that
  `grep -v '^--'` over the diff comes to nothing, so the committed fixture is
  still real output from the query that produced it. Do the same.
close_reason: PR #92 merged: the recipe ships -X -t -A, each justified by measurement. My brief was wrong that -t alone fails, and the psqlrc override is real once a width is set.

title: The sqlcmd recipe the SQL Server query prints does not work
description:
`dbmd query --engine sqlserver` prints a comment block telling the user how to
save its result. One of the two routes it gives is:

```
--   * sqlcmd: `sqlcmd -S server -d yourdb -y 0 -Y 0 -i query.sql -o model.json`.
--     Without -y 0 sqlcmd truncates at 256 characters.
```

**Run exactly that and `dbmd import` refuses the file.**

Verified end to end on 2026-09-07 against a real SQL Server 2022 (16.0.4265.3) in
a container, following the printed instruction verbatim:

```
$ sqlcmd ... -y 0 -Y 0 -i query.sql -o model.json
$ dbmd import --file model.json --dir out
dbmd: model.json is not JSON: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON at position 2315
```

The cause is not truncation and not the provider. sqlcmd appends its row-count
line to the output file:

```
...NO_ACTION"}]}]}\n\n(1 rows affected)\n
```

2333 bytes, of which the JSON is the first 2315. **The payload is perfect.** Cut
the trailing 18 bytes and the same file imports, `dbmd check` is clean and
`--strict` exits 0, with `nvarchar(max)`, `datetimeoffset(7)`, `decimal(12,2)`
and the composite unique index all correct.

## Why this matters more than its size

This is the **first step of the journey** for one of the two supported engines,
and the instruction is one this tool prints itself. A user follows it, gets a
parse error, and the message they get says "the usual cause is a paste that
stopped early" — which is true in general and wrong here. They will go looking
for a truncation that did not happen.

It is also the message `dbmd import` points at when it says "the comment above
the query you ran says how to save its result rather than copy it". That
cross-reference was built deliberately and it currently points at a recipe that
fails.

## The fix, proven

Prepending `set nocount on;` to the query makes the same invocation produce 2314
bytes ending `}]}]}\n`, which imports first try. Tested.

## Watch out for

- **The query is deliberately "one statement and no meta-commands"** so it pastes
  whole into SSMS, DBeaver and a JDBC console alike. `SET NOCOUNT ON` is a second
  statement. Check that adding it does not break the paste-whole property those
  clients rely on, and if it does, fix the recipe rather than the query.
- **`-h -1` also suppresses the row count and conflicts with `-y 0`.** sqlcmd
  refuses both together, so that is not the way out.
- **The "Save Results As" route through SSMS is probably fine** and is how this
  was verified before. Check it rather than assuming, and say which routes you
  tested.
- **The Postgres query does not have this problem** because it gives no client
  invocation at all, only "save that value to a file". Consider whether that
  asymmetry is right: one engine gets a copyable command that must stay correct,
  the other gets none.
- The query text lives in `src/import/providers/sqlserver.ts` as
  `INTROSPECTION_QUERY`, and `dbmd query` prints it verbatim.
close_reason: PR #86 merged: the recipe is fixed rather than the query, because an existing test already forbids SET in it. Verified the guard fails on a revert to the one-file form.

title: A class name used by both the canvas and the inspector has now broken the page twice
description:
The studio's stylesheet is one block for two independent scenes: the canvas, and
the inspector panel. **A bare class selector matches both**, and on 2026-09-07
that cost two defects hours apart.

- **dbmd-34.** The canvas note element used class `note`, which `#inspector .note`
  also matched. Every explanatory sentence in the panel became absolutely
  positioned and stacked in the page corner. Fixed by renaming the canvas element
  to `note-card`.
- **dbmd-49.** `.notes` was the canvas note *layer* and the inspector's red
  validation paragraph, and the unscoped rule was
  `position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0`. Neither `#inspector .notes` rule sets
  `position`, so nothing overrode it. **Every red validation paragraph in the
  panel had been rendering behind the toolbar**, including the create form's
  "there is already a table called ...". Fixed by scoping the three scene layers
  to `.scene >`.

Singular and plural, one character apart, found by two agents who did not know
about each other. **Twice is a property of the system rather than an incident**,
and the second one hid a message the studio was relying on a user reading.

Neither was visible in a diff or in a test. Both were found by driving the page
and noticing something in the wrong place.

## What is wanted

Something that fails the build when a class name is used by both `canvas.ts` and
`inspector.ts` and the stylesheet has a rule for it that is not scoped to one of
