them. That is checkable without a browser: the class names each file uses are in
the source, and the intersection is what matters.

## Watch out for

- **A shared name is not automatically wrong.** A utility class that both scenes
  are meant to share is fine; what is wrong is a shared name with an unscoped
  rule. The check has to distinguish those, and the simplest honest version may
  be to require every rule in the canvas block to be scoped, rather than to
  reason about intent.
- **`.scene >` is now the convention** and `note-card` is the other half of the
  answer. Whatever you build should make the convention enforceable rather than
  replace it.
- **The comment already in that stylesheet describes the first collision.** Read
  it before designing; it is the closest thing to a statement of the rule.
- **Prove it fails**, in `test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts`, by unscoping a
  rule in a scratch copy. ADR 0034: a guard is not believed until it has been
  seen to fail.
- The studio's stylesheet lives inside `src/studio/client/index.html`, so a CSS
  parser is not available for free. Say what you used and why it is good enough.
close_reason: PR #79 merged: the intersection is checked and anchored, nothing in the stylesheet moved, and .name and .type turned out to be shared and safe only by accident.

title: Nothing checks that a command the documentation names exists
description:
`dbmd query` was named by four error messages, the opening line of
`docs/import-format.md`, ADR 0007 and `AGENTS.md`. It did not exist, and the tool
rejected it as an unknown command. It survived because every reference agreed
with every other, so there was nothing inconsistent to notice.

I swept the whole repository by hand afterwards. **It is the only one**, and the
sweep is the point: nothing repeats it.

What I checked, across every tracked markdown file:

- every `npm run <script>` against `package.json`
- every `node scripts/<name>.mjs` against the filesystem
- every `dbmd <subcommand>` against the CLI's command list

All clean today. The three apparent misses are `dbmd fmt` and `dbmd fix`, and
each is explicitly written as hypothetical: "a future `dbmd fmt`", "That is a
`dbmd fix` command".

## Scope

A check that fails the build when documentation names a command, script or npm
task that does not exist. It belongs beside `check:adr` and `check:reviewable`,
and `test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts` is where its own failure is proved.

## Watch out for

- **The hard part is the hypothetical reference, and it is the whole design.** A
  record that says "a future `dbmd fmt` will want this" is correct and must not
  fail the build. Deciding how to tell those apart is this item. A marker the
  author writes is honest and costs a convention; inferring it from nearby words
  like "future" or "would" is clever and will be wrong.
- **Consider inverting it.** Rather than parsing prose for commands, take the
  known list and check every reference resolves. That is the same job with a
  much smaller surface, since the set of commands is small and closed.
- **Prose is full of false positives.** My own sweep matched "dbmd describes",
  "dbmd reads", "dbmd can". Anything matching a bare `dbmd <word>` will need to
  distinguish a command from a verb, which is another argument for the inversion
  above.
- **Do not check decision records for currency.** A record describes what was
  true when it was decided and this repository never edits one. If the check
  cannot tell a stale record from a stale instruction, exclude
  `docs/architecture/decisions/` and say so.
- **Fail with the file and the line.** A build that says "something in the docs
  names a command that does not exist" is worse than the defect.
- **Prove it can fail**, in the guards suite: name a command that does not exist
  in a scratch copy of a page and watch the check refuse. That suite exists
  precisely so a new guard is not believed until it has been seen to fail
  (ADR 0034).
close_reason: PR #73 merged: a backtick is the claim, a marker is the exemption and it is checked in both directions. 233 references, zero false positives.

title: Nothing checks that the checks can fail
description:
ADR 0001 makes a handful of scripts the layer that decides what lands. Every one
of them was mutation-tested by hand on 2026-09-07 and every one failed correctly:

| Guard | Mutation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check-reviewable.mjs` | NUL byte in a tracked file | exit 1, names the file and the offset |
| `check-adr-numbers.mjs` | two records claiming 0033 | exit 1, names both files |
| `check:pack` | `dist/studio/client/**` excluded from `files` | exit 1, says the page would be blank |
| the init scaffold's guard | `pk: true` removed | one test red |
| `guard-merge.mjs --probe` | run directly | refused, which is the answer |

**That is the problem, not the reassurance.** All of it is true today because
somebody spent an hour breaking things on purpose, and nothing repeats it. The
scaffold guard in that table is in the list precisely because it spent weeks
unable to fail: removing the primary key left 622 tests green until dbmd-54.

This repository has now found **four** tests that had stopped testing something.
The guards are the last line, and they are the least exercised code in the tree,
because a guard that never fires looks identical to a guard that cannot.

## Scope

A suite that breaks each guard on purpose in a scratch copy and asserts it
fails. Not a rewrite of the guards.

## Watch out for

- **Assert the exit code and something about the message.** dbmd-54 is the
  precedent: a smoke test that could not see a warning was made to read the
  words. A guard that exits 1 for the wrong reason is still broken.
- **Each mutation must be reverted even when the assertion fails**, or one red
  test leaves the tree dirty and every later run is meaningless. A scratch copy
  or a worktree is safer than mutate-and-restore in place.
- **`check:pack` is slow**, since it builds a tarball, installs it and starts the
  studio. It may deserve to be opt-in rather than part of every `npm run check`.
  Decide and say which; do not silently make the common path slower.
- **Do not test `merge-pr.mjs` by merging anything.** Its refusals are the
  interesting part and they are reachable without a merge: behind, red, stale.
- **`guard-merge.mjs --probe` cannot be tested from inside a test**, because the
  thing it detects is a hook in the harness rather than anything in the tree.
  Leave it out and say so, rather than writing something that passes vacuously.
- The studio agent holds `src/studio/` and `test/studio/`. This item is
  `scripts/` and a new test file.
close_reason: PR #58 merged: 15 tests plus a pack-guard wrapper, verified by neutering two guards and by disabling only the bundle assertion to prove the wrong-reason case is caught.

title: A blank line in the model union silently shrinks what format.md guarantees
description:
`test/docs/format.test.ts` reads `ModelDiagnosticCode` out of the source and
asserts every member has a row in `docs/format.md`. It slices the union at the
**first blank line**, which makes the formatting of that declaration
load-bearing in a way nobody would guess.

**Reproduced against `main`.** A blank line inserted at `src/diagnostics.ts:130`,
which is the kind of thing somebody does to space out a long doc comment, drops
`primary-key-missing` and `group-empty` from the checked set:

```
Tests  14 passed (14)
```

Fourteen passing, and the guarantee now covers two fewer codes than it says it
does. Nothing reports anything.

**The sanity guard only catches the gross case.** `expect(codes.length)
.toBeGreaterThan(10)` does fire if the blank line lands near the top of the
union: a blank line at line 49 truncates the list to one and the test fails with
`expected 1 to be greater than 10`. Near the bottom, the count stays above ten
and it passes. So the guard makes this look defended while leaving the realistic
case open, which is worse than having no guard, because it is the reason nobody
looks again.

This is the fourth test in this repository found to have stopped testing
something, and the second one whose failure mode is a guarantee quietly covering
less than it claims.

## The fix already exists in this repository

`test/import/docs.test.ts`, added by dbmd-46, slices at the **next top-level
`export`** instead. I planted the same blank line inside `ImportDiagnosticCode`
and it still found all fifteen codes. Copy that.

## Watch out for

- **Add the reverse direction while you are there.** The import-half test asserts
  every row also names a real code, and the model-half test does not. That is the
  case a rename produces: the page keeps a row for a code that no longer exists,
  and a reader looks up something that cannot happen.
- **Then delete the `toBeGreaterThan(10)` line, or replace it with the real
  count.** Once the slice is robust the guard defends nothing, and a control that
  no longer prevents anything is a maintenance cost pretending to be safety.
- **Prove it the way this was proved.** Plant the blank line near the end of the
  union, not the start, and show the test going red. A fix verified with a blank
  line at the top would pass for the wrong reason.
- `src/diagnostics.ts` holds both unions plus `DiagnosticCode`, so check whether
  the new slice stops at the right `export` for the first union rather than
  running into the second.
close_reason: PR #53 merged: slices at the next top-level export, matches a table row rather than a substring, and asserts the exact count of 30.

title: The README says the import path is not finished, and it is
description:
`dbmd import` landed on 2026-09-07 in PR #45. The README has not caught up, in
two separate places.

**It calls the command unfinished.** Under "What it does not do":

> **It does not connect to a database.** Not to read one and not to write one.
> The import path, **which is not finished**, reads a JSON file that a person
> produced by running a query themselves...

The surrounding paragraph is right and should stay: dbmd genuinely does not
connect to a database, and that is a decision rather than a gap. Only the clause
is wrong.

**It documents four commands and there are five.** The reference section has
entries for `dbmd init`, `dbmd studio`, `dbmd check` and `dbmd export`, and none
for `dbmd import`. `AGENTS.md` already says five.

## Why this is worth an item rather than a quiet fix

A stated invariant that is not true is worse than an absent one, and this
repository has already paid for that exactly once: `AGENTS.md` claimed the
package was published to npm, and a CI recipe then invented a version number to
match. This is the same defect in the same class of file.

It is also the worst possible claim to have stale. A reader deciding whether the
tool is worth trying meets "not finished" next to the feature that closes the
whole argument, which is that a database becomes markdown becomes a picture you
can drag.

## Watch out for

- **`dbmd import` writes the engine's own type with its modifier**, not the
  normalised vocabulary. `character varying(32)`, `nvarchar(max)`, `order_state`.
  That is ADR 0029 and it is what a user's first diff looks like, so the entry
  should show one.
- **The refusal to write into a non-empty directory names dbmd-42**, which is
  the difference between unimplemented and forbidden. Worth a sentence, because
  re-import is the obvious next question a reader will have.
- **Do not promise a `dbmd query` command.** `introspectionQuery()` exists in the
  source and the command does not.
- Every command the README names should be run and its real output pasted, which
  is the standard dbmd-51 set for that file. Do not write it from the ADRs.
- The README was being edited by the dbmd-34 agent when this was filed, for the
  separate reason that it promises notes and groups the canvas does not draw.
  **Check whether that landed first and build on it.**
close_reason: PR #57 merged: the unfinished clause is gone, dbmd import is documented as the fifth command, and it does not promise dbmd query.

title: A composite foreign key warns twice on every import
description:
Import a real database with a composite foreign key and `dbmd check` reports two
`ref-target-not-unique` warnings, one per column. Both are true. The format
declares a relationship per column and has no way to say that a pair of columns
is unique together, so the validator is correct and the model is correct and the
output is still noise.

The consequence is specific: a freshly imported model is never *silent*, only
error-free, and `dbmd check --strict` fails it. That makes the first thing a new
user does produce warnings they cannot act on, which teaches them that warnings
here are decoration.

Found by dbmd-41 against the SQL Server fixture, which is real catalogue output.

## Watch out for

Two shapes, and they are different decisions rather than two implementations of
one.

- **A composite ref in the format.** Says the true thing, and it is a format
  change: `docs/format.md` is executable, so every fenced block and the
  round-trip writer move with it. It also changes what the studio has to draw,
  because an edge would stop being one column to one column.
- **A validator that recognises a covering set.** No format change: if the refs
  from a table name a set of columns that together are the target's key, warn
  once or not at all. Cheaper, and it leaves the model unable to *say* the thing
  while quietly knowing it.

Prefer the second unless somebody wants composite refs for their own sake.

Do not silence the code. It is right in the single-column case and that is the
common one.
close_reason: PR #48 merged: a covering set silences the composite case; verified that no-key, partial-cover, laundering and expression-key cases all still warn.

title: One file-name rule, spelled once
description:
﻿The studio spells the file-name rule a second time, now that the writer owns it.

Flagged by the dbmd-19/23 agent, who could not fix it because another agent held
`src/studio/` at the time:

> `isSafeSegment` should become `isFileName` plus its two suspicions.

## What changed under it

dbmd-23 moved `isFileName` out of `src/model/write.ts`, where it was private, into
`src/model/paths.ts`, and made it refuse everything `open` refuses on any
platform: `< > : " / \ | ? *`, control characters, and a name too long. The
sentence that settled it is in ADR 0026: **a name the writer cannot write is a
fact about the model however far down the stack it surfaces**, so it is a
`WriteSkip` naming the object rather than an exception.

`src/studio/safe-path.ts` predates that and carries its own `isSafeSegment`, which
overlaps most of it and then adds two refusals of its own: Windows device names,
and trailing dots or spaces. Those two are **suspicion at an HTTP boundary**
rather than duplication, and dbmd-18''s review established they should stay: the
server takes names from a web page and cannot know which path handling the next
reader of the directory will use.

`src/studio/edits.ts` already imports from `paths.ts`, so the seam exists.

## The live consequence, which is small and real

**The studio''s length limit is now looser than the writer''s.** The studio allows
255 characters; the writer refuses beyond 210, because its own temporary file is
42 characters longer than the file it stands in for. So a 230-character table
name is accepted over HTTP and then silently skipped by the writer.

Nobody will type one. It disappears the moment the two rules are one.

## Scope

- `isSafeSegment` becomes `isFileName` plus the studio''s two extra refusals.
- **Keep the studio''s refusals and keep them labelled as suspicion**, with the
  reason. Deleting them would be reading this item as "make them identical",
  which it is not.
- The studio''s message is good and users see it. Whatever the shared rule
  refuses, the HTTP answer should still explain it in the studio''s own words.

## Watch out for

- **Do not weaken the writer to match the studio, or the reverse.** They are
  deliberately different at the edges and the same in the middle.
- The reader also has a rule, that a file whose name starts with `.` is not part
  of a model. That is a **third** thing and not part of this: dbmd-36 established
  that the reader and a directory listing want different halves of it.
- `docs/format.md` has a naming section describing both layers and what each
  refuses. If the numbers change, it changes.
close_reason: PR #63 merged: one decision point, and it closed a silent 201 for five characters the writer refuses. Reproduced on main before merging.

title: CI builds on a Node that is past end of life
description:
﻿The project builds and tests on a Node that is past end of life.

Observed by the dbmd-53 agent while moving the workflows off a deprecated
*action* runtime, and deliberately left alone there because it is a different
question:

> `node-version: 20` is untouched in all three workflows — that is the project''s
> own Node, not the action runtime, and `package.json` says `>=20`. Node 20 is
> past end of life even though the actions no longer run on it.

## The two things this is about, and they are separable

1. **What CI builds and tests on.** All three workflows pin `node-version: 20`.
   That is the version every pull request is judged on, and it no longer receives
   security fixes.
2. **What the package claims to support.** `package.json` says `"node": ">=20"`,
   which is a promise to users rather than a CI setting. Raising the floor is a
   decision about who can run the tool; raising the CI version is not.

**Do not conflate them.** It is entirely reasonable to test on a current Node
while still supporting 20 for the people who have it, and it is also reasonable
to raise the floor. They want separate sentences.

## Why this is not urgent and is worth doing

Nothing is broken. Node 20 still runs the tool and CI is green on it. What has
changed is that a version past end of life stops getting security fixes, and
`AGENTS.md` names Node 20 or later as the environment, so the claim is load
bearing for anybody reading it.

Development happens on Node 24 on Windows and CI runs 20 on Linux, which
`CONTRIBUTING.md` presents as a feature: both ends of the supported range are
exercised rather than promised. **That argument is worth preserving.** If CI
moves to a single current version, the range stops being tested at all, and the
honest fix is probably a matrix rather than a bump.

## Scope

- Decide what CI runs on. A matrix over the floor and a current version keeps
  `CONTRIBUTING.md`''s claim true and costs a little time per run.
- Decide separately whether the supported floor moves, and if it does, say so in
  `package.json`, `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` together, since all three
  state it.
- **Do not raise the floor silently as a side effect of changing CI.**

## Watch out for

- **`check.yml` is the merge gate**, required green with an empty bypass list. A
  matrix changes what "the check" means to the ruleset; confirm the required
  check still resolves rather than becoming several checks none of which is the
  required one. That would block every pull request.
- Verify by running, not by reading. dbmd-53 set that standard for workflow
  changes and it holds here.
- `docs/ci.md` is the recipe this project publishes and it names a Node version
  for somebody else''s CI. That is a third, separate claim.
close_reason: PR #42 merged: Node matrix over 20/22/24, rollup gate proven red rather than skipped.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eleven, 2026-09-07

Branch: `dx/55-node-versions`. **ADR number 0032 is yours** if the decision
deserves a record, and it might. Do not take a different number; 0029, 0030 and
0031 are handed to agents working right now and `npm run check` fails a
collision.

### This is two questions and the item says so. Keep them apart.

1. **What CI builds and tests on.** All three workflows pin `node-version: 20`.
   That is the version every pull request is judged on and it no longer receives
   security fixes.
2. **What the package promises.** `package.json` says `"node": ">=20"`, which is
   a promise to users. Raising it is a decision about who can run the tool.

**Raising the second as a side effect of fixing the first would be the failure
here.** They deserve separate sentences and possibly separate answers.

### The argument you have to preserve or deliberately overturn

`CONTRIBUTING.md` presents the current split as a feature:

> CI builds and tests on Node 20 on Linux for every pull request, and this is
> developed on Node 24 on Windows, so both ends of that range are exercised
> rather than promised.

**That claim is load bearing and it is currently true.** If CI moves to a single
current version, the supported floor stops being tested at all and that sentence
becomes false. So the honest shape is probably a matrix over the floor and a
current version, rather than a bump. Say which you chose and why, and if you
bump rather than matrix, fix that sentence in the same commit.

### The thing that could break everything, and it is not the Node version

**`check.yml` is the merge gate.** A ruleset on `main` requires it green with an
empty bypass list, and ADR 0001 makes it the layer that decides what lands.

**A matrix changes what "the check" means to that ruleset.** One job named `check`
becomes several named `check (20)`, `check (24)` or similar, and the required
status check may then never report, which does not fail loudly: it blocks every
pull request until somebody works out why. dbmd-53's item named this exact hazard
about a different change.

So: if you build a matrix, **confirm the required check still resolves**. Push the
branch, open a pull request, and look at what the ruleset says about it rather
than assuming. If the name changes, either keep a single required job that
depends on the matrix, or say clearly in the pull request that the ruleset needs
updating by hand and exactly how, because that is an owner action and I need to
know before merging.

### Watch out for

- **Verify by running, not by reading.** dbmd-53 set that standard and it holds:
  a workflow change that has never executed is a guess. Link green runs for all
  three workflows.
- **Three places state the version claim**: `package.json`, `AGENTS.md` and
  `CONTRIBUTING.md`. If the floor moves, all three move together. `docs/ci.md`
  names a Node version for somebody else's CI, which is a **fourth, separate**
  claim about their environment rather than ours.
- dbmd-53 just moved every action to its current major. Do not undo that, and do
  not conflate an action's runtime with the project's Node.
- Three agents are working, in `src/cli/` with `src/import/`, in `src/studio/`
  with `test/`, and in `src/model/`. Stay in `.github/`, `package.json` and the
  documentation.

### Evidence bar

- **Green runs for all three workflows**, linked, on a real push.
- **The required check, named**, and evidence it still resolves for the ruleset.
  If it does not, say so plainly and say what the owner must change.
- If you matrixed: the run showing both versions actually ran and both passed.
- The three, or four, claim sites listed, with what each says after your change.
- If you did **not** move the floor, say why, because leaving a promise at a
  version past end of life is also a decision.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: The smoke test checks an exit code where it should check the words
description:
﻿The tarball smoke test asserts an exit code, so a warning is invisible to it.

Found by the dbmd-25 agent, who looked at what the green actually asserted
rather than trusting the colour.

## What it does now

`scripts/smoke-pack.mjs` packs a tarball, installs it, and drives every command
the binary offers. For `check` it does this:

    const checked = await dbmd(install, ['check', model])
    if (checked.code !== 0) { failures.push(...) }

**Exit code only.** `dbmd check` exits 0 for a model with warnings, by design
(ADR 0020: errors fail, warnings print, `--strict` moves the boundary). So the
model `dbmd init` writes could start producing warnings and this test would stay
green while every new user''s first command printed them.

That is not hypothetical: dbmd-25 added an `empty-value` warning and the question
"does the scaffold trip it" had to be answered by hand, because the smoke test
could not answer it.

## Why the gap is narrow but worth closing

`test/cli/cli.test.ts` already asserts `expect(diagnostics).toEqual([])` on what
`init` writes, which is exact and catches this regardless of severity. So the
property **is** guarded; it is guarded from the source tree rather than from the
tarball.

The smoke test exists because the source tree hides a broken `bin` and a missing
`files` entry. Its job is "the installed thing behaves", and "prints no problems"
is part of behaving.

## Scope

- Assert the **text** for at least the clean case: `dbmd check` on the scaffold
  says `no problems`. Do the same under `--strict`, which is where a warning
  actually changes the exit code.
- Look at the other commands in the same file for the same shape. `export` and
  `init` may have the same "exit code only" assertion, and the question is not
  whether they have been unlucky yet.
- Do not turn it into a second copy of the unit tests. The smoke test''s value is
  that it runs the *installed* binary; it should assert the few things that
  differ from a source run, not everything.

## Watch out for

- **Keep it fast.** It already added about seven seconds to `npm run check`, and
  the gate is run on every commit by every agent. A smoke test nobody wants to
  wait for gets removed from the gate, which is the ADR 0017 argument in a
  different costume.
- The text it asserts is user-facing prose and will change. Assert the part that
  carries the meaning, not the whole line, or this becomes a test that fails
  every time somebody improves a message.

title: Every workflow targets a deprecated action runtime
description:
﻿GitHub warns that all three workflows target a deprecated action runtime.

Observed by the dbmd-71 agent while running its own workflow, and it applies to
every workflow in the repository rather than to the new one:

> the runner now warns that `actions/checkout@v4`, `setup-node@v4` and
> `upload-artifact@v4` target the deprecated Node 20 *action runtime*. It applies
> to `check.yml` and `provenance.yml` identically.

## Why this is worth an item rather than a shrug

**`check.yml` is the merge gate.** ADR 0001 makes it the layer that decides what
lands, and a ruleset on `main` requires it green. When GitHub retires that
runtime the gate stops running, and a gate that cannot run is not a gate that
fails loudly: it is a required check that never reports, which blocks every pull
request until somebody works out why.

There is no urgency and there is a deadline somebody else controls. That is
exactly the shape of thing that should be an item rather than a memory.

## Scope

- Move all three workflows to whatever the current major of each action is.
  `checkout`, `setup-node` and `upload-artifact` at minimum; check for others.
- **Do not change what the workflows do.** This is a runtime bump, not a
  redesign, and `check.yml` in particular should come out behaving identically.
- Note that `model.yml` runs the recipe this project publishes, so if an action
  version appears in `docs/ci.md` it changes there too and the two must not
  drift. dbmd-71 made keeping them in step the point of that file.

## Watch out for

- **Verify by running, not by reading.** These are workflows; a version bump that
  has never executed is the same guess dbmd-71''s item warns about. Push the
  branch and link the green run for all three.
- `provenance.yml` is layer 3 from ADR 0001 and it audits `main` after the fact.
  Confirm it still reports the same thing rather than merely exiting 0.
- The pinning argument from ADR 0028 is about `npx dbmd@version` in somebody
  else''s CI and is separate from action versions here. Do not conflate them.

title: Four small wrongnesses in the studio confirmations and labels
description:
﻿Four small things a hunting pass found in the studio, none of them data loss.

Grouped because each is a few lines and they are all in the same two files. Take
them together or split them; do not let the small ones rot because the list has
a big one in it. **None of these is urgent and none should be done ahead of
dbmd-48.**

## 1. Confirm, then fail

Renaming `orders` to `products`, a name already taken, shows the **full**
confirmation:

> This writes tables/products.md and deletes tables/orders.md. 2 refs point here...

and only after pressing Rename says:

> Could not rename orders: there is already a table called `products`

Same for a name `safe-path` refuses, such as `con`. Both refusals are correct and
nothing is written, so this is not a correctness bug. **The dialog states
something untrue at the moment the user decides**, which is the one moment the
dialog exists for. The names in the model are already in the page, so the clash
is knowable before the confirmation is drawn.

## 2. "1 ref point at it"

`src/studio/client/inspector.ts` pluralises the noun and not the verb:

    `${n} ref${n === 1 ? '' : 's'} point at it`

Both the delete and the rename confirmations have it. These are the two most
carefully worded sentences in the product and one of them does not parse.

## 3. A self-reference is listed as an "other file"

Renaming `addresses`, which has `superseded_by` referencing `addresses.id`, says:

> This writes tables/postal_addresses.md and deletes tables/addresses.md.
> 2 refs point here ... which edits 2 other files: tables/addresses.md, tables/orders.md

The **outcome is correct**: a three-line diff and git detects the rename. The
sentence is not: the file being renamed is not an other file.

## 4. The wrong reason on an unanchored edge

Put `type: 42` on a column so its table fails to parse. The canvas replaces the
table''s rows with the did-not-parse message, and the edge''s accessible label
reads:

> Drawn at the table''s name because there is no api_keys.account_id.

`account_id` is still in the model. The cause is that rows are not drawn for an
incomplete table, not that the column is missing. ADR 0018 was explicit that a
fallback which looks like something else is the original bug in disguise, and
this is a smaller version of that: the fallback is right and its explanation is
wrong.

## Watch out for

- **dbmd-48 is a P0 in the same two files** and rewrites how the client learns
  about the model. Do not start these while that is in flight.
- Items 1 and 3 are both about a confirmation being accurate. The confirmations
  are the best thing in the inspector and the reason it is trustworthy, which is
  exactly why a sentence that is wrong in one costs more than it looks.
- Item 4 needs a distinct message rather than a reworded one: "this table did not
  parse" and "this column does not exist" are different facts and a reader acts
  differently on each.
close_reason: PR #67 merged: four fixed, the con case deliberately left, and a fifth found where every inspector validation paragraph rendered behind the toolbar.

title: One frontmatter error per file, not forty
description:
﻿Cap `frontmatter-invalid` at the first one per file, in the reader.

Decided in dbmd-12 and deliberately not built there, because it is a behaviour
change to the reader inside an item about the validator. ADR 0017 records the
argument in full so it does not have to be re-derived.

## What happens now

One invalid file produced **41 diagnostics**, 40 of them distinct. An
unterminated flow sequence swallows the rest of the document, so the YAML parser
reports a genuine and different complaint on nearly every remaining line:

    frontmatter-invalid|4|Implicit keys of flow sequence pairs need to be on a single line
    frontmatter-invalid|5|Block collections are not allowed within flow collections
    frontmatter-invalid|6|Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings
    ... 37 more

Every line is true. The first is the only one worth reading; the rest describe
the wreckage rather than the mistake.

## The decision, from dbmd-12

**The cap belongs in the reader, at `parseFrontmatter`, and reporting the first
`frontmatter-invalid` per file is a truer statement than reporting forty.** After
the first syntax error the remaining output is a consequence of it rather than an
independent fact, so collapsing them is not tidying, it is accuracy.

`src/model/read.ts` already makes that exact argument one function lower for
`kind-mismatch`, so this is a pattern the file has rather than a new one.

Ruled out, with reasons worth keeping:

- **Not the validator.** It produces no cascades: one mistake is at most one
  diagnostic there.
- **Not presentation.** ADR 0006 and ADR 0011 exist to stop the studio and the
  CLI disagreeing about output. A cap applied at printing time either makes
  `--json` disagree with the text form or makes it lossy in a way nothing can
  detect.

## Scope

- Report the first `frontmatter-invalid` per file and stop.
- Decide whether the message says that more were suppressed. Saying so costs a
  clause and stops a reader wondering whether the file has one problem or thirty.
  Saying nothing is defensible if the first message is genuinely sufficient; pick
  one and say why.
- The diagnostic is user-visible in two places now, the studio's panel and
  whatever `dbmd check` prints, so it is worth looking at both.

## Watch out for

- **Do not cap anything else.** Every other code reports one fact per mistake and
  a cap there would hide real problems. This is specifically about a parser
  cascade from a single syntax error.
- `docs/format.md` describes the diagnostics and has a test behind its table. If
  the behaviour changes, check whether the page's wording still holds.
- The page's own examples are now validated as well as read, so an example that
  demonstrates a cascade would have to be an expected-error block.
close_reason: PR #43 merged: one frontmatter error per file, chosen by character position so the tab wins, with a suppression count.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eleven, 2026-09-07

Branch: `format/24-one-error-per-file`. **ADR number 0031 is yours** if this needs
one, which it may not: ADR 0017 already records the argument. Do not take a
different number; 0029 and 0030 are handed to agents working right now and
`npm run check` fails a collision.

### Read the item, then read this, because I measured something that changes it

The item says: cap `frontmatter-invalid` at **the first one per file**, on the
grounds that after the first syntax error the rest is a consequence rather than
an independent fact. That reasoning is right and ADR 0017 has it in full.

**But "the first" is not always the useful one.** I broke a file the most ordinary
way there is, one tab character instead of two spaces, and ran `dbmd check`:

```
tables/t.md
  6  error  Implicit keys need to be on a single line (frontmatter-invalid)
  6  error  Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings (frontmatter-invalid)
  6  error  Tabs are not allowed as indentation (frontmatter-invalid)
  7  error  Implicit keys need to be on a single line (frontmatter-invalid)
  ...
7 frontmatter-invalid diagnostics from one tab character
```

**The message that names the actual mistake is third.** The first two are the
parser describing what the tab did to its state machine. A naive first-only cap
would report `Implicit keys need to be on a single line` for a file whose problem
is a tab, and hide the one line that says so. That is worse than forty true
messages, because it is one confidently wrong one.

So the item's intent is right and its literal instruction is not sufficient.
**Decide what to keep, not merely how many.** Some possibilities, and you may find
better:

- Keep the first diagnostic **at the earliest line**, and prefer within that line
  by something other than parser order.
- Keep the first, and any others **on the same line**, which in the example above
  yields exactly the three that describe the real point of failure.
- Keep the first, and say how many were suppressed, so a reader knows there is
  more rather than believing they have the whole picture.

Whatever you choose, **show it against the tab case**, because that is the break
people actually make.

### What has changed since the item was written

- **`dbmd check` exists** and groups by file, so you can see the effect directly
  rather than through a test.
- **The studio shows diagnostics in a panel**, so this is user-visible in two
  places. A cap improves both.
- **dbmd-25 added `empty-value`**, a warning, in the same reader. Do not cap that
  or anything else: this is specifically about a parser cascade from one syntax
  error. Every other code reports one fact per mistake.

### Watch out for

- **`docs/format.md` is executable.** Fenced blocks tagged `dbmd:` must read and
  validate clean; `dbmd-error:` blocks must produce **exactly** the codes they
  name. If any of those blocks currently relies on a cascade, capping changes what
  it produces and the build will tell you. There is also a test asserting every
  diagnostic code has a row in the page.
- The reader already makes this exact argument one function lower for
  `kind-mismatch`, so this is a pattern the file has rather than a new one. Find
  it and be consistent with it.
- Do not lose the line number. It is the most useful part of a syntax
  diagnostic and dbmd-12 established that a wrong one is worse than none.
- Two agents are working, in `src/cli/` with `src/import/`, and in `src/studio/`
  with `test/`. Stay in `src/model/` and `docs/`.

### Evidence bar

- **The tab case, before and after**, pasted in full. Before is seven; after is
  whatever you chose, and the message a reader is left with must name the tab.
- A second break of a different shape: an unterminated flow sequence, which is
  what produced the original 41, and a missing closing `---`.
- If you report a suppression count, show it.
- `examples/shop` still silent, and `docs/format.md`'s per-code test still
  passing, with a note on whether you had to touch the page.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: The import format page has no per-code table, and no test behind it
description:
﻿`docs/import-format.md` has no per-code table, and nothing stops it going stale.

Found in review of dbmd-13, by its own agent, and correctly left out of scope
there because that item changed no diagnostic codes.

## The asymmetry

`docs/format.md` landed with a row for every `ModelDiagnosticCode` and a test
that reads the union out of the source and fails if a code has no row. A code
cannot be added to the model reader without the page changing in the same
commit. That guarantee survived dbmd-13 moving the union to a new module, which
is exactly the kind of change that could have left the test green and the
guarantee gone.

`docs/import-format.md` documents the introspection contract and has no such
table and no such test. The import half now has its own codes, prefixed
`import/`, and nothing connects them to the page.

## Why it matters more now than when the page was written

The import codes were internal when `docs/import-format.md` was written. Two
things changed:

- **dbmd-13 made the diagnostic shape one public type.** Both halves travel in
  the same list, sorted by the same comparator, and `dbmd check --json` will
  print them together. A consumer meeting `import/wrong-type` has one page to
  look it up in and that page does not list it.
- **The contract is the thing a human satisfies by hand.** ADR 0007 has the
  import path read a JSON file a person produced by running a query themselves,
  so the diagnostics are read by somebody debugging their own file rather than
  by a developer reading source. That is the same audience `docs/format.md`
  exists for.

## Scope

- A row per `import/` code: what it means, and what to do about it.
- A test that reads the union and fails on a code with no row. `test/docs/format.test.ts`
  already does this for the model half and is the pattern to copy, not to
  generalise prematurely; two similar tests are cheaper than one clever one
  until there is a third.
- Check the rest of the page against the code while you are there. It had one
  paragraph describing field names that dbmd-13 had already changed, which was
  caught by hand rather than by anything mechanical.

## Watch out for

- **Do not merge the two pages.** They have different audiences: `docs/format.md`
  is for somebody writing markdown by hand, this one is for somebody producing or
  debugging a JSON document. ADR 0007 keeps the provider seam separate for a
  reason and the docs should follow it.
- The model page's test slices its union at the first blank line in the type
  declaration, which is a real constraint on how that source is formatted. If you
  copy the approach, copy that awareness too, or write something less fragile and
  say why.
close_reason: PR #50 merged: fifteen codes with rows, a test that fails in both directions, and a slice that survives a blank line in the union.

title: writeModel throws where it should skip an unsafe name
description:
﻿`writeModel` throws EINVAL on a name it should have skipped as `unsafe-name`.

Found by the dbmd-15 agent probing the writer's naming rules to document them,
and confirmed in review. Reported rather than fixed, because it was out of that
item''s scope.

## What happens

`isFileName` refuses the empty string, `.`, `..`, and anything containing `/` or
`\`, and an object whose name fails it is skipped with `unsafe-name`. That is the
right shape: a model problem becomes a `WriteSkip` the caller can report, and
`writeModel` does not throw for anything about the model.

A name containing `:` passes `isFileName` and then fails at the filesystem. On
Windows an object named `a:b` makes `writeModel` throw `EINVAL` out of the write
call. The same class covers a control character, a name over the path limit, and
on some filesystems a trailing dot or space.

## Why it matters more than the name suggests

`writeModel`''s contract is that a failure to write is an exception and a problem
with the model is a skip. Getting a raw `EINVAL` for a bad table name puts a
model problem on the exception path, where the caller has no `WriteSkip` naming
which object caused it. ADR 0010''s reasoning is that a caller carrying on after
a failed write has told the user their work is saved when it is not, and an
exception with no object name is the version of that which is hardest to act on.

The studio survives this only because `src/studio/safe-path.ts` refuses `:`
first, at the HTTP boundary. So today the guard that saves the writer belongs to
one of its two callers, and the other caller does not exist yet.

**dbmd-41 is the caller that will hit it.** An importer takes names from a
database catalogue rather than from a person, and a table name a catalogue is
happy with is not automatically a file name. That is the third caller and it has
no boundary guard of its own.

## Scope

- Decide where the rule lives. Duplicating `safe-path.ts` into the writer is two
  spellings of one fact, which is the entropy question dbmd-19 already asks about
  a different pair. Sharing it is better and needs somewhere for it to live that
  the studio and the model layer can both import.
- Whatever the answer, a name the writer will not write should produce a
  `WriteSkip`, never an exception.
- **The related gap is that `unsafe-name` has no diagnostic code**, so a refusal
  is silent to a reader and could not be reported by a future `dbmd check`.
  `docs/format.md` says so out loud today, which is the honest thing to do and
  not a fix. Decide whether a code is warranted here or belongs to dbmd-12.

## Watch out for

- A hand-author cannot reach this: the filesystem refuses the name before dbmd
  gets a chance, so no model on disk contains it. This is entirely about a model
  built in memory, which means an importer or the studio.
- Do not go looking for a Windows device-name hazard here. It was measured during
  review on Windows 11 with Node 24 and `nul.md`, `con.md` and a trailing space
  all wrote and read back as ordinary files. The reserved-name problem is real in
  other path-handling contexts and is not what this item is about.

title: on delete on a ref, and where the model-not-migration line is
description:
`on delete` on a ref, which is the first thing the format would say that the
database *does* rather than *is*.

Named by the dbmd-61 agent writing `examples/shop`, deferred by dbmd-14 with the
reasoning below, and filed here so it is not discovered a third time.

## What is missing

A `ref:` carries a table and a column and nothing else. `ON DELETE CASCADE`,
`ON DELETE SET NULL` and `ON DELETE RESTRICT` are three different promises about
what happens to a child row, and the markdown cannot tell them apart.

The introspection contract already can: `ForeignKey.onDelete` is a
`ReferentialAction` and both providers populate it. So this is the same shape of
gap dbmd-14 closed for uniqueness — the wire carries it, the markdown cannot
receive it, and an import silently drops it.

## Why this one is an ADR and the other two were not

dbmd-14 handled `unique` as a key, because a unique constraint is a fact about
what the data *is*. `on delete` is a fact about what the engine *does when
something happens*, and ADR 0003's premise is that this is a model rather than a
migration: **it describes a schema, it does not generate or apply DDL.**

That premise is not obviously violated by recording a referential action, since
the action is part of the schema as much as the reference is. But it is the
first key that makes the file describe behaviour, and the line between "the
model records what the database does" and "the model tells the database what to
do" is exactly the line ADR 0003 drew. It should be drawn again deliberately
rather than crossed by adding a key.

The answer is quite possibly "record it, it is part of the schema, nothing about
recording it generates DDL". If so, the ADR is three paragraphs and the code is
an afternoon. That is a good outcome and it still wants writing down, because
the next behavioural key will cite it.

## Scope

- An appended section on ADR 0003 saying where the line is now, with the
  reasoning. A new record if it turns out to be a new pattern rather than an
  amendment.
- If it is recorded: the key on a `ref:`, read, written and validated, mapped to
  and from `ForeignKey.onDelete`, and `examples/shop` using it where it is true.
  `orders` to `customers` is the interesting case, since an erasure request there
  deliberately does not delete the row.
- `ON UPDATE` is the same question and should be answered in the same breath,
  even if the answer is that nobody uses it.

## Watch out for

- Touches the reader, the writer, the validator and the contract seam together,
  so it cannot run alongside work in any of them.
- Do not let this become a DDL generator. If the discussion reaches "and then we
  could emit the `ALTER TABLE`", that is a different product and ADR 0003 already
  refused it.
- `check` constraints are the *other* half of what dbmd-14 deferred, and they are
  **not** this item. They are engine-native SQL that dbmd can neither read nor
  compare, which makes them dbmd-18's question about how opaque engine text lives
  in the markdown, not this one's.
close_reason: PR #107 merged: the line is that dbmd writes facts down and never writes statements out. Verified the rename data-loss bug it found, the vocabulary errors, and the round trip.

title: A group's computed box encloses non-members
description:
A group's computed box encloses things that are not members, and nothing says so.

Reported by the dbmd-61 agent, who hit it laying out `examples/shop` by hand and
restructured the model twice because of it.

## What happened

It wanted a three-member `settlement` group over `orders`, `order_items` and
`shipments`. It worked the bounding box out on paper, realised the box would
enclose `products`, which is not a member, and eventually settled for a
two-member group in a corner of the canvas. The model that shipped is shaped by
this constraint rather than by the domain.

The same hazard applies to notes: a note is not a member, so a note dropped into
a convenient gap can land inside a group's computed box and read as though it
belongs to it.

## Why this is not simply "ADR 0005 was wrong"

ADR 0005 argues no-coordinates from two angles and both are correct: a stored box
can disagree with its members, and a stored box puts a shared file in the path of
every layout change. Neither is undermined by this.

What the record does not mention is that **the author of a member has to reason
about a non-member's enclosure**, and that the cost falls almost entirely on
hand-authors. A studio user sees the box redraw as they drag. A person writing
frontmatter sees nothing until something renders.

## Scope, which is to decide rather than to build

Options, roughly in order of how much they cost:

1. **Nothing but documentation.** Say it plainly in the format reference and
   accept it. Defensible: the studio makes it visible, and hand-laying-out a
   canvas is a niche activity.
2. **A validator warning** when a non-member's box falls inside a group's
   computed bounds. Cheap, and turns an invisible problem into a diagnostic.
   Needs a box size for a table, which does not exist yet.
3. **An optional `layout` on a group that overrides the computation.** ADR 0005
   names this as its own revisit path and warns that the moment it exists it can
   disagree with reality.
4. **Render groups so enclosure is visually unambiguous** regardless of overlap,
   which is a studio problem rather than a format one.

Recommendation: 1 now, 2 when a renderer exists to define a table's box, and 3
only if somebody asks. Argue with that.

Whatever is chosen, append it to ADR 0005 rather than editing it, and add the
hand-author cost to that record, because it is a consequence the record does not
currently list.
close_reason: PR #60 merged: the box now cuts a clearing round every non-member it covers, verified by building the three-member settlement group that was previously impossible.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
﻿## Refinement note, 2026-09-07: this is blocked, not merely unrefined

The item lays out three options and asks which. **One of them cannot be judged
yet, and it is the cheapest one.**

Option 1 is "nothing but documentation", defended on the grounds that *the studio
makes it visible*. When this was filed there was no studio. There is one now, and
it is good: the canvas draws tables, anchors edges to column rows, and redraws
live as you drag.

**It does not draw groups at all.** dbmd-34 is the item that adds notes and groups
to the canvas and it has not landed. So option 1''s entire defence is still
untestable: nobody can yet see whether watching the box redraw while dragging
makes the enclosure problem obvious or leaves it just as invisible as it is in
frontmatter.

Marking this blocked on dbmd-34 rather than leaving it labelled for refinement.
The refinement question is real and the answer depends on a thing that does not
exist.

## What else has changed since it was filed

- **Option 2 wanted a box size for a table, "which does not exist yet".** It
  still does not exist as a *model* fact, and dbmd-37 established why it cannot
  cheaply become one: a box''s size is measured from the rendered DOM and moves
  with zoom, with fonts, and whenever a column is added or removed. A validator
  running with no browser has no honest way to compute it. That makes option 2
  more expensive than the item''s ordering suggests, not less.
- **`docs/format.md` now exists**, so option 1 has somewhere concrete to live,
  which it did not when this was written.
- The hazard the item names for notes is now sharper: a note dropped into a
  convenient gap can land inside a group''s computed bounds and read as a member.
  Once dbmd-34 draws both, that is visible rather than theoretical.

## When dbmd-34 lands, the question to ask

Open the studio on a model with a group whose computed box encloses a non-member,
and see whether a person notices without being told. That is one session with the
real thing and it settles an item that has been three hypotheses on paper since
August.

title: The SQL Server provider
description:
The SQL Server provider.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0007-engines-are-providers.md` and
`docs/import-format.md` from dbmd-40 first. This is the item that proves the
seam was real rather than Postgres wearing an interface, so a change forced into
`contract.ts` here is a finding worth reporting, not a nuisance.

## Scope

- `src/import/providers/sqlserver.ts` implementing `EngineProvider`.
- One statement, printed by `dbmd query --engine sqlserver`, returning the
  envelope as JSON via `FOR JSON PATH`.
- `parse` and `normaliseType`, plus `[bracket]` quoting.
- A committed fixture and unit tests over it.

## Watch out for

- **SSMS splits `FOR JSON` output across rows at about 2000 characters.** A user
  copying the grid gets truncated JSON that looks complete and fails to parse
  somewhere in the middle. This is the single most likely support question this
  feature will ever generate. Say so in the printed output above the query, not
  only in the documentation, and make the parse failure name it as a likely
  cause.
- `FOR JSON` needs SQL Server 2016 or later. Say what happens on older versions
  rather than producing a syntax error nobody can interpret.
- `nvarchar(max)` reports `max_length` as -1, and `nvarchar` reports bytes rather
  than characters, so a `nvarchar(50)` reads as 100.
- `sys.indexes`, `sys.index_columns` and `sys.foreign_key_columns` carry what
  `information_schema` does not, including included columns and whether an index
  is the clustered one.
- Default constraints arrive wrapped in extra parentheses, `((0))` for zero.
  Decide whether to unwrap and be consistent.
- Collation is case-insensitive by default, so two tables differing only in case
  cannot normally exist. Do not build that assumption into the contract, and do
  not build the opposite one either.
- `dbo` is the default schema and is not the same as "no schema".

## Evidence bar

Run it against a real SQL Server, on a schema with a composite primary key, a
multi-column foreign key, an `nvarchar(max)` column and a non-`dbo` schema.
Paste the JSON, and say which SQL Server version and which client you used. If
no instance is available, say so plainly rather than inventing output, and say
what that leaves unproven.

Separately, and this is the architectural part: report every change this item
forced on `contract.ts` or on `EngineProvider`. That list is the measure of
whether ADR 0007's seam was in the right place.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Resolved ahead of this item by dbmd-40, which merged the contract first.

This item's brief says "default constraints arrive wrapped in extra
parentheses, `((0))` for zero. Decide whether to unwrap and be consistent."
That decision has now been taken the other way: the contract stores default
expressions **verbatim**, `((0))` included, and `docs/import-format.md` says so.

So this item does not decide it. If the SQL Server provider has a reason to
disagree, the change is to the format doc and the contract, argued in the pull
request, not an unwrap inside the provider. A provider that quietly normalises
what the contract says is verbatim is the exact drift the seam exists to stop.

One other thing settled since this was written: `EngineProvider.normaliseType`
returns the closed `NormalisedType` union rather than ADR 0007's `string`, with
`other` as the escape hatch. ADR 0009 has the argument.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Cross-provider consistency, found while reviewing dbmd-43 against a live database.

**A temporal type's modifier landed in `scale`, and you must match it or the two
providers disagree silently.** The Postgres provider reports `timestamptz(3)` as:

```json
{"native":"timestamp with time zone","normalised":"timestamp","scale":3}
```

SQL is not consistent about whether that modifier is a precision or a scale.
Postgres documents `timestamp(p)` as precision; SQL Server documents
`datetime2(n)` as fractional seconds precision, and its catalog reports it in
`scale`. The contract has both fields, so nothing mechanically stops the two
providers putting the same fact in different places, and nothing downstream
would notice until a model imported from one engine looked different from the
same model imported from the other.

Match the Postgres provider unless you think it is wrong, in which case say so
and both change together. Either way, `docs/import-format.md` should state which
field a temporal precision goes in, because right now it does not and that is
how this happened.

Related: dbmd-18, filed from the same review. An expression index currently
arrives as a column whose name is the expression, which is ambiguous. It is a
contract question rather than a provider one, so do not solve it inside the SQL
Server provider.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave nine, 2026-09-07

Branch: `import/44-sqlserver-provider`. **ADR number 0026 is yours** if you need
one. Do not take a different number; 0023, 0024 and 0025 are handed to agents
working right now and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### Why this item matters more than its P2

Your own item says it: **this is what proves the seam was real rather than
Postgres wearing an interface.** ADR 0007 claimed a third engine is one file and
one registry line. Nobody has tested that claim. You are the test.

So **a change forced into `src/import/contract.ts` is the most valuable thing you
can report**, not a nuisance to route around. If SQL Server needs something the
contract cannot express, say so loudly and precisely rather than bending the
provider to fit. That finding is worth more than the provider.

### What changed under this item, and it is recent

**dbmd-18 landed hours ago and moved the contract.** An index key is now a
column *or* an expression: `IndexKey` is `{ column } | { expression }`, and a key
claiming both is an `import/conflicting-fields` error. Read that code and ADR
0022 before writing your query.

This matters to you specifically because **SQL Server has computed columns**, and
an index over one is the same question in a different dialect. ADR 0022 also
fixed the spelling for two things that are decided and not built: `checks:` on a
table, and a markdown key for `filterExpression`. **Do not build either.** If
your engine makes one of them urgent, report it.

### The traps in your item, and the first one is the whole support burden

- **SSMS splits `FOR JSON` output across rows at about 2000 characters.** A user
  copying from the grid gets truncated JSON that looks complete. Your item calls
  this the single most likely support question this feature will ever generate,
  and it is right. Say so **in the printed output above the query**, not only in
  documentation, and make the parse failure name it as a likely cause. Somebody
  hitting this is looking at an error message, not at a doc page.
- `FOR JSON` needs SQL Server 2016 or later. Say what happens on older versions
  rather than emitting a syntax error nobody can interpret.
- `nvarchar(max)` reports `max_length` as `-1`, and `nvarchar` reports **bytes**,
  so `nvarchar(50)` reads as 100. Get this wrong and every string column in every
  imported model is twice its real size.
- `sys.indexes`, `sys.index_columns` and `sys.foreign_key_columns` carry what
  `information_schema` does not, including included columns and whether an index
  is really a constraint. The contract has `isUnique` and `isUniqueConstraint`
  precisely because those are different things.

### How the Postgres provider set the bar

Read `src/import/providers/postgres.ts` and the review record on its pull
request. Two things it did that you should match:

- **It was driven against a live database**, not against a fixture. ADR 0007
  expects that for a query change, and dbmd-18 did the same against PostgreSQL 16
  in Docker. If you can run SQL Server 2019 or later in a container, do; if you
  genuinely cannot on this machine, **say so plainly and say what you did
  instead** rather than implying more than you ran.
- **Reviewing it against a live database is what found dbmd-18**, the expression
  index that was indistinguishable from a column. Expect to find something
  similar. Looking for it is part of the work.

### Scope

The provider, the query, the registry line, a committed fixture, and tests.
`docs/import-format.md` has to say whatever your engine forced.

**Not the import itself**, which is dbmd-41 and is still blocked. Stay out of
`src/model/`, `src/cli/` and `src/studio/`: agents are working in all three.

### Evidence bar

- **The query, run somewhere real**, with its raw output pasted. If that is a
  container, say which image and version.
- The envelope that comes out, through `readEnvelope`, with its diagnostics.
- **A table that exercises the traps**: an `nvarchar(50)`, an `nvarchar(max)`, a
  computed column, a unique constraint and a unique index that is not a
  constraint, a composite foreign key, and a bracketed identifier that needs
  quoting.
- **Paste the truncation warning** exactly as a user sees it above the query, and
  the parse failure a truncated paste produces, showing it names the cause.
- **Say what the contract could not express**, or say plainly that it expressed
  everything. Either is a real result and the second one is the claim ADR 0007
  made.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: The Postgres provider
description:
The Postgres provider.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0007-engines-are-providers.md` and
`docs/import-format.md` from dbmd-40 first.

## Scope

- `src/import/providers/postgres.ts` implementing `EngineProvider`.
- One SQL statement, printed by `dbmd query --engine postgres`, returning one
  JSON value in the envelope shape.
- `parse` and `normaliseType` turning that into the canonical shape.
- A committed fixture of real output, and unit tests over it that need no
  database.

## Watch out for

- One statement. No psql meta-commands, no temporary tables, no `\gset`. It has
  to paste into pgAdmin, DBeaver, a JDBC console and `docker exec psql` alike.
- **Read-only, and visibly so.** Somebody is going to run this against
  production, and they should be able to satisfy themselves by reading it. Do not
  make that hard to see.
- Exclude `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` from the results, or the first
  import produces four hundred tables.
- `information_schema` does not carry usable index metadata. `pg_index`,
  `pg_class` and `pg_attribute` do. It is also materially slower on large
  catalogs.
- Identity columns and `serial` produce different defaults for the same intent.
  Decide what the model should say and be consistent.
- Case. Postgres folds unquoted identifiers to lower case, so a table created as
  `"Orders"` is a different table from `Orders`. The JSON must carry what is
  actually there, not what somebody typed.

## Evidence bar

Run it against a real Postgres, on a schema with at least one composite primary
key, one multi-column foreign key, and one quoted mixed-case identifier. Paste
the JSON. If no database is available, say so plainly and do not substitute a
schema you invented: a fixture proves the normalisation and never the query, and
that distinction is in ADR 0007.
close_reason: Merged in PR #9. Query verified by extracting it from the built dist and running it read-only against a postgres:16 container over an orchestrator-written schema: composite PK order and case preserved, cross-schema multi-column FK with actions, identity distinguishable from serial, generated column, partial unique index with INCLUDE, view and catalog tables excluded, zero diagnostics.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

The claim was that the query is read-only and proven against a real database, so
I proved it again independently rather than reading the evidence.

I pulled `postgresProvider.introspectionQuery()` out of the **built** `dist`, so
what I ran is the string that ships, then ran it against a `postgres:16`
container over a schema **I** invented, in a session with
`default_transaction_read_only=on` where any write errors. Exit 0, empty stderr.
Static checks on the shipped string first: one statement, no psql
meta-commands, no write verb outside a comment.

My schema was not the one in the fixtures: a cross-schema composite foreign key
with `on delete cascade on update restrict`, quoted mixed-case identifiers
(`"Ops"."Ledger"` on `("TenantId","Code")`), an identity column and a `serial` in
the same table, a stored generated column, a `text[]`, a `timestamptz(3)`, a
column with an explicit collation, a partial unique index with `INCLUDE`, an
expression index, a check constraint and a view.

Fed through `readIntrospection`, zero diagnostics, and every hard case correct:

- `pk: {"columns":["TenantId","Code"]}` — composite, in declaration order, case
  preserved exactly.
- the foreign key carries both columns, the referenced schema, and
  `"onDelete":"cascade","onUpdate":"restrict"`.
- `identity:{"generation":"always"}` on the identity column, while `serial`
  arrives as `default:{"expression":"nextval('entry_legacy_id_seq'::regclass)"}`.
  The two are visibly different, which is the whole argument in the report.
- `generated:{"expression":"(qty * 100)","persisted":true}`, `collation":"C"`,
  and the partial index with `includedColumns`, `isUnique` and
  `filterExpression`.
- `text[]` comes back `{"native":"text[]","normalised":"other"}`. Honest.
- Two tables returned. The view is excluded and so is every catalog table.

Refusing to map `serial` onto `identity: byDefault` is the right call and the
reason given is the right reason: the same default appears on any column drawing
from a sequence for another reason, so the mapping would be a guess dressed as a
normalisation.

Regenerating `postgres-raw.json` from a real database instead of keeping the
guessed one is worth more than it sounds. The guess had doubled parens on a check
expression that `pg_get_expr` does not actually emit. A fixture that was invented
is a test of somebody's imagination.

## Code

Two observations, neither blocking, both filed rather than left in this comment.

**An expression index is indistinguishable from a column with a strange name.**
`entry_lower_code` comes back as `columns:[{"name":"lower(ledger_code)"}]`. A
consumer cannot tell that from a real column called `lower(ledger_code)`, and
`dbmd import` will eventually have to, because the markdown format's `indexes`
takes column names. Filed as dbmd-18.

**A temporal precision landed in `scale`.** `timestamptz(3)` produced
`{"native":"timestamp with time zone","normalised":"timestamp","scale":3}`. SQL
is not consistent about whether that modifier is precision or scale, and the
contract has both fields, so the two providers can disagree in a way nothing
catches. Recorded on dbmd-44 so it matches rather than discovers.

## Architecture

The seam held under its first real load, which is what this item was the test of.
Nothing in `contract.ts` was changed and nothing in it fought the provider. The
observation that `identity.seed`, `identity.increment` and `default.constraintName`
are the only fields Postgres has no truthful answer for, and that all three are
documented as SQL Server's, is the seam working exactly as ADR 0007 intended.

Correcting `registry.test.ts`, which asserted the real registry was empty, is
right: that assertion was only ever true while no provider existed, and it now
builds its own empty registry to test the same thing.

## Verdict

Merge after a rebase. `main` moved when PR #8 landed.

title: The GitHub Actions recipe: check, and publish the diagram
description:
The GitHub Actions recipe: check the model, and publish the diagram.

The pipeline caller from ADR 0006, made concrete. Two jobs a team would actually
want, documented well enough to copy.

## Scope

- A documented workflow snippet that runs `dbmd check` on a repository's model
  and fails the build on an error.
- A second that runs `dbmd export` and uploads the result as a build artifact,
  so a pull request can carry the current diagram without anyone committing a
  generated file if they would rather not.
- Both in the README or a `docs/ci.md`, as copy-paste YAML with the version
  pinned, not as prose describing what you could do.
- This repository uses its own recipe on `examples/shop`, which is how it stays
  true.

## Watch out for

- `npx dbmd@latest` in someone's CI is a supply chain decision made by accident.
  Pin a version in the recipe and say why.
- No TTY, so anything that assumed one shows up here first. This item is the
  real test of dbmd-70 and should be treated as such.
- An artifact upload that silently uploads nothing when the export produced
  nothing is worse than a failure. Make the export's exit code meaningful.

## Evidence bar

The workflow runs in this repository, on a real push, and goes green. Link the
run and paste the artifact's contents. A YAML file that has never executed is
not evidence.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave nine, 2026-09-07

Branch: `cli/71-ci-recipe`. **ADR number 0028 is yours** if this needs one, which
it may not. Do not take a different number; 0024 through 0027 are handed to
agents working right now and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### Both halves you need landed today

- **`dbmd check`** (dbmd-21): reads a model, runs the validator, groups by file,
  errors exit 1 and warnings exit 0 with `--strict` moving the boundary. ADR 0020
  has the exit-code contract. `--json` exits non-zero exactly like the text form.
- **`dbmd export`** (dbmd-22): writes a mermaid `erDiagram` into a README between
  markers, or prints it with `--stdout`. It **refuses a model with errors**, exit
  1, writing nothing. It does not rewrite the file when the diagram has not
  changed.

Read `src/cli/check.ts` and `src/cli/export.ts` before writing YAML. Their exit
codes are the entire contract you are building on.

### This item is the real test of the output contract

Your item says so and it is right. **There is no terminal in a workflow runner**,
so anything that quietly assumed one appears here first. Colour detection,
narration on the wrong stream, a command that waits for input: all of it shows up
in CI before it shows up anywhere else.

If you find such a thing, that is a finding worth more than the recipe. Report
it; do not paper over it with a flag.

### The three traps, and the first is a real decision

- **`npx dbmd@latest` in somebody's CI is a supply chain decision made by
  accident.** Pin a version in the recipe and say why in the surrounding prose.
  Note that this package is **not published to npm** and is deliberately still
  marked private, so a recipe telling people to `npx dbmd@0.1.0` today would be
  telling them to run something that does not exist. **Say what the recipe will
  be, and be honest about what it is until publishing happens.** Using this
  repository's own checkout is a legitimate way to make the recipe real now.

title: Publishable package, verified from a tarball
description:
Make the package installable and `npx`-able.

## Scope

- `bin`, `files`, `exports`, `engines` set correctly. Drop `private: true`.
- The client bundle is built before pack and included in the tarball.
- `prepublishOnly` runs `npm run check`.
- A smoke test that packs the tarball, installs it into a temporary directory
  and runs `dbmd --version` and `dbmd init`, wired into `npm run check` if it is
  fast enough and into its own script if it is not.

## Watch out for

- `files` omissions are invisible locally and fatal for users. The source tree
  has everything; the tarball is what ships. Test the tarball.
- The shebang must survive the build, and the built file needs to be executable
  on a POSIX install even though it is produced on Windows.
- `npx dbmd` on a machine with no cache downloads the tarball. Every dependency
  is start-up latency for a first-time user; check the packed size and say what
  it is in the pull request.

## Evidence bar

From a directory outside this repository, install the packed tarball and run
`npx dbmd init` and `npx dbmd studio`. Paste both, and the packed size.

**Do not drop `private: true`.** The item says to, and I am overriding that.

Publishing to npm has never been asked for by the owner. It is the one open

line: an npm account with rights to the name, whether `dbmd` is still free, a
version that is not `0.0.0`, and anything else you find. That turns an open
question into a decision somebody can make in a minute.

`dbmd-20` set `bin`, `files: ["dist"]` and a `prepack` that builds, and proved a
tarball install works. Since then the package has grown a studio client bundled
by esbuild, three commands, and a library surface in `src/index.ts`. Nobody has
checked the tarball since.

The known gaps, from that item's own report:

- **No `main`, no `exports`.** `src/index.ts` exports the reader, the writer and
  the types, and the studio server is importable at `src/studio/index.ts`. Today
  a consumer cannot `import` any of it from the package, only run the binary.

  legitimate answer if you argue it.
- **`files: ["dist"]` ships `.js.map` files whose `sources` point at a `src/`
  the tarball does not contain.** Harmless and dead weight. Narrow it or ship
  the sources, and say which.

### The traps in the item, all real

- **A `files` omission is invisible locally and fatal for users.** The source

  executable on a POSIX install even though it is produced on Windows.
- **Every dependency is start-up latency for a first-time user** running `npx`
  with no cache. Report the packed size and the unpacked size, as numbers.

### Scope

The package, its scripts, and a smoke test. Not the README, which is dbmd-51.

title: The README a stranger reads
description:
The README a stranger reads.

## Scope

- The workflow, in the order a real user meets it: install nothing, run
  `npx dbmd init` or `npx dbmd import`, run `npx dbmd studio`, edit, `git diff`,
  commit, pull request.
- One screenshot of the studio and one real markdown file, side by side. That
  pairing is the whole product and no paragraph explains it as well.
- What it is not: not a migration tool, not a database client, does not connect
  to anything.
- A link to the format documentation and to ADR 0003.

## Watch out for

- The README currently claims a status that will be wrong the moment this
  lands. Do not leave a status line that quietly becomes a lie.
- Do not write the README from the ADRs. Write it from having run the tool, and
  paste what you actually saw.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave ten, 2026-09-07

Branch: `publish/51-readme`. **No ADR.** A README decides nothing. Do not take a
number; 0025 and 0026 are handed to agents working right now.

### Why this is dispatchable now and was not this morning

I held this item back three times today because the product kept moving under it.
It has stopped. Four commands are on `main` and none of the three branches still
in flight changes what a user does: one fixes a studio data-loss path, one
settles two format spellings, one bumps action versions.

**So write it from the tool as it is, and expect it to stay true.**

### One thing in the item is out of date, and it matters

The scope says `npx dbmd init` and `npx dbmd studio`. **This package is not
published to npm.** `package.json` is `"private": true` on purpose, nobody has
asked for it to be published, and the name was free as of 2026-09-07. `AGENTS.md`
now says so plainly.

I corrected the README's worst offenders an hour ago: the opening block says
`dbmd studio`, followed immediately by a note that this is what the command will
be rather than what you can type today, pointing at `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the
checkout route. **Keep that honesty and improve on it if you can.** A README that
tells a stranger to run something that does not exist is the exact failure this
project has already paid for once: a false claim in `AGENTS.md` is why the CI
recipe invented a version number.

`npx dbmd import` in the scope line is worse: that command does not exist at all
and is still blocked. Do not mention it as though it does.

### The item's real instruction, which I am holding you to

> One screenshot of the studio and one real markdown file, side by side. That
> pairing is the whole product and no paragraph explains it as well.

**Do that.** Not a description of it. Run the studio on `examples/shop`, take a
screenshot, and put it next to the actual frontmatter of a table in the picture.
Commit the image. The global `playwright-cli` is how you take it; the browser
automation MCP server is not connected.

> Do not write the README from the ADRs. Write it from having run the tool, and
> paste what you actually saw.

Also that. Every command you name, run first, and paste its real output rather
than a plausible one.

### What the product actually is today, so you can check yourself against it

`dbmd init` scaffolds a model. `dbmd check` validates it and exits non-zero on an
error, with `--strict` promoting warnings, and `--json` for scripts. `dbmd export`
writes a mermaid diagram between markers that GitHub renders. `dbmd studio` opens
a canvas where you drag tables, edit columns, indexes and prose, rename a table
across every file that references it, and create and delete tables.

What it is not, and both are decisions rather than gaps: **it does not generate or
apply DDL**, and **it does not connect to a database**. The import path reads a
JSON file a person produced by running a query the tool hands them. ADR 0003 and
ADR 0007 are the arguments.

### Watch out for

- **The status line.** The item warns that it will quietly become a lie. It has
  already been rewritten twice today for exactly that. Prefer a shape that stays
  true: say what works and how to run it, rather than a status that ages.
- The studio has a known data-loss path being fixed right now: a page open while
  you edit files by hand can overwrite your edit. **Do not advertise editing by
  hand and in the studio simultaneously** as a workflow until that lands.
- `examples/shop` has **uncommitted edits from the owner**, who has a studio open
  on it. Do not commit them, do not revert them, and take your screenshot from a
  copy if you would rather have a clean one.
- Link `docs/format.md`, `docs/ci.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and ADR 0003. Do not
  restate them.

### Evidence bar

- **The screenshot and the markdown, side by side, in the README**, showing the
  same table.
- Every command you name, with the output you actually got, from a checkout.
- Say which parts of the README you ran and which you asserted. If you assert
  nothing, say that.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: dbmd import into an empty model
description:
