`dbmd import`: turn the introspection JSON into a model directory.

## Scope

- `dbmd import --file schema.json [--dir db-model]`, and reading stdin when no
  file is given, so a pipe works.
- Writes one markdown file per table, through the canonical writer (dbmd-11).
- Tables are laid out on a deterministic grid. There is no auto layout in the
  MVP and the developer arranges them once.
- Refuses to write into a non-empty model directory. The message names dbmd-42
  as the merge that does not exist yet, so the user knows the difference between
  unimplemented and forbidden.
- The generated prose body is a single line saying the table was imported and
  nobody has documented it yet. That is a prompt, and it is the point.

## Watch out for

- Do not invent prose. An imported model with a paragraph of generated
  description per table teaches the reader that the prose is worthless, which
  destroys the one thing this format has that a diagram does not.
- Types come back from Postgres as things like `character varying` and
  `timestamp with time zone`. Decide once whether to normalise them and say so
  in the pull request; whichever you choose, be consistent, because this is what
  every user's first diff looks like.
- A foreign key with no matching table in the JSON is a bad export, not a bad
  model. Diagnose it, do not write a dangling ref silently.

## Evidence bar

Import the fixture from dbmd-40 and paste `dbmd check` output on the result: it
should be clean. Then open the studio on it and include a screenshot.
close_reason: PR #45 merged: dbmd import, verified by importing both fixtures with dbmd check exit 0, plus the refusal, the truncation and the stream split.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Two things settled by dbmd-61's hand-authoring findings, before this item starts.

**ADR 0009's two type names have one key to go into.** The import contract's
`ColumnType` carries `native` and `normalised`, both required, and ADR 0009
argues at length that losing `native` is unrecoverable: a model written without
it cannot get it back without a re-import against a database the user may no
longer have. `Column.type` in the markdown model is one string.

So this item cannot avoid deciding what the markdown holds. It is a format
question, not an importer question, and answering it inside the importer is how
the two drift. Settle it, in an ADR, and say which of these it is:

- one key holding the native type, with `normalised` recomputed on demand
- one key holding the normalised type, accepting that `native` is lost, which
  ADR 0009 explicitly argues against
- two keys, at the cost of a line per column in every table file forever

**Unique constraints are blocked on dbmd-14.** Both engines report them and the
introspection contract carries them, but the markdown cannot express them yet,
so an import today would silently drop a constraint the database enforces. This
item is now behind dbmd-14 for that reason.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eleven, 2026-09-07

Branch: `import/41-import-into-an-empty-model`. **ADR number 0029 is yours.** Do
not take a different one; 0030 is handed to another agent right now and
`npm run check` fails a collision.

### This is the last unbuilt piece of the original product

It has been blocked since August behind five items and all five have landed:
uniqueness the format can say, a nullability key that reads forwards, expression
indexes, one word per fact, and a writer that reports an unwritable name instead
of throwing. **Everything you need exists and is proven.** Read what they left:

- **`src/import/contract.ts`** is the introspection contract, with two providers
  behind it. dbmd-44 added SQL Server with **zero lines changed** in that file,
  which is the strongest evidence the shape is right.
- **`src/import/providers/`** has `postgres.ts` and `sqlserver.ts`, both driven
  against live databases in containers.
- **`writeModel`** is canonical and refuses a name it cannot write with a
  `WriteSkip` naming the object. ADR 0026 has the reasoning.
- **`dbmd check`** exists, so your evidence bar is runnable.

### The three traps in the item, and the first is the one that matters

- **Do not invent prose.** An imported model with a generated paragraph per table
  teaches the reader that the prose is worthless, and the prose is the only thing
  this format has that a diagram does not. One line saying the table was imported
  and nobody has documented it yet **is a prompt, and it is the point.**
- **Type normalisation is a decision, not a detail.** Postgres returns
  `character varying` and `timestamp with time zone`. Decide once, say so in the
  pull request, and be consistent, because **this is what every user's first diff
  looks like.** Note that `Column.type` in the contract already carries both a
  native and a normalised spelling; read why before choosing.
- **A ref with no matching table in the JSON is a bad export, not a bad model.**
  Diagnose it. Do not write a dangling ref silently and leave `dbmd check` to
  find it later.

### What has changed under the item since it was written

- **`unsafe-name` has no diagnostic code and that is deliberate.** ADR 0026 says a
  filesystem refuses such names before dbmd is involved, so no model on disk can
  hold one and a reader could never raise it. **You are the caller that can.** A
  catalogue will hand you a table name a file cannot hold: dbmd-44 imported one
  literally called `Ledger [Entry]`, and a colon in a name on Windows silently
  opens an alternate data stream rather than failing. **Turning a `WriteSkip`
  into an `import/` diagnostic naming the table is your job**, and ADR 0026 says
  so explicitly.
- **The parse seam.** dbmd-44 found that a provider never sees the raw text, so it
  cannot own its own most likely failure: a truncated paste. You write that call
  site. **Name truncation as a likely cause when `JSON.parse` throws**, and do it
  **without knowing the engine**, because sniffing an engine out of the text puts
  an engine name outside `providers/`. The SQL Server provider's own query header
  explains the 2033-character split; do not duplicate that, point at it.
- `dbmd query` does not exist. `introspectionQuery()` is ready for it and it is
  not yours.

### Watch out for

- **`--dir` defaults and stdin.** A pipe must work, which means nothing may prompt
  and narration must stay on stderr. ADR 0006 and ADR 0011, and the gate will
  fail the build on a stray write.
- The refusal to write into a non-empty directory **must name dbmd-42** so a user
  knows the difference between unimplemented and forbidden. That sentence is in
  the item for a reason.
- Deterministic layout on a grid. Same input, same bytes. No auto-layout.
- One agent is in `README.md` and another in `test/studio/`. Stay in `src/cli/`,
  `src/import/` and `docs/`.

### Evidence bar

The item's bar, and I am holding you to all of it:

- **Import the committed fixture and paste `dbmd check` on the result.** Clean is
  the answer. Use the SQL Server fixture too; it is real catalogue output and has
  the awkward names.
- **Open the studio on what you imported and include a screenshot.** That is the
  moment this project's argument closes: a database becomes markdown becomes a
  picture you can drag.
- A model with a ref to a table the export does not contain, showing the
  diagnostic rather than a dangling ref.
- A table name a file cannot hold, showing the diagnostic naming the table.
- A truncated JSON paste, showing the parse failure names truncation.
- Say what you decided about type normalisation and why, and paste a table's
  frontmatter so a reviewer can see what a user's first diff looks like.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: The introspection contract and the provider seam
description:
The introspection contract and the provider seam. No engine.

The first of three: this item defines the shape and the registry, dbmd-43 is
Postgres and dbmd-44 is SQL Server. Doing the seam first is deliberate. A
contract extracted from one working engine is that engine wearing an interface.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0007-engines-are-providers.md` first.

## Scope

- `src/import/contract.ts`: the canonical introspection shape, as types plus a
  validator. It is the **union** of what Postgres and SQL Server can say, not
  the intersection and not Postgres with room bolted on the side. Composite
  primary keys, multi-column foreign keys, schemas and index metadata are all in
  it because both engines have them.
- The envelope: `{ dbmdIntrospection: 1, engine: "...", ... }`, so a pasted file
  says what produced it and `dbmd import` cannot be handed the wrong provider.
- `src/import/providers/index.ts`: the registry. Adding an engine is one file
  and one line here, and nothing outside this directory learns an engine's name.
- `EngineProvider` as ADR 0007 declares it: `introspectionQuery`, `parse`,
  `normaliseType`, `quoteIdentifier`.
- `docs/import-format.md`: the contract as documentation, with a worked example.
  This is what somebody writing the third provider reads.
- A deliberately fake provider in the tests, so the registry and the envelope
  dispatch are tested without either real engine.

## Watch out for

- Designing this from Postgres alone. Open the SQL Server catalog before fixing
  the shape: `nvarchar(max)` reporting length -1, and `sys.*` carrying index
  information that `information_schema` does not, are both things that change
  what the contract needs to hold.
- A normalised type vocabulary that silently loses information. Decide now
  whether the native type string is kept alongside the normalised one. ADR 0007
  flags this as a revisit trigger, which means it is cheaper to get right here.
- The version number is not decoration. Write the code path that rejects an
  unknown `dbmdIntrospection` with a message naming the version it got and the
  version it wanted, and test it, or the field is a comment.

## Evidence bar

Two hand-written fixture files, one shaped like each engine's output, and the
fake provider resolving both through the registry from the envelope alone. Paste
the diagnostic produced by a file with an unknown version and by a file with an
unknown engine.

## Out of scope

Any real SQL. That is dbmd-43 and dbmd-44.
close_reason: Merged in PR #6. Contract verified bi-engine by driving it: -1 length rejected, max accepted, empty schema rejected, explicit nulls stripped so null and absent are identical.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Marked blocked by dbmd-91 rather than briefed to assume Postgres.

The JSON contract is reusable across engines but the query itself is not, so a
wrong guess here throws the whole item away rather than costing an assumption.
That is the "refuse to start work whose inputs are missing" case, not the "state
your assumption and carry on" case.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

Drove the contract myself against documents I wrote, not the fixtures in the PR.
Compiled `dist` and called `validateIntrospectionDocument` and
`readIntrospection` directly.

The claim this item lives or dies on is that the shape is genuinely the union of
two engines rather than Postgres with room bolted on. Checked the SQL Server
half specifically, because that is the half that cannot be reached by
imagination:

- `length: -1` is rejected, and the message names why it exists:
  ``` `length` must be a non-negative whole number or the string "max", got -1;
  SQL Server reports -1 for the max forms and a provider translates that here ```
- `length: "max"` is accepted with no diagnostics.
- `schema: ""` is rejected. `dbo` being a schema name rather than "no schema" is
  enforced, not just documented.
- Explicit `null` on `comment`, `default`, `identity`, `collation` and
  `primaryKey` produces no diagnostics and the nulls are **stripped** from the
  validated value, so null and absent really are the same thing. That is the
  `FOR JSON` behaviour the report claims, and it is the one that a
  Postgres-first design would have got wrong by making null significant.
- Version 0, version 7 and an unknown engine produce the exact diagnostics
  reported, including the "this build has no engine providers at all" branch,
  which is `main`'s honest state today.

Verified independently: this is a bi-engine contract.

## Code

**The seam is real, and one claim in the report is understated rather than
overstated.** The report says `contract.ts` contains no engine name. It contains
twenty-one, and all of them are in comments and one diagnostic message,
explaining *which engine each field exists for*. None is in logic. That is
better than the claim, not worse: a field like `generated.persisted` is
incomprehensible without the sentence saying Postgres generated columns are
always stored. Leave them in.

`engineProviders` is an empty array on `main` with the one-import-one-line
pattern shown directly above it, and the empty-registry path has its own test.
A registry that is honestly empty beats one pre-seeded with providers that do
not exist yet.

`normaliseType` returning the closed `NormalisedType` union instead of ADR
0007's `string` is a deviation from a written interface, and it was reported
rather than slipped in. It is also the right call: an open return type cannot
be switched on, which is the only reason a normalised name exists at all, and
`other` is the escape hatch. ADR 0009 records it against 0007 explicitly, so
the next reader does not have to work out which document is wrong.

## Architecture

ADR 0009 settles the question ADR 0007 left open, and settles it on the argument
that matters: the asymmetry is recovery. A model written without the native type
cannot get it back without a re-import against a database the user may no longer
have, so keeping both is the choice that cannot be regretted.

Three of the four assumptions are the right kind. Check constraints being in the
contract, unnamed by this item, is justified by the alternative being a contract
change during dbmd-43. The `--engine` override landing as a warning before the
flag exists is the kind of thing that is normally scope creep and here it is
what stops dbmd-41 reaching past the seam.

What it hands the two provider items is stated as a list of things they will
have to fight, including that expressions stay verbatim and `((0))` is not
unwrapped. dbmd-44's brief says "decide whether to unwrap"; the contract has
decided. That is a contradiction between an open item and a merged decision, and
it is resolved the right way round: if dbmd-44 disagrees it changes the format
doc rather than unwrapping quietly. I will update dbmd-44 to say so.

## Verdict

Merge. No changes requested.

title: dbmd export to mermaid
description:
`dbmd export --format mermaid`: a diagram other people can read on GitHub.

The cheapest possible answer to "so other devs can see", and it works inside a
pull request without anyone installing anything, because GitHub renders mermaid
in markdown.

## Scope

- Writes `db-model/README.md` containing a mermaid `erDiagram` block generated
  from the model, between markers, so the rest of that file stays a place for
  humans to write.
- `--stdout` prints instead of writing.
- Deterministic output: same model, same bytes. Sort tables and relationships.

## Watch out for

- Mermaid's ER syntax is fussy about names. A table or column with a space, a
  hyphen or a reserved word breaks the whole diagram, and the failure is a blank
  box on GitHub rather than an error anywhere you will see it. Escape or quote,
  and put a table named `order-items` in the fixture.
- A large model produces an unreadable diagram. That is acceptable, and worth
  one sentence in the generated file rather than a layout algorithm.
- Regenerating must not disturb prose outside the markers, and must not rewrite
  the file at all when the diagram has not changed.

## Evidence bar

Paste the generated block, and confirm you viewed it rendered rather than
reading the source. A markdown preview that renders mermaid is enough.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Orchestrator brief, wave eight, 2026-09-06

Branch: `cli/22-export-mermaid`. **ADR number 0023 is yours** if this needs one.
Do not take a different number; 0021 and 0022 are handed to agents working right
now and `npm run check` fails a collision.

### Why this item matters more than its P2 suggests

This project's whole argument is that the model is markdown so the diff is the
review. **This is the item that makes that true for people who do not read
YAML.** A pull request that changes a table shows a changed diagram on GitHub,
rendered, with nobody installing anything. It is the cheapest possible answer to
"so other devs can see", and the item says so.

### What landed while this was blocked, and what you must reuse

`dbmd-21` merged an hour ago and `dbmd check` is the command most like yours.
**Read `src/cli/check.ts` before writing anything.** It shows the shape:

- A `Command` plus one line in `COMMANDS` in `src/cli/main.ts`.
- `src/cli/output.ts` is the only module in `src/` allowed to write, and a gate
  fails the build on a bare `console.log` anywhere. A command ends with
  `return out.report({ code, text, json })`, so the exit code, the prose and the
  payload come out of one value.
- Exit `2` means the command line was wrong and nothing ran. `1` means the
  command ran and could not do what was asked. ADR 0020 has the boundary.

If you find yourself inventing an envelope or a way to print, go and find the one
that landed.

### The three traps, and the first one is the item

- **Mermaid's ER syntax is fussy about names, and the failure is invisible.** A
  table or column with a space, a hyphen, or a reserved word breaks the whole
  diagram, and what GitHub shows is a blank box rather than an error anywhere you
  will look. **Put a table named `order-items` in your fixture** and make the
  diagram survive it. This is the entire risk of the item: everything else fails
  loudly and this fails silently, in somebody else's pull request.
- **Regenerating must not disturb prose outside the markers**, and must not
  rewrite the file at all when the diagram has not changed. That second half is
  the same property `writeModel` already has and for the same reason: a tool that
  touches a file it did not need to touch puts noise in a diff, and this project
  keeps filing items about that.
- **Deterministic output.** ADR 0006's fourth rule. Sort tables and
  relationships; same model, same bytes, every time.

### A gap worth deciding rather than inheriting

The item says a large model produces an unreadable diagram, that this is
acceptable, and that it is worth **one sentence in the generated file** rather
than a layout algorithm. Agree or disagree, but decide it deliberately and say
which. Do not build a layout algorithm.

### What to do about the parts the format has and mermaid does not

The model carries notes, groups, layout coordinates, unique indexes and prose.
Mermaid's `erDiagram` has none of that. Decide what is dropped and say so in the
generated file, because a reader looking at a diagram that silently omits a
grouping box will trust it more than they should.

### Scope

`dbmd export` with mermaid as its format. Not a second format, not the GitHub
Actions recipe, which is dbmd-71 and is blocked on you.

Stay out of `src/model/`, `src/import/` and `src/studio/`: agents are working in
all three. You should need none of them; you are a consumer of `readModel`.

### Evidence bar

- **Paste the generated markdown for `examples/shop`**, in full, as text. It has
  eight tables, a self-reference and a unique index, so it is a real test.
- **Paste it again for a model containing a table named `order-items`** and a
  column name with a space in it. If the diagram survives, say how; if you refuse
  such a name instead, say why that is better.
- **Run it twice and show the second run wrote nothing.** Then change one column
  and show it wrote once.
- **Put prose above and below the markers, regenerate, and show the prose
  untouched** by pasting the diff.
- Show `--stdout` printing rather than writing, with nothing on stderr.
- **Actually look at the rendered diagram.** Paste the mermaid into something
  that renders it, or open it in a browser with the global `playwright-cli`, and
  say what you saw. A block of syntactically valid mermaid that renders as a
  blank box is precisely the failure this item warns about, and no test catches
  it.

You do not merge. Push the branch, open the pull request, report, stop.

title: Owner: which database engines the import must cover
description:
Owner decision: which database engines the import has to cover.

dbmd-40 builds the Postgres introspection query on the assumption that Postgres
is the one that matters first. That assumption is not derivable from anything in
this repository.

## What is needed

Which engines do the applications you would point this at actually use, in
order? Postgres, MySQL or MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite, something else.

## Why it matters now rather than later

The JSON contract in dbmd-40 is designed once. A contract shaped by one engine
grows warts when the second arrives, and the two that would shape it most
differently are SQL Server, whose schema and identifier rules do not match
Postgres, and SQLite, which has no information schema at all.

Naming the second engine now costs an hour of design in dbmd-40. Discovering it
after dbmd-41 costs a rewrite of both.

## Recommendation

Postgres first, and tell me the second one even if it is months away. If the
answer is genuinely "only Postgres", say so and the contract gets simpler.

## Meanwhile

dbmd-40 proceeds on Postgres and is briefed to keep the JSON shape engine
neutral where that is free, which is most of it.
close_reason: Answered: Postgres and SQL Server, behind a provider seam. ADR 0007, and dbmd-40 split into 40, 43 and 44.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Answered by the owner on 2026-08-25: Postgres and SQL Server for now, with a
proper provider pattern so a third engine is additive rather than a rewrite.

Recorded as ADR 0007. Two engines chosen up front is the number that forces the
design: one lets you call a single query an architecture, and three would be a
rewrite of whatever one produced.

dbmd-40 is rewritten as the contract and the provider seam with no engine in it,
and split from dbmd-43 (Postgres) and dbmd-44 (SQL Server). The seam comes first
deliberately, because a contract extracted from one working engine is that
engine wearing an interface.

title: Import from a live database
description:
Bootstrap a model from a database that already exists.

The shape is deliberately borrowed from ChartDB and it is the best idea in that
product: the tool never connects to the database and never asks for credentials.
It prints a query, the developer runs it themselves with whatever client they
already trust, and hands back the JSON it produced.

That keeps database drivers out of the dependency tree, keeps secrets out of the
tool entirely, and works through a bastion host or a VPN without any of it being
our problem.
close_reason: All eight children closed. The journey runs end to end: dbmd query prints your engine's introspection SQL, you run it with the client you already trust, dbmd import turns what came back into a model directory, and as of dbmd-42 a re-import over that directory computes a delta, itemises it and writes nothing until somebody confirms it. Prose, layout and group membership are never touched, and a file no item on the list names is never opened. Two providers behind one contract, both driven against live databases in containers. dbmd never connects to a database and that is a decision rather than a gap.

title: Publishable as npx dbmd
description:
Make `npx dbmd` work for somebody who has never seen this repository.

Publishing to npm is the owner's step and is not something the loop does on its
own. What this epic covers is everything up to that: the package being correct,
the binary resolving, the bundle being present in the tarball, and a README that
shows the real workflow rather than an aspiration.
notes:
## Answered by the owner, 2026-09-07: "Yes let's publish to npm"

Asked five times across the day and now answered. `"private": true` comes out
of package.json.

Removing that line is the decision; it is not the whole of the work, and the
rest is derivable and mine:

- The package must be publishable by a person rather than by the loop. A
  release workflow that publishes on a tag is the shape, and the npm token is
  the owner's to add as a repository secret. That is an owner action and the
  pull request has to name it plainly rather than assume it.
- `docs/ci.md` says the recipe does not run as written because the package is
  not published. That sentence has to change in the same commit that makes it
  false, and so do the equivalents in `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and
  `README.md`, which all say the tool is not on npm.
- `check:pack` already proves the tarball installs and the studio starts out of
  it, so the evidence that publishing works exists. What it does not prove is
  that `npx dbmd` resolves for a stranger, and only a real publish does.
- The name was free as of 2026-09-07. Confirm it still is before pushing a tag.
close_reason: All four children closed. The package is publishable and the path to a release exists: private came out, the version is 0.1.0, and .github/workflows/release.yml publishes on a pushed v* tag and on nothing else, refusing a tag whose version disagrees with package.json and a tag on a commit that is not an ancestor of main. check:pack now reads private and bin out of the manifest inside the tarball, because npm publish --dry-run exits 0 on a private package and is not a rehearsal. Nothing is on the registry: the token and the tag are the owner's, and PR #118 numbers the steps.

title: probe
close_reason: Probe of explicit ids. They work, so the backlog uses readable sequential ids rather than hashes.

title: AGENTS.md says two invariants and lists five, in the file whose counts a record calls perfect
design:
`AGENTS.md`'s Invariants section opens:

> Two, and both are about this repository rather than about code that does not
> exist yet.

**There are five.** Agents do not land code; decision record numbers are handed
out; every tracked source file has to be readable as a diff; a command in
backticks is a claim that it exists; a command that exists owes the README an
entry.

## Why this is worth filing rather than fixing quietly

ADR 0043 stakes an argument on a count in this exact file:

> `AGENTS.md` has carried a count of the commands through five arrivals, from
> two to seven, and has never once been wrong, because its count and its list
> are the same sentence: editing the list puts your cursor next to the number.
> The README heading counted entries that ended two hundred lines below it, and
> it was wrong twice out of three chances.

**The commands count is still right.** Line 54 reads "it has seven commands:
`dbmd init`, `dbmd query`, `dbmd import`, ..." and there are seven. Count and
list, one sentence, exactly as the record says.

**The invariants count is wrong, and it is wrong for the README's reason rather
than in spite of it.** "Two" sits in a lead-in sentence and the five invariants
are five separate bold paragraphs below it. Adding one does not put your cursor
anywhere near the number. So this does not refute ADR 0043, it sharpens it: what
is reliable is the sentence shape, not the file.

ADR 0043's revisit condition says what to do when a count in this file goes
wrong, and it is about the commands count rather than this one, but the answer
transfers:

> **`AGENTS.md`'s count goes wrong.** It never has. The day it does, the answer
> is the one taken here: the sentence loses its number, rather than gaining a
> check.

## Watch out for

- **Take the number out, do not correct it to five.** That is the record's own
  stated answer, and correcting it to five recreates the same trap with a
  different number in it. The lead-in still has a job: it says the invariants
  are about this repository rather than about code that does not exist yet, and
  that sentence survives without a count.
- **Leave the commands count alone.** It is right, and it is right structurally.
  Removing it would delete the evidence ADR 0043 rests on.
- **Amend ADR 0043 by appending.** Records here are never edited. What this adds
  is that a second count in the same file went wrong while the first did not,
  and that the difference was the sentence shape the record already named. That
  is worth an entry because it is the record's own prediction coming true in a
  place the record did not look.
- **`check:commands` cannot see this** and should not be taught to. It resolves
  commands, not counts, and a check that counted bold paragraphs would be
  guessing at what a list is.

title: check:commands cannot see a backticked script path, and one of them is wrong
design:
ADR 0036's "Revisit when" asks for exactly this and says how to handle it:

> **A reference is found that this check cannot see.** That is the case worth
> writing down rather than fixing quietly: it says which shape to add, and the
> list above is meant to grow from evidence rather than from imagination.

Here is the evidence. `scripts/guard-merge.mjs` names
`` `scripts/command-reader.test.mjs` `` in a comment, as the test that catches
drift between the copies of its command reader. **That file does not exist in
this repository**, and it is the reason `dbmd-x58` exists.

`check:commands` scanned that file and did not see the reference. Its script
shape is `/node\s+(scripts\/[\w.-]+)/g`, so it reads an invocation and not a
path. A comment that names a sibling script without telling anybody to run it
falls straight through.

## The shape to add, and what it costs

A backticked bare path into `scripts/`: `` /`(scripts\/[\w.-]+)`/g ``, resolved
against the filesystem the same way the existing script shape is.

Measured against `check-commands.mjs`'s own file set, which is tracked `.md`,
`.ts` and `.mjs` minus `docs/architecture/decisions/`, `.beads/` and
`test/guards/`:

 files scanned | backticked `scripts/` paths that do not resolve
---------------|-----------------------------------------------
 174           | 1

The one is the defect above. No false positives to weigh.

## Do not generalise it to every path

I ran the wide version first, every backticked repo-relative path, and it found
six, of which one was this defect and five were correct prose: a hypothetical in
ADR 0043's revisit clause, a branch name that begins with `docs/`, two
historical mentions inside backlog bodies, and a sentence in
`orchestrating.md` that names `docs/process/gotchas.md` precisely in order to
say the file no longer exists.

**That last one is the argument against the general rule**, and it is not an
edge case. The honest way to record that a file was removed is to name it, so a
check demanding every backticked path resolve would push writers toward vaguer
history. ADR 0036's shapes all read a *command*, which is a claim that something
is runnable now; a path is often a claim about what happened. Keeping the new
shape scoped to `scripts/` keeps it on the runnable side of that line.

## Watch out for

- **Append to ADR 0036, do not edit it.** Records here are amended by appending.
  The revisit condition being satisfied is itself the thing worth recording, and
  a future reader should be able to see the condition and its answer as two
  entries rather than one rewritten one.
- **`test/guards/` is excluded on purpose** and holds this check's own wrong
  fixtures. A new shape wants a new fixture there, and adding it is what proves
  the shape fires.
- **The exclusion list is the risk.** `docs/architecture/decisions/` is excluded
  because a record is history, and history is exactly where a stale
  `scripts/` path would be harmless. That exclusion is right and the new shape
  should keep it rather than quietly widening the scan.
- **Fixing `dbmd-x58` may delete the reference this fires on.** If it does, the
  new shape has nothing left to catch and the fixture in `test/guards/` becomes
  its only evidence that it works. Land them in an order where that is true on
  purpose rather than by accident.

title: merge-pr.mjs knows which branches it is about to make stale and does not say
description:
`docs/process/orchestrating.md` has a section called "Hold every merge while
anything is rebasing". **I broke it twice on 2026-09-07**, the second time
within an hour of writing about the first, and the second time I made two agents
rebase, one of them twice.

The section is right and the instruction is not the problem. **An instruction is
not a control**, which is a lesson already written down in this repository about
a different rule, and the answer to a rule broken by accident and repeatedly is a
linter, a hook or a type rather than a firmer sentence.

## What the wrapper already knows

`scripts/merge-pr.mjs` calls the GitHub API to decide whether the pull request in
front of it is mergeable. **In the same breath it could ask which other pull
requests are open**, and every one of those is a branch its merge is about to
make stale, because the wrapper's own refusal is "the required checks are green,
but the branch is behind main, so that green is stale".

So the cost is knowable at exactly the moment somebody chooses to pay it, and
right now it is invisible until an agent reports and gets sent back.

## What to build, and it is small

Before merging, print the other open pull requests and say plainly that each one
now needs a rebase and a re-verify. Something like:

```
Merging #128 will make 2 other branches stale:
  #129  tooling/86c-a-check-that-reads-lines
  #130  docs/wie-a-number-that-was-never-run
Each needs a rebase and a re-verify before it can land.
```

**Do not add a prompt and do not refuse.** Merging while others are open is
often the right call: the alternative is a queue that never drains. What is
missing is that the cost is currently paid by somebody who is not in the room.

## Watch out for

- **Do not make it a gate.** `merge-pr.mjs` already refuses four things and a
  fifth that is a judgement call would get bypassed, which is worse than a line
  of output.
- **It must not fail the merge if the listing call fails.** A merge that works
  today must not start depending on a second API call, so wrap it and say
  nothing if it cannot answer.
- **`test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts` does not cover this script**, and
  ADR 0034 says so and calls it a gap rather than a decision, because its
  decisions need the network. dbmd-76x is about that gap and this change makes
  it slightly worse. Say so in the pull request; do not try to fix both here.
notes:
## The cancelled agent left a finished commit, and here is what it is

`tooling/what-a-merge-costs-and-what-nobody-breaks`, commit `2f69db1`. Never
pushed, so **no CI run and no review**. Assessed on 2026-09-07 so that deciding
what to do with it is cheap.

| file | lines changed |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/merge-pr.mjs` | 444 |
| `test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts` | 552 added, to 1,731 |
| `scripts/check-main-provenance.mjs` | 258 |
| two new decision records | 151 |

**It is much more than this item asked for.** It took dbmd-76x's larger option
as well: separating each script's decision from the network, which is what
closes ADR 0034's revisit condition and is why both scripts moved so far.

Both files parse. That is the only thing verified about them.

## Why resurrecting it is not cheap, and that is the decision

**A 444-line change to `merge-pr.mjs` is the riskiest change this repository
can take**, because it is how everything lands, including its own fix. There is
no path where it goes in unreviewed.

`test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts` growing by 552 lines is the right shape
for that risk and is also 552 lines of unreviewed test. The guard suite is the
thing that proves the guards work; a change to it needs the same scrutiny as a
change to a guard.

## The options, and what each costs

- **Resurrect it as a fresh agent's rebase-and-re-verify.** Cheapest in machine
  terms: the branch exists, so the work is done and what is bought is CI and a
  review. The agent has to be told plainly it did not write this.
- **Discard it and do this item small**, printing the stale branches and nothing
  else, leaving dbmd-76x separate. Loses real work; gains a change that can be
  reviewed in one sitting.
- **Leave it.** Nothing on `main` is worse for it, and the item stays true.

**Owner's call, and it is a judgement about appetite for risk in the merge path
rather than about the code.**
## The work exists, on a local branch, and starting from scratch would waste it

`tooling/what-a-merge-costs-and-what-nobody-breaks` carries commit `2f69db1`,
"dbmd-nm5, dbmd-76x: what a merge costs, and the guard nobody had broken". It
was never pushed, so it has never seen CI and has never been reviewed. Its agent
was stopped by the owner over machine resources rather than for anything about
the work.

 file                                    | lines
-----------------------------------------|-------
 `scripts/merge-pr.mjs`                  | 444
 `test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts` | 552
 `scripts/check-main-provenance.mjs`     | 258
 ADR 0034, appended                      | 29
 ADR 0058, new                           | 122

1,158 insertions and 247 deletions in five files.

Its commit message says what it does: `merge-pr.mjs` names the branches a merge
is about to make stale and says what each one owes, without prompting and
without refusing, with the listing wrapped whole so a merge that worked
yesterday does not start depending on a second API call. Then, because that
second call went into a script nothing tested, both network-dependent guards
move their decisions into exported functions whose facts are arguments and their
`gh` calls into a `main()` that runs only when the file is the entry point, so
the four refusals in `merge-pr.mjs` and the one rule in
`check-main-provenance.mjs` become ordinary tests.

## State, measured 2026-09-07

- **Six commits behind `main`**, and it conflicts. A merge preview reports
  conflicts touching `check-main-provenance.mjs`, `merge-pr.mjs` and
  `broken-on-purpose.test.ts`, which are the three files it rewrites most.
- **ADR 0058 is claimed by this branch.** Do not hand 0058 to anything else
  while this exists. 0057 and 0059 are already spoken for by other work.
- **It does not collide with the recovered documentation work**, which touches
  `README.md`, five other ADRs and `test/docs/readme.test.ts`.

## Watch out for

- **This is not blocked on the owner and it never was.** I filed it that way. The
  owner's stop was about resources, and reviving a branch is ordinary sequencing.
  What it needs is an agent to rebase it and push it, because a rebase of a
  1,158 line change across three conflicting files is implementation work.
- **Sequence it after the open pull requests land.** It rewrites the tool every
  merge goes through, so landing it while other branches are waiting means every
  one of them merges through a script that has never merged anything. Let the
  queue drain first, then rebase this against a quiet `main`.
- **The worst case is that nothing can merge.** `merge-pr.mjs` is the only
  sanctioned path and `guard-merge.mjs` refuses the alternatives. Whoever lands
  this should merge one throwaway pull request with the new script before
  trusting it with a real one.
- **`check-main-provenance.mjs` is also what `dbmd-rjd` will want to extend.**
  Two changes to one file, so they want an order rather than a race.

title: The README's opening block claims to be a file and is not
description:
Found by the dbmd-wie agent while writing the assertion for the rest of that
page, and correctly left alone.

`README.md` line 21 shows a block claiming to be
`examples/shop/tables/shipments.md`. **It is stale against the committed file**:
the real one has `on delete: restrict` on `order_id` and the block does not.

## Why it was not fixed with the rest

dbmd-wie made every block in the `dbmd import` walkthrough either a real run, a
byte-for-byte file assertion, or a sketch marked as one. This block is outside
that walkthrough and it has a property none of the others do:

**It carries a `layout:` line.** `layout: { x: 900, y: 640 }`. Asserting the
block byte for byte would mean that **dragging that table in the studio turns the
build red**, which is an absurd thing to do to somebody arranging a diagram, and
the example exists to be arranged.

## Three ways out, and the third is probably right

- **Correct it and leave it unasserted.** Cheapest, and it goes stale again the
  next time anything about `shipments` changes. That is exactly how it got here.
- **Assert it and accept the red build on a drag.** Not defensible. The owner
  drags this model.
- **Assert the block minus the volatile lines.** It is already a prefix rather
  than a whole file, so the page has half-accepted that idea. A `dbmd-file:` tag
  that stops at a named line, or ignores `layout:`, keeps the claim honest about
  the part that is a claim.

Whichever wins, **correct the missing `on delete: restrict` in the same change**,
because it is wrong today either way.

## Watch out for

- **ADR 0056** landed with dbmd-wie and defines the three tags and the rule that
  every block in the walkthrough carries one. This block is outside that page
  section, and the record names it as deliberately uncovered. If you cover it,
  amend the record by appending rather than editing.
- **`layout:` is the line a reviewer learns to skip** (ADR 0003). Anything that
  makes it load-bearing in a test is working against that.
- The same reasoning applies to any future block showing a table file, so decide
  the rule rather than this one block.
notes: Pinned down on 2026-09-07 so whoever takes this is not hunting: the difference is exactly one line. The block goes from `ref: orders.id` straight to `- name: carrier`; the committed file has `    on delete: restrict` between them. Nothing else in the shown prefix differs. That one line arrived with ADR 0046, which is also why the block cannot simply be regenerated and left unasserted: the same thing will happen the next time a key is added to a ref.
close_reason: Closed

title: Four revisit conditions describe work that has already happened
description:
When the owner said "yes let's publish to npm", ADR 0024's first revisit entry
fired and dbmd-5.1 appended a correction to it. That was the right move and it
was the only record that got one.

**Two others describe the same event and were left alone, and my brief is why.**
I told that agent "0024/0028/0039 are not edited, per the repo's
superseded-records-stay rule", which was correct about not editing and wrong
about not appending. They followed it exactly.

## ADR 0028, first revisit entry

> **`dbmd` is published, if it ever is.** The "not on npm" section of
> `docs/ci.md` comes out, the placeholder becomes whatever the real first
> version turned out to be...

Both halves are already done:

- **The "not on npm" section of `docs/ci.md` is gone.** #118 removed it this
  morning. A reader following this on release day will look for a section that
  gone, and conclude the record is describing a different repository.
- **`0.1.0` stopped being a placeholder.** ADR 0051 chose it, and `docs/ci.md`
  now says so in the section that replaced the one above.

## ADR 0039

> **Somebody publishes the package.** The skill's opening section is written
> around `npx dbmd` not working. It should stop being written that way on the
> day it starts.

Also done. `.claude/skills/dbmd/SKILL.md` now says `npx dbmd` "resolves whatever
is on the registry, and `npm view dbmd versions` is what says which releases
exist", which is written to be true on both sides of a first release rather than
around it not working.

## What is genuinely still pending, and must survive

**Nothing is on the registry.** The condition in both records, *published*, has
not fired: the decision fired. So neither entry should be deleted, and neither
record's argument changes. What is stale is the **instructions** attached to
them, which now name work already carried out.

## What to do

Append to each, in the shape ADR 0024 and ADR 0003 already use, and say plainly:
the decision to publish was taken on 2026-09-07, these instructions were carried
out then, and what remains on the day of a real release is whatever is left over.
Point at ADR 0051. **Do not edit a word of what is there** and do not delete the
entries.

## Watch out for

- **Check the rest of both revisit lists** while you are in them, not only the
  entry named here. The same change may have half-fired something else, and a
  second pass is cheaper than a second item.
- **Do not touch `docs/ci.md` or the skill.** They are already correct; this is
  about the records that describe changing them.
- `npm run check` runs `check:adr` and `check:commands`. A record naming a
  section that does not exist is not something either catches, which is why this
  had to be read.
notes:
## The cancelled agent finished this, and it found more than my sweep did

Its work is saved as a 526-line patch in the session scratchpad under
`cancelled-work/`. It covers this item **and dbmd-5pj**, which were briefed
together.

Appendices to five records, not four: 0013, 0028, 0029, 0039 and an amendment to
0056. **My sweep found four fired conditions and it found at least six**,
including one I missed entirely, a composite-foreign-key warning condition under
ADR 0029 that had also come true.

The prose is the right shape. From the 0029 appendix:

> Appended rather than edited, because everything decided here about what an
> import writes is unchanged ... The refusal this record calls a placeholder has
> been replaced, so the paragraph above headed "It refuses a directory that is
> not empty" reads as history.

It names the fired condition, points at the successor record, says what became
history rather than what is wrong, and does not touch a word above.

## Risk, which is the opposite of the other cancelled piece

| | this | the merge-cost one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what it touches | five records, `README.md`, one test file | `merge-pr.mjs`, the guard suite |
| worst case if wrong | a record reads oddly | nothing in the repository can merge |
| lines added | 322 | 1,158 |

**Nothing here is in the product or the merge path.** The 80 lines in
`test/docs/readme.test.ts` are the only executable part, and they extend a
mechanism that landed the same day in #130.

## Recommendation

**Resurrect this one.** It is finished, low risk, better than the brief asked
for, and the alternative is redoing a sweep it has already done more thoroughly
than I did. A fresh agent rebases it, runs the check, and reports; it must be
told plainly that it did not write this.

Still the owner's call, because the harness treats work they stopped as
cancelled and will not resume it.
close_reason: Closed

title: The list of guards nobody breaks on purpose is missing one, and it is the detection layer
description:
`test/guards/broken-on-purpose.test.ts` opens with a section called WHAT IS NOT
HERE, AND WHY. It is the best thing in that file: it names `smoke-pack.mjs`
(covered by `check-pack-guard.mjs` instead), `guard-merge.mjs --probe` (absent on
purpose, with a real argument) and `merge-pr.mjs` (**"absent too, and that one is
a gap rather than a decision"**).

**There are two network-dependent guards and the list names one.**
`scripts/check-main-provenance.mjs` is neither covered by the suite nor
mentioned in that section, and ADR 0034 does not discuss it either.

## Why it matters more than a missing sentence

That script is the **detection** half of the merge gate, and its own header says
so: `merge-pr.mjs` and `guard-merge.mjs` prevent and can be bypassed, "a layer
that can be bypassed cannot tell you it was bypassed", and this one runs on the
result so it cannot be. It runs in CI through `.github/workflows/provenance.yml`
and I run it by hand after every merge.

**Nothing has ever proved it detects.** If it silently stopped failing on a
direct push, every run would print the same reassuring line it prints today, and
the claim that every commit came through a pull request would become a promise
again rather than an audit.

The gap is the same one ADR 0034 already records for `merge-pr.mjs`, for the same
reason: the decision needs the GitHub API. **The list is just short by one**, and
a list that presents itself as exhaustive and is not is the failure this
repository keeps paying for.

## Two sizes of fix, and the small one is not enough on its own

- **A sentence.** Add it to the WHAT IS NOT HERE section and to ADR 0034, so the
  list is honest. Ten minutes, and it fixes the false impression rather than the
  gap.
- **Separate the decision from the network.** For both scripts. The rule here is
  one line, *a commit associated with no pull request is a violation*, and it is
  testable the moment the API call is a parameter. ADR 0034 already names this
  refactor under "Revisit when" for `merge-pr.mjs` and says it is worth doing for
  this reason. **Doing it for both closes that revisit condition rather than
  half of it.**

Do the sentence whatever else happens.

## Watch out for

- **Do not move `BASELINE`.** The script says why in a comment: moving it forward
  is how a real violation gets absorbed into history nobody looks at.
- **Do not make the check pass by weakening it.** If the refactor changes what it
  decides, that is a finding, not a detail.
- The suite's own rule is that nothing mutates the working tree: every mutation
  happens in a temporary directory or on a value in memory, because a
  half-restored file on Windows is easy to make and hard to notice.
notes:
Checked on 2026-09-07 so the item is not overstated: check-main-provenance.mjs does run in CI, on every push to main, through .github/workflows/provenance.yml, and the last six runs all succeeded. So the gap is exactly and only that nothing has ever proved it detects. It is not orphaned and it is not unrun; it is untested, in the one file whose whole job is to say which guards are untested and why.
The same branch carries this item's work: tooling/what-a-merge-costs-and-what-nobody-breaks, commit 2f69db1, never pushed. See the note on dbmd-nm5 for its state, its conflicts and the order it wants. The two items land together or not at all, because the change that widens the guard suite is the same change that made the second network call needing it.

title: check:scenes reads a line at a time, so a rule spread over five lines is invisible to it
description:
Found by the dbmd-fnl.1 agent and confirmed by them rather than reasoned about.

`scripts/check-scene-classes.mjs` enforces ADR 0037: a class name that both the
canvas and the inspector write must have every rule anchored to one scene. It
exists because two scenes once shared a stylesheet and broke the page twice in
one day, the second time invisibly.

**It reads a line at a time.** `ref` is a class both scenes now write, and has
been since dbmd-32. Both rules are anchored, `.box li .ref` and
`#inspector ol > li .ref`, so the invariant holds. But the inspector writes its
ref field through a `textField(...)` call spread over five lines, and the check
never sees the class and the scene on one line, so it reports **three shared
names where there are four**.

Confirmed by collapsing that call onto one line: the check then reports `.ref`
and still passes.

## Why this matters more than a miscount

The check is the detection layer under a bug that was invisible in a diff and in
a test, and was only ever found by driving the page. **A detection layer with a
formatting-dependent blind spot is one Prettier setting away from silence.** The
count being wrong is the symptom; the gap is that a correctly anchored rule can
become an incorrectly anchored one without the check noticing, if the call that
writes the class is wrapped.

## Watch out for

- **Do not fix this by asking people to write one-line calls.** That is a rule
  nobody can enforce and Prettier will undo.
- The check has to read the source as a tree rather than as lines, or read the
  built client bundle where the call is already collapsed. Say which you chose
  and what it costs.
- **Whatever changes, prove the check still catches what it caught.** ADR 0034's
  guard suite is the pattern: break the anchoring on purpose and show the failure.
- The count in its output is a claim. If the number moves, say so in the pull
  request, because a reviewer who remembers three will wonder.
close_reason: Landed as PR #129. The hole was live rather than hypothetical and I proved it before reading the diff: on main, check:scenes reported three shared class names, missed .ref, and let me rewrite the inspector's anchored rule as a bare .ref with exit 0, which is the exact defect ADR 0037 exists to forbid. The fix reads both scene files as a tree and fails that same mutation with both writing sites named. On main now it reports four names. The agent's caveat that reproducing it needed the canvas half added locally was right and is what stops the next reader running the steps, seeing nothing and calling the item bogus. Twelve guard cases from eight, four of which fail against the old script, checked by swapping the old script in rather than asserted.

title: One number in the README's import walkthrough cannot have come from running it
description:
Found on 2026-09-07 by running the README rather than reading it.

**`README.md` line 339 says:**

```
$ dbmd import --file next-release.json --dir shop-model
shop-model already says what this postgres import says: 4 tables, nothing to change.
```

The walkthrough above it imports `test/import/fixtures/postgres-raw.json` into
`shop-model` and reports **2 tables, 3 files**, which is true: I ran it. The
delta block between them removes one table and changes two columns, and adds
none. So the model in that walkthrough has two tables, or one after the delta,
and never four.

The real output is:

```
shop-model already says what this postgres import says: 2 tables, nothing to change.
```

## Why this is worth an item when everything around it is right

**Every other output block in the README is real.** `examples/shop: 8 tables, 2
notes, 1 group, no problems` matches to the character. So does the import block.
I checked. That is what makes the wrong one misleading rather than obviously
decorative: a reader has no way to tell which blocks were run.

The delta block itself cannot be real, because `next-release.json` is a database
that does not exist as a fixture, and that is a fine thing for a walkthrough to
do. **The problem is that a hypothetical block and a real one look identical**,
and one of the hypothetical numbers does not follow from the story.

## Two ways to fix it, and the second is the one that lasts

- **Correct the number** to what the walkthrough would actually print. One
  character, and it goes stale again the next time the fixture changes.
- **Make the blocks that can be real, provably real.** `docs/format.md` already
  works this way: its fenced blocks are executed and must produce exactly what
  they claim. The two blocks in this walkthrough that use a committed fixture
  could be asserted the same way, and the hypothetical one marked as such.

**Recommend both.** The mark on the hypothetical block is what tells a reader
which is which, and it costs a sentence.

## Watch out for

- **Do not make the hypothetical block real by inventing a fixture.** The point
  of that block is a database that changed, and a second fixture is a second
  thing to keep in step with the first.
- The README documents all seven commands and `scripts/check-commands.mjs`
  asserts that. It does not read output blocks, which is the gap.
- Paths in output are absolute when a real run prints them, and the README shows
  them relative. Whatever asserts a block has to account for that, and ADR 0006
  is why the difference exists.
close_reason: Landed as PR #130. I verified the detection rather than the correction: putting 4 back makes the test fail naming the command and the line, which is the difference between a corrected page and a page that stays correct. The agent went past the brief three times and was right each time: the block I asked to have corrected is now a real run, because an unchanged database printing one line is a second run of the first command with nothing written in between; the formatter had quietly rewritten a quoted value inside a fenced block so the page and the writer disagreed and nothing could tell; and the convention is guarded as well as the content, so removing a tag or the reader-facing word sketch both fail.

title: The group in the shipped example is called Wr
description:
Measured against `git archive HEAD`, which is what a stranger clones, at
1600x1000 fitted:

- The group label reads **`Written by the depot handheld`** and is 151 pixels
  wide.
- A note covers **136** of those pixels.
- What the canvas shows is `Wr...`.

The group is the one thing on that picture that explains why two tables are
boxed together, and its name is unreadable. Everything else in the shipped
layout is clean: **zero overlaps between the ten boxes**, notes ending exactly
where the tables begin. Somebody arranged this carefully and one label lost.

## Two ways to fix it and they are not the same item

- **Move the note.** Forty pixels in `examples/shop/notes/*.md`. Cheap, fixes
  the demo, changes nothing about the tool.
- **Stop a note being able to cover a group label.** That is behaviour, it is
  the notes-render-in-front question in the parent epic, and it is the owner's.

**Do the first.** Do not do the second under this item, and say in the pull
request that you did not.

## Watch out for

- **The owner has four uncommitted `layout:` edits** in
  `examples/shop/tables/` in the parent checkout: `addresses`, `orders`,
  `shipments`, `stock_movements`. Never commit them, never revert them, and
  **do not touch any file under `examples/shop/tables/`**. Only `notes/` is
  yours here.
- **Check the fix against the committed tree, not the working tree.** That is
  the mistake that produced this item's parent in the wrong shape: I measured a
  working tree mid-arrangement and reported it as what ships. Use
  `git archive HEAD examples/shop`.
- Re-measure the overlap after moving: the group box is the bounding box of its
  members plus padding, so moving a note near it can change what the label bar
  reports as covered.

## Evidence bar

- **The label's covered pixels, before and after**, from the same probe: the
  `.group-label` rectangle against every `article` rectangle.
- **A screenshot of the committed tree, before and after**, same window size.
- **Zero overlaps still**, between the ten boxes.
- `dbmd check examples/shop` clean, and `npm run check` green.
notes: Not dispatched yet, and the reason is collision. dbmd-fnl.1 is looking at every layout in examples/shop right now to check that a box-width change does not move what overlaps what. Two agents in that model at once would fight. Dispatch this once fnl.1 has landed.
close_reason: Landed as PR #128, two lines in two note files. I measured it on the branch's example rendered by main's build, because the change is data rather than code: the label went from 136 of its 151 pixels covered to zero, with zero overlapping pairs before and after, and the covers-2-non-members badge went with it. The useful part was the agent working out that the geometry is 54 pixels rather than the 40 I guessed, because coverage here is all-or-nothing horizontally and a 40 pixel move would have changed nothing.

title: Nothing wakes the studio when a file stops being unreadable
description:
Found while dbmd-e6e was being driven.

A lock being released is not a filesystem event, so nothing tells the watcher.
The session goes on holding the file as unreadable until something else under
the model directory moves, or a flush happens to re-read. Editing any other
table clears it.

**Low priority, and here is why it is not zero.** dbmd-e6e's message says "try it
again once the file can be read", which is good advice a person can follow: their
next edit is the flush that re-reads. So the stuck state is not stuck for anybody
who does what they were told. What it does leave is a diagnostics panel showing
an error that is no longer true, for as long as nobody touches anything.

## Options, and what each costs

- **Re-read on a timer while any object is unreadable.** Simple, bounded, and it
  polls a disk that is usually fine. A second or two is probably invisible.
- **Re-read when the page regains focus.** Free, and it matches when a person
  comes back from whatever had the file open.
- **Nothing, and say so in the record.** The advice already works and an error
  that clears on the next action is a small lie for a short time.

**Recommend the focus one** if it is cheap in this codebase, because the gesture
that releases a lock is usually closing the other program, and the gesture after
that is clicking the page.

## Watch out for

- **Do not poll unconditionally.** Only while something is actually unreadable,
  and stop when it clears, or this is a watcher that never sleeps for a state
  almost nobody is ever in.
- Whatever wakes it must go through the same read the flush uses, or the two
  paths will disagree about what the disk says, which is the class of bug
  dbmd-e6e just closed.
notes:
## Re-verified on 2026-09-07, after three studio changes landed, and still true

Three things touched this area that day, dbmd-e6e, dbmd-062 and dbmd-c7q, so the
item was worth re-checking before dispatching against it rather than assuming.

Measured on `git archive HEAD examples/shop`, with a real exclusive lock:

| | revision | diagnostics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| while locked, after a flush | 1 | 1 |
| lock released, nothing touched | 1 | 1 |
| six seconds later, still nothing touched | 1 | 1 |
| after appending to a **different** file | 2 | **0** |

**Both halves of the item hold.** A release is not a filesystem event so nothing
wakes the watcher, and the session goes on reporting the file as unreadable
indefinitely. Touching any other file under the model directory clears it in one
revision.

## What this changes about the item

Nothing about the diagnosis, and one thing about the priority. The stale state
is **indefinite rather than brief**: it does not time out on its own, which the
item guessed at and did not know. Fifteen seconds was as long as this was worth
measuring, and there is no reason to think a longer wait behaves differently,
because there is nothing in the loop to fire.

The recommendation stands: re-read when the page regains focus, if that is cheap
here, because the gesture that releases a lock is usually closing the other
program and the gesture after it is clicking the page.

title: An object the studio could not read is reported as one that did not parse
description:
Found while dbmd-e6e was being driven, and left deliberately because it is the
same defect one layer over.

Follow the new advice, edit again while the file is still unreadable, and the
next edit is refused `incomplete` with **"`tables/orders.md` did not parse ...
Fix the file and reload"**. It parsed fine. Nobody can fix it, because there is
nothing wrong with it: something else has it open.

The canvas and the inspector say the same thing, so a person is told a third
false reason after dbmd-e6e removed the first two.

## Why it was left rather than folded into dbmd-e6e

Fixing it means the page knowing **why** an object is incomplete rather than only
that it is, and that is plumbing a reason through two scene files. dbmd-e6e was
one sentence in the write path and keeping it that size was right.

## What a fix has to keep

- **`incomplete` is a real state and must stay one.** A file that genuinely did
  not parse is the common case and its message is correct.
- **The reason comes from the reader**, the way dbmd-e6e's does: repeat the
  clause, name no cause, so `EBUSY` and a permission change read the same.
- **The three surfaces must agree.** dbmd-e6e's own finding was that a status
  line can stand over a list saying the opposite. Check the canvas, the inspector
  and the footer together, in a browser, not one of them in a test.

## Watch out for

- `.scene >` is the convention and `npm run check:scenes` enforces it. This one
  touches two scenes by definition, which is exactly where that check exists.
- The test belongs at the seam with `node:fs/promises` mocked, because CI runs
  Linux and a Windows lock proves nothing there.
close_reason: Landed as PR #131. I proved the before state on main with a real lock rather than taking it: main said a file that parsed perfectly did not parse and told the reader to fix it and reload, which is advice nobody can take. The branch says it could not be read and quotes the reader's clause. I then put a tab in another file's frontmatter and the branch still answers incomplete with the old sentence word for word, so the two cases came apart rather than merging. The locked file was byte-identical throughout. The diagnosis is the good part: complete: false was two facts wearing one flag, which is why one change fixed three surfaces, and the agent found main.ts keeping its own inline copy of the question that did not count a kind directory which would not list.

title: The two ways to create a table disagree about whether a new one says it is undocumented
description:
Found by driving the greenfield journey on 2026-09-07: `dbmd init`, then a table
created entirely through the studio, then `check`, `refs` and `export`. The whole
loop works. This is the one thing the two creation paths do differently.

**`dbmd import` writes a prompt line into every table it creates**, and the
argument for it is recorded: an imported model with a generated paragraph per
table teaches the reader that the prose is worthless, but one line saying nobody
has documented this yet is a prompt, and the prompt is the point. `dbmd init`
does the same in spirit: its scaffolded tables carry real prose.

**A table created in the studio gets nothing.** `blankObject` in
`src/studio/edits.ts` sets `body: '\n'`, with a comment explaining only the blank
line after the closing `---`. So the file is:

```
---
kind: table
table: sessions
columns:
  - name: id
    type: ""
    pk: true
layout: { x: 651, y: 457 }
---
```

Nothing on disk says this table is undocumented, and nothing ever will.

## The question, which is not "make them the same"

The studio case is genuinely different and this might be right as it is. You are
looking at the canvas with the inspector open and can type prose immediately, so
a prompt line could be noise you delete every time. That is a real argument and
nobody has made it in writing.

What is not defensible is that the two paths differ **by accident**. No decision
record covers the empty body, and the comment in `blankObject` explains the
newline rather than the emptiness.

So: decide it, and write down whichever way it goes. If the studio should write a
prompt line, it should read like the import one and not be a second spelling of
the same idea. If it should not, say why the studio is the exception, because the
next person to notice this will otherwise file it again.

## Watch out for

- **`dbmd check` already warns about the empty `type`** on the column a create
  starts with, and the studio shows that diagnostic in its panel. A second nag
  about an empty body may be one too many at exactly the wrong moment.
- Whatever is decided, a created table must still round trip: `writeModel`
  concatenates rather than pads, which is what the existing comment is about.
close_reason: Landed as PR #121. The decision went the other way from the obvious one and is better for it: the studio is the exception, the file a create writes is byte for byte unchanged, and the panel says nothing has been written yet. I drove it and watched the line appear on a created table, vanish on the first keystroke without reselecting, and come back when the prose was cleared. The agent also found that a textarea placeholder would have been invisible here, because a created body is one newline and a textarea holding a newline is not empty, which is the ADR 0030 class of defect and only findable by driving.

title: Nothing has ever parsed the diagram dbmd export writes
description:
`dbmd export` exists to write something GitHub renders. **The one property that
matters is asserted nowhere.** A diagram mermaid's grammar cannot spell produces
no error in this repository: `npm run check` is green, the `draw the diagram`
job uploads it as an artifact, and the failure appears as a blank box in
somebody else's pull request.

This is known and written down. `test/export/mermaid.test.ts` opens with it:

> The claim every test here is really making is that the emitted diagram
> **parses** ... There is no mermaid parser in this repository to assert that
> against, and adding one would be a dependency the size of a browser, so what
> these tests assert is the shape the diagram was measured to need.

So the prevention is careful and reasoned: ADR 0023's escape-or-quote rule,
entity names always quoted, attributes rewritten where mermaid allows no quote,
the true name kept beside the rewritten one. **What is missing is the
detection**, and a preventive rule with no detection is silent exactly when it
is wrong.

## The item is to settle the parenthetical, not to assume it

The reason recorded is "a dependency the size of a browser". That may still be
true and it may not, and nobody has checked since it was written:

- Rendering mermaid needs a DOM. **Parsing may not.** Find out whether a
  parse-only package exists that covers `erDiagram`, which is the only grammar
  this tool emits.
- It would be a **devDependency**, never shipped: the `files` allowlist decides
  what a stranger downloads and tests are not in it. Weigh the cost against
  that, not against the published tarball.

**Either answer closes this.** If a parse-only dependency exists and is
reasonable, add it and assert against the awkward cases rather than the tame
ones: a table name with a space, a quote, a `#`, a bracket, a control
character, and the imported name `Ledger [Entry]` that dbmd-44 met in a real
catalogue. If it does not, say so with what you looked at, and amend that doc
comment so the next person does not re-derive it.

## Watch out for

- `examples/shop` has tame names, so a test that only draws it proves the least
  interesting case. The gap is in the names an import produces.
- Do not weaken ADR 0023's escaping to make a parser happy. If the parser
  disagrees with the ADR, that is a finding and the ADR is the thing that gets
  amended, by appending.
notes: Not dispatched yet, and the reason is sequencing rather than doubt. It edits package.json, and dbmd-5.1 is in that file right now removing "private": true and settling the files allowlist, the bin entry and the first version. Two branches in one package.json is a package-lock.json conflict nobody needs. Dispatch this once dbmd-5.1 has landed.
close_reason: Landed as PR #122, and it found a live defect rather than only closing a question. I verified both halves myself: mermaid imports and parses in a bare Node process with document and window undefined, so the recorded reason for not having a parser was true of rendering and false of parsing; and main's own output for a column typed [int], the SQL Server catalogue's spelling, was rejected outright by mermaid with a caret under the bracket. The branch's output parses. I reverted the leading-character rule to its old shape and the test written for it failed. The best thing in it is a finding rather than a fix: a bare entity name now parses in mermaid 11 as an entity plus an alias, so dropping the quotes would give a confident picture of a table nobody has rather than a blank box.

title: The stale-edit notice tells a person to read /api/model, then says the same thing again in English
description:
Found by driving the studio on 2026-09-07, not by reading code. The refusal
itself is right and the behaviour is right; this is only the sentence.

Edit a table's file by hand while a studio page holds it, then edit that table
in the page. The server refuses with 409, nothing is written, the hand edit
survives, and the page re-reads. Correct in every respect. The status bar then
shows this, verbatim:

> this patch names revision 2 and this studio is on revision 3, so it was made
> against a model that is no longer what the files say. Nothing was written.
> Read /api/model again and make the edit on top of what it says now. The page
> will re-read the model; make the edit again on top of what it then shows.

Two problems, and both come from one seam.

**It tells a person to read `/api/model`.** That is an instruction to a program.
The person reading it has no way to act on it and no reason to know what it is.
`src/studio/edits.ts` builds that sentence in `requireCurrent`, where it is
right, because the same words are the API's answer to a script.

**It then gives the same advice twice.** `src/studio/client/main.ts` appends
"The page will re-read the model; make the edit again on top of what it then
shows." to the server's sentence, which already ended with "make the edit on top
of what it says now". A reader gets the instruction, then the instruction again,
and the second one is the useful one because it says who does the re-reading.

The fix is probably that the client renders the *code* rather than concatenating
the server's prose. `RequestFailed` already carries `code` alongside the words
and its doc comment says exactly why: "The words are for the developer and the
code is for the page." The page then reads the code and is quietly not doing it
here.

Small. The reason it is worth an item at all is that this is the one message a
developer sees at the exact moment they think they have lost work.
close_reason: Landed as PR #120. I found this by driving the studio and read the new sentence off the page myself: it names no URL and no revision, says the change on disk is intact, and gives one instruction once. The developer's detail, code and both revisions, moved to the console. The API's own 409 string is byte-identical, which was the thing most at risk. The agent also found the delete path was saying the same thing under a 'could not' heading for something that did not fail, which I had missed, and re-drove that path unasked.

title: npm run backlog cannot run, and the export it would produce already happens
description:
`package.json` line 65 defines `"backlog": "bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl"`.
It fails in both shells on this machine:

```
$ npm run backlog
'bd' is not recognized as an internal or external command
```

`bd` lives at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\beads\bd.exe` and that directory is on
no PATH here, in bash or in PowerShell. So the script has never worked from a
plain checkout.

**And it does not need to.** `.beads/issues.jsonl` is already current: updating
dbmd-42 at 13:24:52 wrote the item's new `updated_at` into the file without
anyone running an export. Beads exports on write.

So this is a script that cannot run, doing a job that is already done, sitting
in a file people read to learn how the project works. That is the shape this
repository has paid for twice: a page saying a thing exists, and somebody
building on it. Either delete it, or make it resolve the binary the way every
other caller in the repo has had to.

Small, and worth doing only because the next reader will try it.
notes: Not dispatched yet, and the reason is sequencing rather than doubt. It edits package.json, and dbmd-5.1 is in that file right now removing "private": true and settling the files allowlist, the bin entry and the first version. Two branches in one package.json is a package-lock.json conflict nobody needs. Dispatch this once dbmd-5.1 has landed.
close_reason: Landed in the same pull request. Verified independently: an item filed minutes earlier was already in the committed .beads/issues.jsonl with nobody running an export, so the script was doing a job already done and could not run anyway. check:commands is what surfaced the stale sentence in orchestrating.md the moment the script was deleted, and that paragraph now says what changed rather than being quietly removed.

title: ADR 0023's list of what the diagram drops is missing the referential actions
description:
ADR 0023 exists to say what `dbmd export` drops, and it enumerates it:

> **A model carries things `erDiagram` has nowhere to put.** Sticky notes,
> grouping boxes, layout coordinates, prose bodies, nullability, defaults, and
> every index that is not a single-column unique one.

`on delete` and `on update` landed after that was written. The diagram drops them
too, and the list does not say so.

Verified: `dbmd export --stdout examples/shop` renders
`"orders" ||--o{ "order_items" : "order_id"` and nothing about `cascade`, though
that ref carries `on delete: cascade`.

## Why an enumeration here earns its maintenance

Most lists in this repository do not, and one was deleted today for exactly that
reason. **This one is different: its whole point is to be complete.** The
paragraph's own argument is that a reader has no way to tell a model with no
groups from a diagram that did not draw them, so a list of what is silently
dropped is the only place that gap is closed. An incomplete one is the trap the
paragraph warns about, one level up.

It is also the same category as two entries already on it. ADR 0046 used
`nullable:` and `default:` to argue that the format has always carried behaviour;
0023 had already filed both as things the picture drops.

## Scope

An appended section on ADR 0023. Records here are amended by appending and never
edited, so do not touch the paragraph: add the two, and say the diagram still
drops them on purpose.

**The decision itself is almost certainly unchanged.** `erDiagram`'s only slot is
the relationship label, that label already carries the referring column, which a
reader needs, and crowding it is a worse diagram. If you agree, say so in three
sentences. If you think the label should change, that is a different item and it
needs the owner.

## Watch out for

- **Do not change what `dbmd export` emits** in this item. `examples/shop`'s
  rendered diagram is committed in `README.md` and in the model workflow, and a
  label change moves both.
- **The studio's canvas also does not show the action, and its panel does.** That
  looked like a third gap and I do not think it is one: the edge is the overview
  and the panel is the detail, which is the same split ADR 0035 uses for a group's
  box and its label. Say whether you agree while you are in the area.
- ADR 0023's revisit list already mentions splitting by group, so it is a record
  that expects to be added to.
close_reason: PR #115 merged: the two keys are on the list, the decision is unchanged, and the clause describing a selection that cannot happen was corrected before it landed.

title: One export message prints a Windows path where every other prints a slashed one
description:
`src/cli/export.ts` has a `slashed()` helper whose own comment says why it
exists:
